articles.title: Ask More of Your UI
articles.description: In my last post, I wrote about moving Forem’s performance and maintenance work into autonomous loops...
articles.body_html:
In my last post, I wrote about moving Forem’s performance and maintenance work into autonomous loops on top of OpenHands. Over a month, those loops shipped 351 pull requests, cut average Rails request time from 70ms to 16ms, and got me out of the business of being a human clipboard between dashboards and terminals.

Stepping out of the day-to-day execution loop immediately creates a different problem: once the factory is running on its own, how do you actually see it?

Text-driven interfaces will always be powerful. The terminal, the prompt box, and the markdown log are native to how language models work and how developers express ad-hoc intent. None of that is going away.

What is strange is how uncreative almost all of the UI surrounding AI tools is right now. We have the most capable software-generating engines in history, and our nearly universal interface for operating them is a dark-mode chat window with a blinking cursor and a scrolling wall of JSON tool calls.

A chat box is a fine place to have a conversation. It is a terrible instrument panel, and every platform looks the exact same.

Scrollback is not observability

With a single interactive session, you can hold the state of the world in your head. You know the branch, the model, and why a test failed because you watched the text stream by.

The moment you move to eight autonomous loops firing every ten minutes across isolated git worktrees, three frontier model subscriptions, and dozens of in-flight pull requests, chat scrollback breaks down. Answering basic operational questions from a list of chat transcripts turns you right back into a meat router:

  • Did the Rust loop stop opening PRs because it ran out of candidates, because its WIP <= 1 gate is full, or because a stale .gitconfig.lock wedged the worktree?
  • Did Claude Opus 5.5 just hit a rate-limit cooldown, and did the router cleanly hand the next tick to Gemini 4 Argon or GPT-6.1 Sol?
  • Is PR #24547 healing itself on its 10-minute CI check-in, or has it burned three repair rounds on the same failing spec?

If you have to click into five conversation logs or run four CLI commands to reconstruct that picture, the interface is failing you. Good observability isn’t about having all the logs somewhere. It’s about shaping the data so you can make a clear decision in five seconds.

Using the tools to build the instrument panel

The irony of bland AI interfaces is that the very tools we are staring at make it trivial to build better ones.

I have no illusion that a dashboard I spin up in an afternoon will rival what the best dedicated AI observability products should look like a year or two from now. We are still in the early days of figuring out the visual grammar for managing autonomous software, and dedicated platforms will eventually nail this.

Until they do, you don’t have to settle for the generic default. A bespoke interface built around your system’s exact levers will beat a one-size-fits-all chat shell every time, and AI coding tools let you iterate on that interface as fast as the underlying system evolves.

In an effort to do more than just complain, I prioritized building a custom control center right alongside the loops themselves.

The Automation Observatory

I ditched the default OpenHands theme and home page for a custom observability platform. I consider this the least I can do, but part of the maintenance itself is improvements in the tooling over time, so this is a work in progress which I hope will yield some creative results. Packaged as a Schema v1 Canvas extension, it survives upstream upgrades without forking the core app.

Every section maps to a concrete decision I needed to make while tuning the factory:

1. The Autonomous Loop Registry. Instead of recent chats, the centerpiece is an Airtable-style ledger table showing all nine workflows (perf-loop, rust-loop, error-loop, test-loop, deps-loop, issue-loop, github-pr-reviewer, pr-merge-loop, and worktree-pruner). Each row shows live status, cadence, WIP cap, and open PRs, with inline controls to pause, trigger a run, or pin a specific model provider.

2. Frontier Subscription Balance and Cooldowns. A three-column sheet tracks our model router across Gemini 4 Argon (agy-acp), Claude Opus 5.5 (claude-acp), and GPT-6.1 Sol (codex-acp), showing run distribution, whether any provider is in an 8-hour cooldown, and a one-click reset when credentials refresh.

3. The Open PR Check-In Radar. Every autonomous PR is watched on a 5 -> 10 -> 20 -> 40 minute exponential back-off schedule for CI failures or review comments. The radar lists every open PR in that queue, its current back-off step, repair rounds attempted, and a live countdown to its next check-in.

4. Ephemeral Worktree Hygiene. A bottom ledger tracks the count and age of isolated /data/worktrees/* checkouts, read-only Postgres health, and Mac bridge status. When parallel git gc runs left orphaned directories behind, it showed up here immediately as worktree ages creeping past an hour.

Designing for human judgment

None of this replaces text. When I want to explore a feed-ranking idea or pair on a four-phase JavaScript asset cleanup, I still click "New Chat" or open a terminal.

But separating conversation from supervision changed how the whole system feels to run. A good interface compresses operational noise into peripheral vision. I can glance at the Almanac over coffee, see that eight loops are green, notice that rust-loop is pinned to Argon with one PR in review, and close the tab.

We are barely scratching the surface of what human interfaces for agentic systems should look like. For now, the best part of having agents that write code is that you don’t have to wait around for someone else to design the cockpit.

articles.title: Top 5 AI Agent Patterns for Frontend Devs
articles.description: When I code, I prompt, wait, and see what comes back. For a bigger feature I might reach for...
articles.body_html:
When I code, I prompt, wait, and see what comes back. For a bigger feature I might reach for something like spec-driven development. Either way, I'm babysitting the coding harness through every interaction.

Don't get me wrong, that can work well. But plenty of problems are too complex to solve with a single prompt. For those, I'd much rather write one prompt, walk away, and come back to finished work. The patterns in this post came out of trying to do exactly that.

There are five of them, each a step past prompting and specs, and together they keep my agent working while I'm off doing something else: scheduled jobs, memory, subagents, workflows, and bots.

I show everything in Kiro Crew, the open source coding harness I know best, and a couple of things in the Kiro IDE. Some of these patterns exist in Claude Code, Codex, and OpenClaw too, so you can check those out as well.

Here's the video if you'd rather watch:

(Full disclosure: I'm a Developer Advocate at AWS, and Kiro is an AWS product.)

How to follow along (If you want to try this yourself)

  • Kiro Crew installed. The install guide covers the desktop app and the one-line CLI install.
  • Optional, the Kiro IDE if you want to try memory and workflows there too.
  • A frontend project to point it at. Mine are a couple of Vue and Vite+ apps.

1. Schedule

The first feature I think everyone should try out is scheduling. Kiro Crew runs on a Gateway that can live on a VPS, a Mac mini, or your laptop, and it can kick off agent runs on a timer. You can set something similarly by running your harness in the cloud as well.

I care a lot about accessibility and Lighthouse scores on my sites. A daily job can run a Lighthouse test on my frontend code and send me a report, or open a pull request with the fixes instead.

The two jobs on my Schedule page right now aren't about code at all. One researches frontend and fullstack news every morning at 7 a.m. The other is a weekly CFP finder that looks for conference talks I could submit to, every Monday at 9.


Both jobs run on their own and drop a report when they finish.

Each job is a prompt plus a schedule. Open one and you get the message, a cron expression, and a timezone. The news job is 0 7 * * *.


Run Now is handy for testing a prompt before you trust it overnight.

You don't have to write cron by hand. Ask in chat, something like "every night at 2, run Lighthouse on /pricing and tell me what dropped," and the agent creates the job for you. The scheduling docs have the CLI version too.

2. Turn on memory

Memory is how your agent remembers who you are and what you're working on. I've been using this a lot. It works really well for remembering my preferences. For example, it knows I am a Vue.js fan, so it starts every project with Vue.js or Nuxt.

In Kiro Crew, memory lives in a folder at ~/.kiro/crew/workspace/memory as plain markdown, with files for your preferences and your projects. It gets pulled into context when it's needed. You can tell it things as you chat. Maybe you like tabs over spaces, or you want the Options API in Vue for some reason. Just say "can you remember this for me?"

The Kiro IDE has memory too, and the setting has four modes.


Off is the default, so you have to turn it on.

I run Use and learn. It can learn per project or globally, so every project shares the same preferences. Here's one it saved for me during a Vite+ project. I'd asked for a diagram, it asked me a bunch of setup questions, and I told it to just make a nice looking image.


I never wrote this rule. It appeared naturally as I was creating my project.

It even saved the tooling workaround it found, so the next diagram didn't hit the same missing dependency. If your harness has memory, turn it on and start telling it your preferences. Kiro Crew will sometimes turn what it learns into a skill on its own as well.

3. Ask for subagents

When you have a few pieces of work that don't depend on each other, they don't need to wait in line. Tell the agent to split it up. "Run three subagents and research this at the same time" is all it takes. *FYI, some harnesses will do this automatically, but it's hit and miss, I would always explicitly tell it to use subagents, and if needed use worktrees

I did that for my tech news. One subagent took markets and big tech, one took AI releases, and one took dev news like Hacker News threads and Vue, Nuxt, and Vite releases.


Three subagents, 35 seconds, 1.73 credits. The main agent combines the reports at the end.

Each subagent gets its own context, so they don't fill up your main chat or trip over each other. This is a lot cleaner than what I saw people doing a while back, opening 10 terminal windows and running an agent in each one. That gets messy fast.

The current models, like Claude Opus 5.5, are good at breaking work down. Kiro Crew also lets you keep several sessions open at once, each working on a different part of the codebase or a different project in the workspace. I like having that in a GUI where I can see everything that's running.

4. Build a workflow for anything you'll do twice

Workflows are harder to describe than the others. A workflow kicks off multiple agents in a set order, fans work out to them, and checks the results.

Let me explain it by using migrations as an example. You can build one workflow and then reuse for every migration. Each step can fan out to several agents or subagents, and usually there's a judge near the end that double checks the results before it's done.

Kiro Crew has a Workflows feature, and so does the Kiro IDE. The IDE ships with recipes you can open and read. Here's feature-pipeline.


Two separate reviewers on the code loop, then an aggregator that merges what they found.

The design and code steps loop, and the code loop runs two reviewers in parallel before an aggregator combines their findings. The recipes are saved as files you can open and change.

There's also a ralph recipe, if you've heard of the Ralph loop. It runs one coding agent through a JSON checklist, one item per pass, up to 200 times, until everything on the list is done. Check the Kiro workflows docs or the Kiro Crew workflows docs for how to write your own.

5. Give one area of your app to a bot

Bots take everything above and put it in one place. A bot is a long-running agent that owns one area of your work. It has its own memory, it can run its own subagents (Kiro Crew calls them workers), it can run on a schedule, and it works toward a goal.

I made one for accessibility and called it A11y. On the Schedules tab there's Heartbeat, which wakes the bot every hour to look for work on its own. For an accessibility bot, that means checking the app every hour as people merge things in. You can add your own schedules here too.


Heartbeat stays off until the bot has a goal.

The Goals tab is where you give it the goal, something like keeping the Lighthouse score above 90. The bot proposes milestones and you confirm them, which works a lot like the steps in a workflow. You can also turn on daily, weekly, or monthly check-ins so it sends you reports.


Each bot gets its own dashboard, and you build it by asking in chat.

Each bot also gets its own dashboard. Ask it to set one up showing what it's working on and what's next, and it builds the page for you.

One thing to know before you go all in on bots. Every Heartbeat wake, every worker, and every scheduled run uses credits. Heartbeat is off by default and you pick the interval, 30 minutes up to 4 hours. Start slow. The how bots work page covers the rest.

Wrap up

If you haven't noticed, the common theme in all these is that you can stop and walk away and things still get done. Scheduled jobs run while I sleep, memory carries what I've told it into the next session, subagents and workflows split the work up, and a bot does all of it for one part of my app.

Which one are you going to try first? Let me know in the comments. I'm curious if anyone is already running bots on a project.

  • Kiro Crew memory
  • Kiro Crew subagents
  • Kiro Crew workflows
  • How bots work
  • Kiro IDE memory
  • Kiro IDE workflows
  • The video on YouTube

articles.title: Google AI Classroom Part 5: Real-Time Multilingual Live Subtitles & Hong Kong Code-Switching with Gemini 4 / 3.8 & On-Device Gemma 4 E2B
articles.description: Inclusive teaching and learning with real-time 9-language live subtitles handling Hong Kong English-Cantonese code-switching via Gemini 4 and Gemma 4 E2B.
articles.body_html:
Author: Cyrus Wong (黃俊彥) — Google Developer Expert - Cloud (AI), Senior Lecturer at HKIIT

1. Problem Statement: Why Standard Speech-to-Text Breaks in Bilingual Technical Classrooms

In bilingual university and polytechnic classrooms across Hong Kong and Asia, lecturers rarely speak monolingual formal prose. Instead, we naturally code-switch between colloquial Cantonese, English, and domain-specific technical terminology within a single breath:

"大家留意呢個 React component，如果你喺 useEffect 入面唔記得 clean up 個 WebSocket listener，就會搞到 memory leak，甚至令個 Docker container OOM crash。"

When we tested standard commercial speech-to-text (STT) and machine translation pipelines on live Hong Kong lectures, they failed in three ways that actively confused students:

  1. Homophone Hallucination: Generic STT engines phonetically force English programming keywords (useState, kubectl, DynamoDB, idempotent) into nonsensical Chinese characters (e.g., turning useState into "要死" or Docker into "多卡").
  2. Colloquial Cantonese Calques: Standard translation APIs struggle with spoken Cantonese particles and idioms ("呢個", "點解", "搞掂", "睇下"), producing broken English or unnatural literal Mandarin translations.
  3. Loss of Cross-Discipline Context: The word "port" means a TCP/UDP network port in Computer Science, a venous access port in Nursing & Healthcare, and a maritime harbor in Logistics. Without discipline-aware context and rolling conversational history, utterance-by-utterance translation loses pronoun referents ("it", "this hook") and domain accuracy.

To solve this for diverse international and mainland/local student cohorts, we engineered a Dual-Engine Real-Time Multilingual Live Subtitle Pipeline supporting 9 simultaneous target languages (zh-Hant, zh-Hans, en, ja, ko, es, fr, de, vi). Instructors can switch seamlessly between:

  • Server Mode (Recommended · Cross-Platform): Powered by Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite (gemini-3.5-flash-lite), Gemini 3.8 Flash (gemini-3.8-flash), or Gemini 4 Argon (gemini-4-argon) via Genkit (translateTeacherSpeech in functions/ai_flows/subtitleFlows.js) with thinkingBudget: 0 for sub-second multi-language structured JSON generation.
  • Client Mode ($0.00 Cloud Cost · Desktop WebGPU/WASM): Powered by on-device LiteRT-LM Gemma 4 E2B (gemma-4-E2B-it-web.litertlm) running inside a dedicated Web Worker (litertGemma.worker.js) with automatic cloud fallback for zero dropped captions.

2. Architectural Deep-Dive: Dual-Engine Live Subtitle Pipeline

In TeacherSubtitleControlModal.jsx and useTeacherLiveSubtitles.js, instructors can toggle between Server Mode and Client Mode, change their spoken source language (zh-HK, en-US, zh-CN), or add/remove target languages on the fly without restarting their microphone stream.

Diagram 1: Dual-Engine Live Subtitle Architecture (Cloud Gemini 4/3.8/3.5 vs. $0.00 Edge Gemma 4 E2B)

2.1 How the Pipeline Captures and Translates Mixed Languages (Code-Switching)

A common question when designing multilingual live subtitles for bilingual classrooms is: how does the system actually handle mixed languages without breaking the ASR or the translation engine?

Our architecture splits this problem into two decoupled stages:

1. Ingestion: Capturing Spoken Mixed Speech (Cantonese + English Technical Terms)

In Hong Kong and international polytechnics, teachers speak Cantonese while using English for technical concepts ("大家留意呢個 React component，如果你喺 useEffect 入面唔記得 clean up 個 WebSocket listener...").

  • Primary Desktop Path (Web Speech API zh-HK): In useTeacherLiveSubtitles.js, Chromium's SpeechRecognition is initialized with recognition.lang = 'zh-HK'. Google's Hong Kong speech recognition acoustic models natively support conversational Cantonese interleaved with English technical loanwords and acronyms.
  • Audio Fallback Path (LiteRT Whisper & Cloud Gemini): When Web Speech is unavailable (e.g. specialized browsers or VAD silence flushes), 16kHz PCM audio buffers are transcribed via on-device LiteRT Whisper Web Worker or Firebase AI Logic (transcribeAudioWithFirebaseAI). The prompt instructs the engine to transcribe verbatim and retain technical vocabulary rather than forcing homophone substitutions.

2. Translation: Why LLM-Driven Translation Replaces Rule-Based MT for Code-Switching

Traditional machine translation engines (such as standard MT APIs) fail on code-switched technical speech because they expect grammatically formal, monolingual source text. When fed mixed Cantonese-English sentences:

  • They mistranslate colloquial Cantonese grammatical particles ("呢個", "點解", "搞掂", "睇下").
  • They attempt to literally translate programming identifiers (useEffect, useState, Docker, Kubernetes) into Chinese characters.
  • They lose pronoun referents ("佢" / "it") across short, choppy speech bursts.

To overcome this, our system forwards the raw bilingual transcript to an LLM (Cloud Gemini 3.5/3.8/4 or On-Device Gemma 4 E2B) configured with tailored system instructions:

  1. Explicit Source Identification: Tells the model that the source is zh-HK containing colloquial Cantonese with English technical code-switching.
  2. Preservation of Technical Terms: Explicitly instructs the model to preserve programming keywords, variable names, framework identifiers, and CLI commands in their original technical English form.
  3. Colloquial-to-Formal Transformation: For Traditional Chinese (zh-Hant), transforms spoken Cantonese grammar into standard formal written Chinese (書面語); for English (en), translates the colloquial framing into fluent, idiomatic English rather than word-for-word calques.
  4. Pronoun & Context Resolution via Rolling History: Injects the preceding 4 speech cues as read-only context (historyText), allowing the LLM to understand what "佢" or "this hook" refers to from the previous sentence.

3. Implementation Walkthrough: Code-Switching Translation with Cloud Gemini & Edge Gemma 4 E2B

3.1 Server Engine: translateTeacherSpeech with Rolling History & thinkingBudget: 0

When translating live speech in a lecture theatre, latency is paramount: if subtitles lag more than 1.5 seconds behind the lecturer's voice, students lose synchronization with the slide pointer.

In functions/ai_flows/subtitleFlows.js, translateTeacherSpeech minimizes multi-language translation latency while preserving technical terminology by combining three techniques:

  1. Zero-Thinking Fast Path (thinkingConfig: { thinkingBudget: 0 }): Disables chain-of-thought reasoning tokens for direct lexical translation while keeping temperature: 0.1 for deterministic technical terminology preservation.
  2. Rolling Conversational History (historyText): Passes the lecturer's preceding 4 utterances (historyBufferRef.current.slice(-4)) strictly as read-only context so the model resolves pronouns ("if we omit it" $\rightarrow$ "if we omit the dependency array") without re-translating old sentences.
  3. Resilient Multi-Model Routing (generateWithResilience): Supports gemini-3.5-flash-lite (default high-frequency workhorse), gemini-3.8-flash, and gemini-4-argon (gemini-4-argon) with automatic region/model failover and per-class FinOps quota enforcement (checkQuota & logJob). 
// From functions/ai_flows/subtitleFlows.js
export async function translateTeacherSpeech({
  classId,
  teacherUid,
  teacherEmail = '',
  text,
  sourceLang = 'zh-HK',
  targetLangs = ['zh-Hant'],
  context = '',
  customPrompt = '',
  historyText = null,
  model = null,
}) {
  const targetModel = model || AI_MODEL;
  const trimmedText = (text || '').trim();
  if (!trimmedText || isSubtitleNoiseOrRefusal(trimmedText)) {
    return { originalText: '', sourceLang, translations: {}, modelUsed: targetModel, cost: 0 };
  }

  const validTargets = Array.isArray(targetLangs) && targetLangs.length > 0
    ? targetLangs.filter((l) => Boolean(l && typeof l === 'string'))
    : ['zh-Hant'];

  const targetDesc = validTargets
    .map((code) => `${code} (${SUPPORTED_SUBTITLE_LANGUAGES[code] || code})`)
    .join(', ');

  const domainContext = context?.trim() || 'General Classroom Instruction';
  let historyBlock = '';
  if (Array.isArray(historyText) && historyText.length > 0) {
    const lines = historyText.map((l) => (typeof l === 'string' ? l.trim() : '')).filter(Boolean);
    if (lines.length > 0) {
      historyBlock = `\nPreceding Speech History (for conversational context, pronoun resolution, and terminology continuity only; DO NOT translate this section):\n${lines.map((l) => `- "${l}"`).join('\n')}\n`;
    }
  }

  const prompt = `You are a real-time lecture subtitle translator for higher education.
Context / Subject Matter: ${domainContext}
Spoken Source Language: ${sourceLang} (May include colloquial Cantonese and English code-switching)
Target Language(s) to produce: ${targetDesc}
${historyBlock}
Current Speech to Translate:
"${trimmedText}"

Guidelines:
1. FULL TRANSLATION MANDATORY: Translate the complete sentence and meaning accurately and naturally into each requested target language.
2. For English ("en"): Translate all spoken Chinese/Cantonese phrases into natural fluent English. NEVER leave untranslated Chinese characters or colloquialisms in the English translation.
3. For Simplified Chinese ("zh-Hans"): Translate Cantonese colloquialisms into standard written Simplified Chinese.
4. For Traditional Chinese ("zh-Hant"): Translate into standard written Traditional Chinese (書面語).
5. Technical Terms: Preserve domain-specific technical keywords, programming syntax, standard formula names, and brand names (e.g. "useEffect", "Firestore", "Docker", "Python", "Kubernetes") in their original technical spelling without unnatural literal translations.
6. Translate ONLY the "Current Speech to Translate", using the Preceding Speech History solely to infer context, resolve pronouns, and maintain terminology continuity.
7. Return a JSON mapping with the exact target language codes as keys.`;

  const translationsSchema = z.record(z.string(), z.string());

  const { response, modelUsed } = await generateWithResilience(
    {
      prompt,
      config: {
        temperature: 0.1,
        thinkingConfig: { thinkingBudget: 0 },
      },
      output: {
        schema: z.object({
          detectedSourceLang: z.string().optional(),
          translations: translationsSchema,
        }),
      },
    },
    targetModel
  );
  // ... [Normalizes language keys and logs exact token usage to classes/{classId}/aiCosts] ...
}

3.2 Client Engine: $0.00 On-Device Gemma 4 E2B in Web Worker with Streaming CacheStorage

For instructors running 3-hour daily lab sessions on desktop workstations who want $0.00 cloud AI expenditure, we integrated Gemma 4 E2B (gemma-4-E2B-it-web.litertlm) via @litert-lm/core inside web-app/src/workers/litertGemma.worker.js.

When the teacher clicks Download & Load Local Gemma 4 (~1.9 GB) in TeacherSubtitleControlModal.jsx, the worker streams the model weights with real-time progress reporting and caches the binary in the browser's persistent CacheStorage (webai-litert-gemma-v1), so subsequent lectures load from local SSD in under 2 seconds:

// From web-app/src/workers/litertGemma.worker.js
export function buildGemmaTranslationPrompt({
  transcript,
  sourceLang = 'zh-HK',
  targetLangs = ['en'],
  courseContext = '',
  customPrompt = '',
}) {
  const sourceName = langNames[sourceLang] || sourceLang;
  const targetList = targetLangs.map((code) => `- "${code}": ${langNames[code] || code}`).join('\n');
  const domainContext = courseContext?.trim() || 'higher education and classroom instruction';

  return `<start_of_turn>user
You are an expert real-time lecture translation assistant for ${domainContext}.
Translate the following spoken classroom transcript from ${sourceName} into the requested target languages:
${targetList}

CRITICAL RULES:
1. FULL TRANSLATION MANDATORY: Translate the entire meaning into each requested target language. For English ("en"), translate all spoken Chinese/Cantonese phrases into fluent natural English.
2. For Simplified Chinese ("zh-Hans" / "zh-CN"), translate into standard written Simplified Chinese. For Traditional Chinese ("zh-Hant"), translate into standard written Traditional Chinese.
3. Preserve discipline-specific terminology, proper nouns, formula/variable names, and standard technical abbreviations (e.g. "useEffect", "Docker", "Python") in their original technical form.
4. Return strictly a single valid JSON object mapping each target language code to its translated text.

Spoken transcript:
"${transcript}"
<end_of_turn>
<start_of_turn>model
`;
}

Crucially, in useTeacherLiveSubtitles.js, if on-device Gemma 4 E2B is still initializing, times out (>10s), or omits one of the requested target languages in its JSON output, translateTranscript automatically backfills only the missing language keys via the Cloud translateTeacherSpeech function—guaranteeing zero dropped captions:

// From web-app/src/hooks/useTeacherLiveSubtitles.js
const result = await gemmaPromise;
const gemmaTranslations = result?.translations || {};
const missingLangs = targetLanguages.filter((l) => !gemmaTranslations[l]);
if (missingLangs.length === 0) {
  return gemmaTranslations;
}

// Hybrid Partial Fallback: Only request missing languages from Cloud Gemini!
const callTranslate = httpsCallable(functions, 'translateTeacherSpeech');
const response = await callTranslate({
  classId,
  text: trimmed,
  sourceLang: speechLanguage,
  targetLangs: missingLangs,
  context: courseContext,
  customPrompt: customPromptText,
  historyText: recentHistoryStrings,
});
return { ...gemmaTranslations, ...(response.data?.translations || {}) };

4. Discipline Glossary Injection & Zero-Restart Dynamic Prompt Propagation

A single university deployment spans multiple faculties—from Computer Science & Software Engineering to Healthcare, Nursing & Medical Sciences, Business & Corporate Finance (EBITDA, IFRS), and Electrical & Mechanical Engineering.

Diagram 2: Discipline Glossary Injection & Zero-Restart Dynamic Prompt Propagation

When an instructor switches the Subject Domain or edits custom prompt instructions inside TeacherSubtitleControlModal.jsx (or ClassManagement.jsx), the update propagates to all active inference workers and student screens via Firestore onSnapshot with 0ms audio interruption:

4.1 Production Prompt Engineering Gallery: Code-Switching & Multi-Discipline Samples

To help educators and AI engineers adapt our subtitle pipeline to their own universities, below are the exact production prompt templates and assembled payloads from functions/ai_flows/subtitleFlows.js, web-app/src/constants/promptRegistry.js, and admin/prompts/translations/.

Sample 1: Full Assembled Server-Mode Prompt (translateTeacherSpeech) with 4-Turn Rolling History & 9-Language JSON Output

When a lecturer speaks in Hong Kong Cantonese mixed with English technical terms, translateTeacherSpeech injects the 4 most recent utterances (historyText) strictly for pronoun resolution ("佢" / "it" $\rightarrow$ useEffect cleanup function) and terminology continuity:

You are a real-time lecture subtitle translator for higher education.
Context / Subject Matter: Cloud Native Architecture, React Hooks & Container Orchestration (ITP4124)
Spoken Source Language: zh-HK (May include colloquial Cantonese and English code-switching)
Target Language(s) to produce: zh-Hant (繁體中文 (Traditional Chinese)), zh-Hans (简体中文 (Simplified Chinese)), en (English), ja (日本語 (Japanese)), ko (한국어 (Korean)), es (Español (Spanish)), fr (Français (French)), de (Deutsch (German)), vi (Tiếng Việt (Vietnamese))

Preceding Speech History (for conversational context, pronoun resolution, and terminology continuity only; DO NOT translate this section):
- "頭先我哋起咗個 Firestore onSnapshot listener 去 subscribe 個 liveSubtitles document。"
- "大家留意下，當個 student component unmount 嗰陣，個 WebSocket connection 其實仲未斷㗎。"
- "如果你喺 useEffect 入面唔記得 return 個 cleanup function 呢，"

Current Speech to Translate:
"佢就會一直食住個 browser memory，搞到 memory leak 甚至令個 container OOM crash 囉！"

Guidelines:
1. FULL TRANSLATION MANDATORY: Translate the complete sentence and meaning accurately and naturally into each requested target language.

5. Edge Cases & Production Failure Modes We Solved

Building a demo speech-to-text app takes an afternoon; making it survive 3-hour lectures across Windows, macOS, iPadOS, and Android hardware in noisy lecture halls required solving five subtle production bugs:

Diagram 3: Out-of-Tab Microphone Silence Watchdog & Mobile iOS Jetsam OOM Guard

Edge Case 1: The Mobile iOS WebKit 1.9 GB Jetsam OOM Crash Guard

iOS and iPadOS browsers enforce a strict per-tab WebContent memory ceiling (~1.4 GB–2.0 GB). If an instructor opens the Teacher Dashboard on an iPad Pro and the browser attempts to auto-download and instantiate the ~1.9 GB gemma-4-E2B-it-web.litertlm model in WASM/WebGPU memory, iOS WebKit immediately kills and reloads the page (Jetsam OOM).

Edge Case 2: Whisper Silence Hallucinations ("Thank you for watching", "♪", Foreign Script Artifacts)

When a lecturer pauses for 5 seconds to write on the whiteboard, whisper-tiny frequently hallucinates YouTube training artifacts such as "Thank you.", "Thanks for watching.", "[BLANK_AUDIO]", or random Korean/Cyrillic/Arabic characters due to background HVAC fan noise. Worse, if a non-empty hallucination string is returned, a naive pipeline treats it as valid speech and skips the Cloud AI audio transcription fallback!

  • Our Fix: Both client (isWhisperNoiseArtifact in useTeacherLiveSubtitles.js) and server (isSubtitleNoiseOrRefusal in functions/ai_flows/subtitleFlows.js) strip these exact hallucination patterns and out-of-script Unicode blocks ([\uAC00-\uD7AF\u0600-\u06FF...]) before deciding whether to invoke transcribeAudioWithFirebaseAI or publish to Firestore: 
// From web-app/src/hooks/useTeacherLiveSubtitles.js
export function isWhisperNoiseArtifact(text, speechLanguage = 'zh-HK') {
  const trimmed = (text || '').trim();
  if (!trimmed) return true;
  if (/^(\[.*\]|\(.*\)|♪+.*♪*|thank you\.?|thanks for watching\.?|you\.?)$/i.test(trimmed)) {
    return true;
  }
  if (
    /please provide the audio|audio recording or transcript|no speech detected|no clear speech|inaudible|ambient room noise|nothing to transcribe|blank_audio|^transcription\s*:/i.test(
      trimmed
    )
  ) {
    return true;
  }
  const normalizedLang = String(speechLanguage || 'zh-HK').toLowerCase();
  if (normalizedLang.startsWith('zh') || normalizedLang.startsWith('en')) {
    // Reject unexpected Hangul, Arabic, Hiragana/Katakana, Thai, or Cyrillic noise tokens
    if (/[\uAC00-\uD7AF\u1100-\u11FF\u0600-\u06FF\u3040-\u30FF\u0E00-\u0E7F\u0400-\u04FF]/.test(trimmed)) {
      return true;
    }
  }
  return false;
}

Edge Case 3: Out-of-Order Async Network Responses & Parallel STT Race Conditions

When running hybrid Web Speech API + WASM Whisper VAD in parallel, two race conditions happen:

  1. Web Speech API finalizes an utterance in 150ms, and 4 seconds later the local WASM Whisper worker finishes processing the same PCM buffer and overwrites the newer subtitle.
  2. Utterance #14 (a long 25-word sentence) takes 800ms to translate in the cloud, while Utterance #15 (a short 3-word phrase) finishes in 300ms. When Utterance #14's HTTP response arrives late, it overwrites Utterance #15 on student screens!
  3. Our Fix:
    • Whenever recognition.onresult emits a final transcript, it sets lastSpeechRecFinalAt = Date.now() and calls clearPendingVadBuffer(), suppressing any trailing Whisper VAD flush within 2.5 seconds.
    • In publishSubtitle, we assign a monotonically increasing sequence number const seq = ++seqCounterRef.current before awaiting translateTranscript(). When the translation resolves, if seq < latestPublishedSeqRef.current, we discard the stale write from touching liveSubtitles/current while still preserving it in recentHistory sorted by seq.

Edge Case 4: iOS Safari WebKit AudioContext.resume() Deadlock & Zero-Gain Pull Node

In Chrome, Safari, and iOS WebKit, calling await audioCtx.resume() inside an async getUserMedia callback when transient user activation has expired returns a permanently pending Promise that deadlocks audio setup forever. Furthermore, on iOS WebKit, a MediaStreamAudioSourceNode connected only to an AnalyserNode or AudioWorklet will refuse to pull PCM frames unless the graph terminates at audioCtx.destination.

  • Our Fix: In useTeacherLiveSubtitles.js and TeacherSubtitleControlModal.jsx, we never await audioCtx.resume(); instead we fire-and-forget tryResumeAudioCtx() alongside passive pointerdown/keydown listeners, and connect the analyser to audioCtx.destination through a 0-gain silent GainNode (silentGain.gain.value = 0) so WebKit pulls hardware audio frames without causing speaker feedback.

Edge Case 5: The Wireless Mic Battery Trap (isMicSilentWarning Watchdog)

Lecturers frequently minimize the browser and spend 40 minutes coding in VS Code or presenting fullscreen PowerPoint slides. If their wireless lapel microphone battery dies or they accidentally hit the hardware mute switch on their headset, they have no idea that student captions have stopped.

  • Our Fix: A 2-second watchdog in useTeacherLiveSubtitles.js monitors both hardware track events (primaryAudioTrack.muted, enabled === false, readyState === 'ended') and RMS voice activity timestamps (lastVoiceActivityAtRef.current). If the hardware track is muted for $\ge 10\text{s}$ or zero speech energy is detected for $\ge 45\text{s}$, isMicSilentWarning triggers a high-visibility alert and native OS notification on top of fullscreen PowerPoint.

6. Architectural Comparison: Server Gemini Models vs. Edge Gemma 4 E2B

Here is how the dual-engine subtitle options compare across execution mode, model configuration, and device requirements:

Server Mode (High-Nuance Flash) gemini-3.8-flash temperature: 0.1, thinkingBudget: 0 Minimal (Stateless HTTPS Callable) $0.75 / $3.75 per 1M tokens
Server Mode (Flagship Reasoning) gemini-4-argon thinkingBudget: 0 (Legacy sampling keys stripped) Minimal (Stateless HTTPS Callable) $2.00 / $10.00 per 1M tokens

7. Key Takeaways

  1. Decouple STT from Multilingual Translation: Running lightweight hybrid STT on the edge (Web Speech API + LiteRT Whisper + noise artifact filtering) and sending clean text strings with a 4-turn rolling history to translateTeacherSpeech eliminates server audio-slicing overhead and keeps latency under 500ms.
  2. Use thinkingBudget: 0 for Real-Time Captioning: When invoking Gemini 4 Argon (gemini-4-argon), Gemini 3.8 Flash, or Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite for live subtitles, setting thinkingConfig: { thinkingBudget: 0 } and temperature: 0.1 delivers flagship lexical accuracy without reasoning-token latency spikes.
  3. Hybrid Edge + Cloud Beats Pure Edge: On-device Gemma 4 E2B reduces cloud FinOps cost to $0.00 on desktop laptops, while automatic partial fallback to translateTeacherSpeech ensures mobile iPads never crash from WebKit memory limits and no target language is ever left blank.
  4. Guard Every Browser Audio Quirk: Non-blocking AudioContext.resume(), 0-gain destination nodes on WebKit, Android SpeechRecognizer mic-seizure avoidance, and monotonic sequence numbers (seqCounterRef) are essential for rock-solid classroom reliability.

articles.title: Does Promise.all() Cancel Other Promises When One Rejects?
articles.description: When Promise.all() rejects, the promise it returns settles with the first rejection reason, and that...
articles.body_html:
When Promise.all() rejects, the promise it returns settles with the first rejection reason, and that is all that changes. Nothing is cancelled. The other input promises keep going, the operations behind them keep running, and any side effect they perform still happens, after your code has already moved on to the error path.

The table comes from a three-operation reproduction on Node.js 22.23.4. Operation A fails early, B succeeds later, and C writes to a store later still. Timings are approximate. The order of events is the result.

What you might ask What the run showed
Did the aggregate promise reject? Yes, at about 50 ms, with the same error object A rejected with
Did B, an input promise, still settle? Yes, it fulfilled at about 150 ms
Did C, the underlying operation, still run? Yes, it wrote to the store at about 250 ms, after the aggregate had rejected
Can B's value be read through the aggregate? No. It is only available from the promise b itself
Did anything cancel B or C? No. Promise.all() has no concept of cancellation

That is where most explanations stop. The more useful question is what your code should do with work that is still running after a failure. The rest of this article covers how the promise combinators differ, what cooperative cancellation with AbortController can and cannot do, how to choose between the options, and why retrying the whole group after a partial failure can duplicate writes.

Why a rejected Promise.all() does not mean the work stopped

Picture a settings page with a Save all button. It sends three requests at once: profile, notification preferences and billing address.

await Promise.all([
  saveProfile(form.profile),
  saveNotifications(form.notifications),
  saveBillingAddress(form.billing),
]);

The billing request fails fast on validation. Promise.all() rejects, the catch block runs, and the page shows "Save failed, please try again." The user reads that as "nothing was saved." But the other two requests were already on the wire, and nothing told them to stop. Assume both complete a moment later. The user clicks Save again, and the same three requests go out a second time.

Nothing in that sequence is a bug in Promise.all(). It did what it is specified to do. The bug is the assumption that a rejected aggregate means the group of operations has stopped. The error described the aggregate promise, and the user took it to describe the work.

The same gap appears when you upload several files, call several endpoints inside an SDK method, or fan out data transforms. Whenever an operation has an effect outside the promise (a write, a message sent, a file created, a charge made), the distance between "the promise rejected" and "the work stopped" is where duplicate writes, stale screens and confusing logs come from. If the operations are pure reads whose results you discard, the same gap costs you some bandwidth and CPU and may not matter at all. The first job is to know which case you are in.

What Promise.all() actually does with its input promises

Three different things hide behind the word "promise" in this problem, and mixing them up causes most of the confusion.

Term What it is What controls it
Aggregate promise The single promise Promise.all() returns Settles once, on the first rejection or when every input has fulfilled
Input promises The promises you pass in Each settles on its own schedule, independent of the aggregate
Underlying operations The real work: a request, a timer, a disk write, a computation Whatever started it. A promise only reports on it

A promise is a report on an operation, not the operation. Its state tells you whether the report has come in. It does not tell you whether the work is running, finished or stopped.

The specification shows why Promise.all() cannot reach into the operations. For each element of the iterable, it converts the element to a promise and calls then on it with two functions. The fulfillment handler stores the value at that element's position and counts down the elements still pending. The rejection handler is the reject function of the aggregate promise itself. The algorithm is PerformPromiseAll in the ECMAScript specification. Four consequences follow.

  1. The first rejection settles the aggregate. The first input to reject calls the aggregate's reject function. Any later call does nothing, because a promise settles only once.
  2. Later successes are never delivered. The aggregate resolves only when a counter of pending inputs reaches zero, and the counter only goes down when an input fulfills. The input that rejected never counts down, so the counter never reaches zero. The values from the other inputs are collected into a list that nothing can read, and the aggregate's resolve function is never called.
  3. Every input counts as handled. Attaching then handlers marks each input promise as handled. MDN states that rejections after the first are ignored and do not trigger unhandledrejection events.
  4. Nothing in the algorithm touches the operations. The only thing Promise.all() does to an input is attach handlers, by calling then on the promise it gets from Promise.resolve(). It has no way to cancel, pause or inspect the work behind it.

One more detail that is easy to miss. In the common pattern Promise.all([a(), b(), c()]), JavaScript calls a, b and c before Promise.all() runs at all. If those functions start their work before they return a promise, which they usually do, that work is already underway when Promise.all() receives the promises. Promise.all() never calls your functions and does not start operations for you. It observes work that is already in motion. The one exception is a lazy thenable, an object whose then method only starts the work when it is called. Promise.all() passes each input through Promise.resolve(), and for a thenable that queues a job which calls its then. I checked this: the work begins a moment after Promise.all() has returned, instead of before. Promises returned by real APIs such as fetch do not behave that way.

MDN also notes that rejecting the aggregate does not unsubscribe the handlers attached to the inputs. Repeatedly passing the same long-lived pending promise to Promise.all() can accumulate handlers on it, even when another input rejects each time. A shared shutdown promise reused inside a loop is one way to run into that.

The smallest reproduction: what happens after Promise.all() rejects

Three timer-driven operations are enough to separate the aggregate, the inputs and the work. A rejects at about 50 ms. B fulfills at about 150 ms with a plain value. C writes to a store at about 250 ms, and the store stands in for anything outside the promise, such as a file, a row or a message. This is the core of 01-lifecycle.mjs, trimmed to the essentials.

import { createTimeline, sleep } from "./lib/timeline.mjs";

const { log } = createTimeline();
const store = []; // stands in for "something outside the promise"

function start(name, ms, behaviour) {
  log(`${name} started`);
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    setTimeout(() => {
      if (behaviour === "reject") {
        reject(new Error(`${name} failed`));
      } else if (behaviour === "write") {
        store.push(name);
        log(`${name} side effect performed (store = [${store}])`);
        resolve(`${name} result`);
      } else {
        resolve(`${name} result`);
      }
    }, ms);
  });
}

const a = start("A", 50, "reject");
const b = start("B", 150, "value");
const c = start("C", 250, "write");

for (const [name, p] of [
  ["A", a],
  ["B", b],
  ["C", c],
]) {
  p.then(
    (v) => log(`${name} promise fulfilled with "${v}"`),
    (e) => log(`${name} promise rejected with "${e.message}"`),
  );
}

const aggregate = Promise.all([a, b, c]);
aggregate.then(
  () => log("AGGREGATE fulfilled"),
  (e) => log(`AGGREGATE rejected with "${e.message}"`),
);

The .then observers on a, b and c only record when each input settles. Promise.all() has already attached its own handlers to the same promises. This is the output from a real run on Node.js 22.23.4. The numbers change from run to run, and the order does not.

    0 ms  A started
    5 ms  B started
    5 ms  C started
   55 ms  A promise rejected with "A failed"
   55 ms  AGGREGATE rejected with "A failed"
  154 ms  B promise fulfilled with "B result"
  256 ms  C side effect performed (store = [C])
  256 ms  C promise fulfilled with "C result"

After 400 ms the script also checks the end state.

aggregate: rejected (A failed)
store: ["C"]
aggregate rejected with the very same error object as A: true
B value, read from the individual promise b: B result

What this shows. The aggregate settled about 200 ms before the last operation finished. B still fulfilled after the aggregate rejected, and C still performed its side effect after the aggregate rejected. The error the caller received is the object A rejected with, not a copy or a wrapper. B's value is still readable, but only from b, never from the aggregate.

What it does not show. These are simulated operations on timers. The run says nothing about how a particular HTTP client, database driver or file API behaves when its caller stops waiting. It also covers only operations that have no cancellation support. The cancellation case comes later.

What happens after the first rejection

A later success

Already covered by the timeline. The operation finishes, its side effect happens, and its promise fulfills. Its value is out of reach of the aggregate. If your cleanup code needs that value, for example the id of a resource that was just created, you have to keep a reference to the input promise yourself, or collect outcomes with Promise.allSettled() instead.

A later rejection, and whether it becomes an unhandled rejection in Node.js

It is easy to assume that once Promise.all() has rejected, the other failures have nobody listening and surface as unhandled rejections. The language-level answer is no, because Promise.all() attached a rejection handler to every input. The second script checks that on Node.js, where unhandled rejection reporting is a runtime feature and not part of the language. Three inputs reject at about 20, 60 and 90 ms, all passed to Promise.all().

Scenario 1: P1, P2, P3 reject at 20/60/90 ms; all passed to Promise.all
   22 ms  aggregate rejected with "P1"
unhandledRejection events in scenario 1: 0
Outcomes read from the individual promises afterwards:
  P1: rejected (P1)
  P2: rejected (P2)
  P3: rejected (P3)

Zero unhandledRejection events, even though two inputs rejected after the aggregate. The control case is a single rejecting promise that is not passed to anything.

Scenario 2 (control): one rejecting promise that is NOT passed to anything
  273 ms  process 'unhandledRejection' event for "LONE"
unhandledRejection events in scenario 2: 1

Node's process documentation says the unhandledRejection event fires when a promise is rejected and no handler is attached within one turn of the event loop. The command-line documentation says the default --unhandled-rejections mode is throw. With no unhandledRejection listener installed, the rejection is raised as an uncaught exception. The script checks that default in two child processes with no listener.

one rejection nobody handles -> exit code 1
Promise.all, a later input rejects -> exit code 0

The second child attaches a .catch() to the aggregate. That matters, because the aggregate is a promise too. If you call Promise.all() and never await it or attach a handler, the aggregate's own rejection is the unhandled one. Siblings are not.

So when an unhandled rejection does show up around a Promise.all() call, a likely cause is a promise that was never an input. That could be a timeout promise created on the side, a helper that returns a rejecting promise nobody awaited, or an aggregate nobody handled.

Multiple failures

The aggregate carries one rejection reason, the first one it observed. The other failures are not lost, since each input promise keeps its own state, and the script reads all three back with Promise.allSettled() after the fact. But that only works if you still hold the input promises. If the application needs every error, for logging, reporting or deciding what to clean up, collecting outcomes up front is simpler than reconstructing them later. Here are the same three failures, collected with Promise.allSettled().

Scenario 3: same shape of failures, collected with Promise.allSettled
  Q1: rejected (Q1)
  Q2: rejected (Q2)
  Q3: rejected (Q3)

Promise.all() vs Promise.allSettled() vs Promise.any() vs sequential await

The third script runs the same three operations under each strategy. A rejects at about 50 ms. B and C succeed at about 150 and 250 ms, and each writes to the store. For every strategy it records when the aggregate settled and which writes landed after that moment. Same Node.js 22.23.4 run.

Strategy Settles at Outcome Writes before it settled Writes after it settled
Promise.all() about 50 ms Rejects with A's error none B, C
Promise.allSettled() about 250 ms Fulfills with rejected, fulfilled, fulfilled B, C none
Promise.any() about 150 ms Fulfills with B's value B C
Sequential await about 50 ms Rejects with A's error none none, because B and C never started

None of the three combinators cancels anything. They differ in when they settle and in what they let you see.

Promise.all() settles as soon as any input rejects, or when all have fulfilled. It exposes the first failure and, on success, every value in input order. It is useful when you need one aggregate result that fulfills only if every input fulfills, and fail-fast rejection is appropriate. It does not give you rollback or atomicity. If the operations have side effects, you still need to decide what happens to the work that remains in progress.

Promise.allSettled() waits for every input to settle and never rejects because an input did. It fulfills with one object per input, in input order, each with a status of fulfilled or rejected and either a value or a reason. The price is time. It settled at about 250 ms in the run above, because it waited for the slowest operation even though A failed at 50 ms. Use it when every outcome matters, and not when you want to fail fast.

Promise.any() settles on the first fulfillment. It rejects only when every input rejects, with an AggregateError whose errors array lists the reasons in input order, not in the order they happened. The script confirms that with a slow first input and a fast second one.

Promise.any AggregateError.errors order: [ 'first input (slow)', 'second input (fast)' ]

MDN documents that fulfilling the result does not cancel the remaining operations, that every input is marked as handled, and that an empty iterable produces an already rejected promise. In the table, C still wrote at about 250 ms after Promise.any() had settled with B's value.

Sequential await is not a combinator, but it is the other way to avoid the problem. It stops later operations from ever starting, so after A fails there is no B or C to worry about. This only holds when you start each operation after the previous await has finished. If you create all the promises first and then await them one by one, everything has already started. Sequential execution does not make failure safer in general. Anything that already ran stays done, and the total time becomes the sum of the operation times instead of the longest one. It is the right choice when operations depend on each other, or when running them together would be wrong for the target system. It is the wrong choice when they are independent and the user is waiting.

How to cancel the remaining requests when Promise.all() fails

Promises have no cancellation mechanism of their own. The platform's answer is cooperative cancellation with AbortController. You create a controller, hand its signal to the operations, and call abort() when you want them to stop. The signal only communicates. As the MDN page for AbortSignal puts it for promise-based APIs, an operation should react to the abort by rejecting its unsettled promise with the signal's reason. Whether it does is up to the operation.

There is a design consequence. In the common pattern, the functions that produce the promises have already been called before Promise.all() receives them, so there is no moment at which you could give them a signal. A cancellation-aware version has to take functions that start the work and accept a signal. That also lets it skip operations that have not started yet when something has already failed.

The repository contains a teaching implementation, runAllOrAbort. Validation and comments are trimmed here, and the full file is in the repo.

export class SiblingFailedError extends Error {
  constructor(cause) {
    super("Aborted because another task in the group failed", { cause });
    this.name = "SiblingFailedError";
  }
}

export class GroupFailedError extends Error {
  constructor(cause, { outcomes, timedOut, whenSettled }) {
    super("A task in the group failed", { cause });
    this.name = "GroupFailedError";
    this.outcomes = outcomes;
    this.timedOut = timedOut;
    this.whenSettled = whenSettled;
  }
}

const isAbortInduced = (reason, signal) =>
  signal.aborted &&
  (reason === signal.reason || reason?.cause === signal.reason);

export async function runAllOrAbort(tasks, { settleTimeoutMs = 5000 } = {}) {
  const controller = new AbortController();
  const { signal } = controller;
  const outcomes = tasks.map(() => ({ status: "not-started" }));
  const snapshot = () => outcomes.map((o) => ({ ...o }));

  let firstFailure = null;
  let markFailed;
  const failed = new Promise((resolve) => {
    markFailed = resolve;
  });

  const running = tasks.map(async (task, i) => {
    if (signal.aborted) return;
    outcomes[i] = { status: "pending" };
    try {
      const value = await task(signal);
      outcomes[i] = {
        status: "fulfilled",
        value,
        observedAfterAbort: signal.aborted,
      };
    } catch (reason) {
      const abortInduced = isAbortInduced(reason, signal);
      outcomes[i] = {
        status: "rejected",
        reason,
        abortInduced,
        observedAfterAbort: signal.aborted,
      };
      if (!abortInduced && !firstFailure) {
        firstFailure = { reason };
        controller.abort(new SiblingFailedError(reason));
        markFailed();
      }
    }
  });

  const allSettled = Promise.all(running).then(() => "settled");

  await Promise.race([allSettled, failed]);
  if (!firstFailure) return outcomes.map((o) => o.value);

  let timer;
  const deadline = new Promise((resolve) => {
    timer = setTimeout(resolve, settleTimeoutMs, "timeout");
  });
  const result = await Promise.race([allSettled, deadline]);
  clearTimeout(timer);

  throw new GroupFailedError(firstFailure.reason, {
    outcomes: snapshot(),
    timedOut: result === "timeout",
    whenSettled: allSettled.then(snapshot),
  });
}

The design choices worth noticing.

  • The first genuine failure triggers the abort. The abort reason is a SiblingFailedError that wraps the original error, so a task can tell why it was stopped.
  • A failure is separated from an abort. A rejection counts as abort-induced only when it is the abort reason itself or carries it as its cause. The name AbortError alone is not evidence, because a task can fail on its own with an error of that name.
  • The caller gets the original error. GroupFailedError.cause is the first genuine failure, along with a snapshot of every task's status.
  • Waiting is bounded. After aborting, the helper waits up to settleTimeoutMs for started tasks to settle, then throws anyway. whenSettled resolves later with the final outcomes.
  • Promise.all() is safe inside it. Every entry in running catches its own errors, so that aggregate never rejects.

The fourth script drives it with five tasks. E finishes before the failure. A fails at about 50 ms. B uses Node's timers/promises setTimeout with a signal, an API that supports abort. C is a hand-written timer that honours the signal. D ignores the signal entirely. Logging is trimmed here.

const tasks = [
  // E: finishes before the failure
  async () => {
    await sleep(20);
    effect("E");
    return "E ok";
  },
  // A: the genuine failure
  async () => {
    await sleep(50);
    throw new Error("A failed");
  },
  // B: a real API that supports AbortSignal
  async (signal) => {
    const v = await timersSleep(150, "B ok", { signal });
    effect("B");
    return v;
  },
  // C: hand-written, honours the signal
  (signal) =>
    new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
      if (signal.aborted) return reject(signal.reason);
      const t = setTimeout(() => {
        effect("C");
        resolve("C ok");
      }, 250);
      signal.addEventListener(
        "abort",
        () => {
          clearTimeout(t);
          reject(signal.reason);
        },
        { once: true },
      );
    }),
  // D: ignores the signal entirely
  async () => {
    await sleep(250);
    effect("D");
    return "D ok";
  },
];

Task C is deliberately minimal. In real code, also remove the abort listener when the timer completes normally, as MDN advises for abortable APIs, so a long-lived signal does not keep it alive. { once: true } only removes the listener if the signal actually aborts.

First run, waiting for every task to settle after the abort (Node.js 22.23.4). The script also prints status tables, which are shown separately below.

   21 ms  E side effect performed
   51 ms  A throws
   52 ms  C received abort and cleared its timer
   52 ms  B rejected: name=AbortError, cause is signal.reason: true
  251 ms  D side effect performed
  252 ms  runAllOrAbort threw: cause="A failed"

Side effects that happened in total: E, D
Task Status when the helper threw Abort-induced Observed after abort
E fulfilled - false
A rejected false false
B rejected true true
C rejected true true
D fulfilled - true

A dash means the field does not apply. Four different things happened, and they are easy to blur together.

  • E finished before anyone asked for cancellation. The abort could not undo it, and its side effect stands.
  • B and C received the signal and stopped. Their 150 ms and 250 ms timers never produced a side effect. This is cancellation working, because each of them cooperates.
  • D received the signal too, because it was passed to every task, and ignored it. It ran to completion and wrote at about 251 ms. The abort request did not stop it.
  • observedAfterAbort is true for D because the helper saw D settle after the abort had been requested. It records what the helper saw, not when the work physically finished.

The second run uses a settleTimeoutMs of 100. The helper aborts, waits 100 ms and then throws without waiting for D. These are the log lines in time order.

   21 ms  E side effect performed
   50 ms  A throws
   51 ms  C received abort and cleared its timer
   51 ms  B rejected: name=AbortError, cause is signal.reason: true
  152 ms  runAllOrAbort threw: cause="A failed"
  251 ms  D side effect performed

Side effects that happened in total: E, D

When the error reached the caller, D's status was pending. That is all the caller could know. Then D wrote at about 250 ms anyway, after the error had been reported. This is the difference between three things that people often treat as one. Stopping the caller's wait (the helper threw), requesting cancellation (the abort), and actually terminating the work (something only the operation itself can do).

One note on the output above. The line B rejected: name=AbortError, cause is signal.reason: true is an observation from Node.js 22.23.4. Node's timers documentation says the promise returned by the timer rejects with an AbortError when its signal aborts, and the section does not mention a cause. The helper accepts both shapes (rejecting with signal.reason itself, or an error that carries it as cause) so it does not depend on one runtime detail. If you adapt it, test it against the APIs you actually call. fetch was not tested here.

Which approach to choose: a decision table

There is no single right answer, because the right answer depends on what the operations do and what a failure means. These five questions get you most of the way. Do you need every result? Do you need to hear about every failure? Do the operations have effects outside the promise? Do they support cancellation? Does one depend on another?

Situation Use What you accept
All operations must succeed, and you do not need to stop the others automatically Promise.all() The others keep running after a failure. Fine for cheap or idempotent work, risky for expensive or side-effecting work. No rollback
Every outcome matters, because you report, retry or clean up per item Promise.allSettled() You wait for the slowest operation. No fail-fast
The first success is enough, such as mirrors or fallbacks Promise.any() The losers keep running unless you cancel them. If all fail, you get an AggregateError with reasons in input order
Remaining work is expensive or useless after a failure, and the operations accept a signal Concurrent tasks with a shared AbortController Tasks that ignore the signal keep running, finished work is not undone, and you need to treat abort errors differently from real ones
Operations depend on each other, or concurrency would be wrong for the target Sequential await Total time is the sum of the parts. Earlier completed steps still stand if a later one fails

Three rules of thumb sit under the table.

Let the rest finish when the work is independent, cheap and still useful. Prefetching three panels of a dashboard is a good example. If one panel fails, the other two results are worth having, and Promise.allSettled() lets you render them.

Request cancellation when the remaining work is expensive or its result is now pointless. Large downloads, heavy computations and long-polling requests are the classic cases. Do it only through APIs that accept a signal, and do not describe it to yourself as stopped until the operation says so.

When cancellation is unsupported, change what you promise. You cannot abort arbitrary JavaScript work from outside it. What you can do is stop waiting, ignore the late result, and make the effect safe to repeat. Mark the operation's state in your own code (for example, a request id that the UI checks before it renders a late response), and use idempotency keys for writes, as the next section shows.

Retrying after Promise.all() fails: why repeating the whole group can duplicate writes

Back to the Save all button. The fifth script reproduces it without a database or a network. An in-memory ledger stands in for any destination where a write has an effect. Three writes run together, and w3 fails once.

function createLedger() {
  const rows = [];
  const seen = new Set();
  let failNextFor = new Set();
  return {
    rows,
    failOnce: (id) => failNextFor.add(id),
    // Without an idempotency key, every call appends a row.
    async write(id, key) {
      await sleep(id === "w3" ? 20 : 60);
      if (failNextFor.has(id)) {
        failNextFor.delete(id);
        throw new Error(`${id} failed`);
      }
      if (key && seen.has(key)) return `${id} (duplicate ignored)`;
      if (key) seen.add(key);
      rows.push(id);
      return id;
    },
  };
}

The first scenario is what the button in the opening example does. It runs Promise.all() on the three writes, and on failure runs the whole group again.

attempt 1 rejected: w3 failed
ledger after attempt 1: [ 'w1', 'w2' ]
ledger after naive full retry: [ 'w1', 'w2', 'w3', 'w1', 'w2' ]

w3 failed first, so the aggregate rejected at about 20 ms. w1 and w2 were already in flight and landed afterwards, which is why the ledger holds them after attempt 1 even though the attempt "failed". The retry then wrote all three again. w1 and w2 now exist twice.

Two other approaches fix it, and they work differently. Giving each write a stable key derived from the logical operation, not from the attempt, lets the receiver drop repeats. Collecting outcomes with Promise.allSettled() lets you retry only what failed.

// Scenario 2: retry the whole group, but every write carries a stable key
const attempt = () =>
  Promise.all(ids.map((id) => ledger.write(id, `order-42:${id}`)));

// Scenario 3: collect outcomes, retry only the failures
const first = await Promise.allSettled(ids.map((id) => ledger.write(id)));
const failedIds = ids.filter((_, i) => first[i].status === "rejected");
await Promise.all(failedIds.map((id) => ledger.write(id)));

ledger after full retry with idempotency keys: [ 'w1', 'w2', 'w3' ]
failed after first pass: [ 'w3' ]
ledger after retrying only failures: [ 'w1', 'w2', 'w3' ]

Both end with each write exactly once. The third approach has a trap, though, which is the fourth scenario. A rejected call does not prove the write failed. A timeout can reject the caller while the write still commits on the other side. The script injects that case. The write commits, but the caller only sees a timeout.

Simulated lost response, the write commits but the caller sees a timeout
  attempt 1 rejected (w1 timed out waiting for the response)
  after a retry without an idempotency key, ledger = [ 'w1', 'w1' ]
  attempt 1 rejected (w1 timed out waiting for the response)
  after a retry with an idempotency key, ledger = [ 'w1' ]

That last scenario is simulated, not measured. It shows the logic, not how often a real system loses a response.

What to take from it.

  • Retrying only the failures is safe only when a failure is known to mean "not applied." A validation error usually does. A timeout does not.
  • Idempotency keys are the safety net, and the receiving service has to enforce them. The Set in the script lives inside one process. Real enforcement has to survive restarts, multiple servers and concurrent requests, so it belongs in the service or database that accepts the write.
  • Do not start a retry while attempt one is still in flight. After a failure, work from the first attempt may still be landing, as w1 and w2 did. If you request cancellation, wait for whenSettled (or accept the risk knowingly) before retrying. The overlap case was not run as a separate script. It follows directly from the lifecycle shown earlier.
  • A cancelled operation may still have committed. Aborting after the request has been sent does not tell you whether the other side applied it.

Limitations

Some of what I wrote here is promised by the JavaScript spec, so it holds in every engine. The rest is just what I saw when I ran the scripts in Node.js, and another runtime could do something different. Here is how I split the two.

  • From the specification and MDN. These come from the documentation, not from my runs. The aggregate settles on the first rejection, nothing gets cancelled, handlers are attached to every input, Promise.any() lists AggregateError reasons in input order, and promise-based APIs are expected to reject with the abort reason.
  • Observed on Node.js only. I only saw these on Node.js, namely the unhandledRejection counts, the exit codes, and the cause on the AbortError from timers/promises. They are runtime behaviour, so they could differ elsewhere. I ran the scripts on Linux with Node.js 22.23.4, 24.22.2 and 26.13.0. The tests and all five scripts also passed on Windows with Node.js 22.22.2, and that run printed the same events in the same order, line for line, once I ignored the elapsed milliseconds. Windows was slower. I did not test any other versions or operating systems, and the output blocks in this article come from one Linux run on 22.23.4.
  • I did not test browsers. MDN documents that Promise.all() marks its inputs as handled and that later rejections do not trigger unhandledrejection. Treat that as MDN's claim, since my runs did not verify it.
  • Only one real cancellable API got tested. That was the timer from timers/promises, plus a hand-written task. I did not test fetch, streams, file APIs or database drivers, so please do not assume they behave like the timer. I did test what an aborted request does to a node-postgres query in an earlier post.
  • I did not look at Promise.race(). It has the same shape of problem, with its own questions about timers and cleanup.
  • The operations are simulated with timers. The timings are approximate, and the order of events is what I am claiming. I ran each script ten times and compared the full output, ignoring the elapsed milliseconds. Every script produced one distinct output, on Linux and also on Windows with Node.js 22.22.2.
  • runAllOrAbort is there to teach the pattern, not to replace a concurrency library. It cannot stop a task that ignores the signal, it cannot undo work that already finished, and whenSettled stays pending if a started task never settles. The failure it reports is the first one it saw, which is not always the one that physically happened first. settleTimeoutMs has to be an integer from 1 to 2147483647. Anything else throws a RangeError, because setTimeout() normalizes out-of-range delays to 1 ms.
  • The ledger in the retry script lives in memory. Real idempotency has to be enforced by the service that receives the write. The lost response in the last scenario is injected, not measured.

Reproduce the examples

Everything above comes from the promise-all-rejection-and-cancellation repository. It is plain Node.js with no dependencies, no network access, no servers and no database. It needs Node.js 22 or newer.

git clone https://github.com/shubhrapokhariya/promise-all-rejection-and-cancellation.git
cd promise-all-rejection-and-cancellation
npm run verify   # helper tests, then all five scripts
npm run repeat   # run each script 10 times and compare the full output, takes about a minute
npm test         # helper tests only
node 01-lifecycle.mjs   # or any single script, 01 to 05
File What it shows
01-lifecycle.mjs The aggregate rejects first, the other inputs still settle, and a side effect still happens afterwards
02-later-rejections.mjs Later input rejections raise no unhandledRejection event in Node, and a rejection nobody handles does
03-combinators.mjs all, allSettled, any and sequential await on the same operations
04-cancellation.mjs A shared AbortController, tasks that honour the signal, one that ignores it, and giving up the wait
05-partial-failure.mjs Full retry versus idempotency keys versus retrying only failures, plus a simulated lost response
lib/run-all.mjs The runAllOrAbort helper, covered by 19 tests in test/run-all.test.mjs

Each line of a timeline starts with elapsed milliseconds. Treat the order of events as the result, since the exact numbers change from run to run. The repository also includes a GitHub Actions workflow that runs npm run verify on Node.js 22, 24 and 26.

Practical takeaway

A rejected Promise.all() ends your wait. It does not end the work. Four facts that look like one are actually separate. The promise rejected, cancellation was requested, the operation stopped, and the effect happened. Your code can observe the first two directly. The last two are known only if the operation tells you.

Before wrapping side-effecting work in Promise.all(), ask three questions. Which of these operations already has an effect outside the promise? Does each one accept a signal and actually honour it? Is the effect safe to repeat if the whole thing runs again? If you cannot answer the third question with yes, fix that first. Cancellation reduces waste. Idempotency prevents duplicate writes.

The only real cancellable API I tested here was Node's timer, and I covered database drivers in an earlier post, so I am curious about everything else. Has an HTTP client, SDK or queue ever kept working after its AbortSignal fired on you? Tell me which one and what you saw in the comments.

Sources

Official documentation and specification pages, checked on 10 November 2026.

  • ECMAScript specification, PerformPromiseAll
  • MDN, Promise.all()
  • MDN, Promise.allSettled()
  • MDN, Promise.any()
  • MDN, AbortSignal
  • MDN, AbortController.abort()
  • Node.js, process, the unhandledRejection event
  • Node.js, command-line options, --unhandled-rejections
  • Node.js, timers, cancelling timers with AbortController

articles.title: I can build the product with AI. Getting the first users is harder.
articles.description: What building Brainy and MoneyBrain taught me about finding early users beyond my LinkedIn network, and what I want to try next.
articles.body_html:
With Brainy and MoneyBrain, getting the first users and growing monthly recurring revenue has been harder than building the software.

At the beginning, I used my circles on LinkedIn. It gave me somewhere to start talking about the products. Expanding beyond that network has been difficult, especially without a large budget.

That is where I want to pick up from my previous post about building products with AI. In that post, I described how I move from a brainstorm to requirements, GitHub issues, implementation, and a reviewed pull request. I can give the implementation work a scope and check the result against it.

Finding users leaves me with questions I am still working through: where to reach people who need the product, and why they would try it, return, and eventually pay.

My network gave me a place to start

Talking about Brainy and MoneyBrain on LinkedIn was a reasonable first step. I already had people I could reach there, rather than starting with an empty account and hoping someone would find a product announcement.

But a professional network is a particular audience. Someone can be interested in how I build software without needing either product. A post about my AI workflow and a post explaining why someone should use an application ask for different kinds of attention.

More visibility for me would be useful, but I also need to understand which people have the problem the product addresses. Otherwise, I could spend more time promoting it and still learn very little about demand.

A screenshot of a SaaS advice post brought this back into focus. It covered familiar recommendations: promote the product, talk to users, keep the first version small, use it yourself, and pay attention to people who leave.

Reading those points alongside my experience, I kept returning to the difficulty of reaching the next group of people without a large budget.

The post puts most of the work after launch into marketing. I would not assign a fixed percentage to it, but I agree with the underlying reminder: launching leaves a substantial amount of work ahead. For my current goal of finding users, time spent explaining the product and following up with people deserves a place in the schedule alongside implementation. Another completed issue does not tell me whether anyone new understood the offer.

Reaching outside my LinkedIn circles

The encouragement to promote the product openly is useful. Staying entirely within my familiar LinkedIn circles would leave the same audience boundary in place. I need to be willing to explain what I have built somewhere people do not already know me, and to hear that it may not be relevant to them.

I could make a long list of places to post. Each one would take time to understand, participate in, and follow up on. I would also have to decide what to say there, because a product announcement that makes sense to my LinkedIn contacts may mean very little to a stranger.

For Brainy and MoneyBrain, I would rather make the next attempt narrow enough to learn from. Pick one product, one specific problem, and one place where people already discuss that problem. Then explain or demonstrate the part of the product that addresses it.

I also need to make that choice separately for each product. The fact that I built both does not mean the same people need both, or that the same explanation will persuade them. Putting their names into one announcement is convenient for me; a potential user needs a reason to care about the particular application in front of them.

I could examine the result: did people recognize the problem, ask how the product handles their situation, or try it?

If the only response is interest in the technology behind it, that would tell me something too. I might have reached other builders, or explained the implementation more clearly than the reason to use the product.

I feel the budget constraint, but I do not want to turn that into a conclusion that growth requires a large advertising spend. I have not established that. Before spending more, I want a clearer idea of whom I am trying to reach and what I can show them.

A useful next asset could be a short walkthrough of one task, using demonstration data and showing the result. I could use it in a relevant conversation, give the landing page something concrete to show, and learn which part needs more explanation. A tutorial answering a question prospective users already ask could also become something they can find or share later. These would give me more to work with than repeatedly announcing that the product exists.

A community, a search-focused article, or a collaboration needs to earn the time I put into it. A channel with no advertising bill still costs time. Participating well in a community means reading the discussions, respecting its rules, and contributing something useful before expecting attention for my application.

The alternative is often something people already do
