Before writing that walkthrough, I need to understand what the person would replace. They might already have a tool, a document, or a routine that handles the task adequately. Moving to my product could mean learning another interface and spending time setting it up before they see a benefit.

My own move from Notion to Brainy is a useful example of an existing workflow being involved. It gives me a case to examine, but another person's reasons to change could be different. I need to ask which part of their current approach is frustrating enough to justify the effort of switching.

That should shape the product description. Explaining the task someone can complete gives them a way to judge the offer. Describing my AI-assisted development process tells them how I made it. I enjoy talking about that process, and it belongs in the previous post, but it may have little bearing on a person's decision to use Brainy or MoneyBrain.

Even the comparison with competitors needs this context. A competing subscription price tells me one thing about the market; a person's current workaround tells me what I would have to improve. If their approach is already good enough, I need to understand that answer instead of assuming another feature will persuade them.

The first visit needs somewhere useful to go

Someone outside my network needs to understand the product without knowing my background. That makes the advice about the landing page and sign-up process more relevant.

A useful check would be to ask someone unfamiliar with the project to look at the page and explain what they think it does. Then ask them to attempt its main task. I would want to see where they hesitate before adding another feature to the backlog.

That is how I read the advice to make a landing page clean, fast, and convincing. Keep the page focused, check how it loads on a phone, and show a concrete use of the product. A polished layout still needs to help that unfamiliar visitor decide whether to try it.

Google login might remove a step for some people. It cannot explain an unclear product promise, and I would not treat it as an automatic requirement for every audience. The question I want to investigate is where a prospective user gets stuck between understanding the offer and experiencing something useful.

Using my own product regularly gives me a way to notice friction in ordinary tasks. In my earlier post about moving to European digital services, I described replacing Notion with Brainy. That is a useful starting point for testing a real workflow. But I know the product's intended behavior and can navigate around something that another person would find confusing. My familiarity is a reason to get an outside view, especially when I am asking that person to trust a new product.

Keeping the minimum viable product small belongs in this discussion too. I want enough functionality to let someone complete the task that brought them there. Adding features before understanding that task could make both the explanation and the first visit more complicated.

The screenshot names MoSCoW as a way to keep that scope under control: Must Have, Should Have, Could Have, and Won't Have this time. The Agile Business Consortium explains those priorities. For a first release, I would ask whether leaving a feature out prevents the intended user from completing the core task. If it does not, I need a good reason to put it ahead of learning from users.

For the first users, I would also consider helping them through that task personally. Paul Graham's essay on doing things that don't scale argues for recruiting early users manually and paying close attention to their experience. I can see a practical application here: offer a short walkthrough, watch where the person needs help, and use that observation to improve the next attempt.

If I have to explain the same step to everyone, that gives me something specific to investigate in the interface or instructions. If each person wants a completely different outcome, I need to revisit the audience and scope. Automating the welcome messages before understanding those differences could leave me sending more people through a confusing experience.

Trust is part of the first useful experience

There is another reason someone might hesitate even after understanding the product: they have to decide whether to put their information into it. A demonstration with sample data can reduce the effort needed to evaluate the workflow, but using the application for real asks for more trust.

For any task involving personal or financial information, I would want the product to explain what it stores, what happens to that information, and how a person can leave. Those explanations need to match the actual implementation. I cannot make a privacy or security promise simply because it would look reassuring on the landing page.

Support belongs in that decision too. A person should be able to find a way to report a problem and understand what help they can reasonably expect. As an independent builder, I need to be honest about that commitment. Offering personal onboarding is useful only if I leave enough time to follow through.

This is part of what makes a small MVP a serious product decision. I can defer optional features while still needing a dependable core workflow. If the application loses the work someone just entered, a smaller backlog does not make their experience acceptable. The scope has to include the behavior people rely on, and I need to check it before asking them to move a real task into the application.

Growing MRR asks more than whether someone signed up

The screenshot recommends charging from day one instead of offering free trials. There is a useful question behind that advice: will someone pay for the outcome? A payment is more direct evidence of willingness to pay than an encouraging comment on LinkedIn.

I would still make the trial decision around the product. If someone needs to use it with their own information or across several days to judge the benefit, a trial could help them decide. If the value can be demonstrated clearly before purchase, charging immediately may make sense. I would not dismiss every free user as unserious; their experience can reveal a problem that also affects paying users.

Monthly recurring revenue is an objective I care about. To make progress toward it, I need to understand what would justify an ongoing payment from the people I am trying to reach. Choosing a price or removing a free trial does not answer that question on its own.

The advice to price based on value is more useful to me than copying another application's subscription page. I would want to ask about the task a person is doing now: how they handle it, what is frustrating, and what a useful improvement would look like. Time saved, a recurring task made easier, or a mistake avoided could give the discussion a concrete basis. Those are possibilities to investigate, not benefits I can assign a monetary value to without talking to people.

Those conversations could happen through a DM, an email, or a short call, depending on what the person prefers. A focused question about what they tried to do would give me more to work with than asking whether they like the product. I would also want to hear from someone who created an account and then stopped, rather than only from people willing to praise it.

This is where retention belongs alongside the work of finding new users. If people try the product and do not return, reaching a larger audience leaves that question unresolved. I would want to understand repeated use before scaling the same acquisition attempt. For a recurring subscription, whether people keep finding a reason to use the product matters to the revenue goal too.

If a person leaves, an optional conversation could help explain what happened. I would make unsubscribing or cancelling straightforward, and respect a person who does not want to explain. An email opt-out might mean they want fewer messages; a product cancellation asks a different question. Either can be feedback, but neither gives me a reason to argue with their decision.

I also need to understand the expected frequency of the task. Someone may get value from a product every week or at a particular point in the month. Daily activity would be a poor way to judge that experience if daily use was never the goal. I would look for people returning when the need occurs and completing the task they came for.

Feedback from those conversations needs a decision attached to it. A request for another feature might reveal a missing step in the core workflow, or it might describe a different product. I would record what the person was trying to accomplish before putting the request into the backlog. That gives me a way to compare it with other needs instead of letting the most recent message determine the next epic.

I need to know where the attempt stops working

Once I start trying channels outside LinkedIn, a total sign-up count will leave too much unexplained. I want enough visibility to distinguish a message that people never saw from a product they tried and then abandoned.

A simple record could follow the path from first contact to continued use:

Step What I would try to learn
Someone encounters the product Which conversation, post, article, or recommendation brought them there?
They visit the page Can they understand the problem it addresses and the next action?
They create an account Where do they hesitate or leave during registration?
They complete the main task Do they get the outcome that made them try it?
They return when needed Does the product fit an ongoing need?
They begin or continue paying What makes the ongoing price worthwhile to them?

That main task needs a definition for each product before its completion becomes a useful signal. Opening a dashboard might only show that registration worked. The meaningful action should reflect what the person wanted to accomplish, and any measurement should collect only the information needed to understand that behavior.

With a small number of users, raw counts and conversations need to sit alongside any percentages. A few people leaving at one step would justify looking at it; it would not give me a reliable explanation of why everyone leaves. The channel context matters too. People arriving from my existing network may behave differently from people encountering the product for the first time.

This could make the next decision more specific. If people understand the offer but cannot finish the task, I have something to investigate in the product. If the people I reach do not recognize the problem, I need to examine the audience or message. Changing both at once would make it harder to understand what helped.

The costs behind the MRR goal

MRR also needs more detail than one rising total. Stripe's explanation of monthly recurring revenue separates growth from new subscriptions and existing customers increasing their subscriptions, and reductions from cancellations or downgrades. Those movements describe different situations that I would want to understand separately.

For example, new subscriptions could increase the total while existing subscribers leave. I would want to see both movements before deciding to repeat the acquisition effort. A larger total on its own would not explain whether the product is keeping the users it already reached.

Then I need to compare recurring revenue with the costs of providing the service. Hosting, payment processing, and support take resources. Where a product uses paid external services, their usage belongs in that calculation too. MRR measures recurring revenue; it does not show what remains after those costs.

The implementation workflow has costs as well, and the time spent helping users has to fit into the week. Even if AI makes an implementation task cheaper for me, I still need to maintain the behavior it introduces and answer questions about it. That is another reason to keep the scope of a growth experiment manageable.

A lifetime deal offered simply to produce early cash would deserve particular scrutiny. An ongoing service creates ongoing work, while a one-time payment has a different revenue shape from a recurring subscription. Before making that offer, I need to understand the support commitment it would create. This is a possible decision to examine; I am not reporting a pricing change to either product.

Ambition needs a reason to continue

The post also encourages builders to aim beyond their first revenue milestone. I like the challenge to think about what a product could become. At the same time, a larger MRR target needs some basis: who else could benefit, how I could reach them, and whether they would keep using it. Changing the number in a goal would leave my current acquisition problem untouched.

For Brainy and MoneyBrain, I want the next milestone to answer one of those questions while leaving room for a bigger ambition.

What I want to do with the next cycle of work

My next useful step would be to give one attempt at finding users the same attention I give an implementation task. Choose a specific audience and problem, make a small attempt to reach them, and leave time to follow up with anyone who tries the product.

A short note for each attempt could record the audience, the message, where I shared it, and what happened afterward. Including the effort spent, even if no money changed hands, would give me something to compare when deciding what to repeat.

For this purpose, focusing on one product at a time would make the follow-up easier to manage. Brainy and MoneyBrain can both remain part of my work, but trying a new audience and message for both simultaneously would divide that attention. AI gives me a way to move implementation forward; I still have to make room in the week to understand the people using the result.

I would set a review point before starting. With a limited budget, I need to consider the time spent as well as the money. Continuing an experiment should depend on what I learn from it; persistence alone would not tell me whether to repeat it, change it, or stop.

That connects two pieces of advice in the screenshot: stay in the game, and consider moving on when the product does not make money. If the goal is a business, revenue and costs need an honest review. Personal usefulness can be a separate reason to maintain it, but it does not establish commercial demand. I want to give a promising idea a fair test without treating every additional month of work as evidence that it will succeed.

I still value the workflow from the previous post. It helps me turn a product idea into software I can review. With Brainy and MoneyBrain, my immediate challenge is to take the next step beyond my LinkedIn circles and learn why someone unfamiliar with me would choose to use what I built.

AI assisted with drafting and editing this post and generating the cover image.

articles.title: You're Still Optimizing Re-Renders Wrong: The Vue 3 Architecture That Outsmarted the Virtual DOM
articles.description: A visual, 10-minute deep dive into Vue 3 internal architecture. Learn how JavaScript Proxies coordinate with the global targetMap, why Compiler-Informed Block Trees crush traditional brute-force VDOM diffing, how to avoid the destructuring trap, and how Vapor Mode compiles directly to the DOM.
articles.body_html:
If you have built applications in modern frontend frameworks, you have almost certainly encountered the re-render nightmare.

In traditional Virtual DOM architectures, updating a single state variable often causes an entire component tree to re-execute from top to bottom. To prevent performance bottlenecks, developers must manually wrap calculations in memoization hooks, carefully manage dependency arrays, and worry about stale closures:

// The manual dependency tightrope
const userProfile = useMemo(() => {
  return calculateComplexMetrics(user, filters);
}, [user.id, filters.activeStatus]); // Miss a dependency, and your UI breaks

One missing dependency in that array creates subtle, agonizing bugs. One unnecessary dependency triggers expensive cascading re-renders across dozens of child components.

Then you look at Vue 3:

// In Vue 3: No dependency array. No manual memoization.
const userProfile = computed(() => {
  return calculateComplexMetrics(user.value, filters.activeStatus);
});

You mutate user.value.name, and only the exact paragraph rendering that name updates. The parent component does not re-render. Sibling components do not recalculate. There are no dependency arrays, no stale closures, and no manual memoization hooks.

To many developers, this behavior looks like magic or dangerous hidden reactivity.

In reality, Vue 3 is powered by one of the most sophisticated engineering architectures in modern software: a fine-grained Proxy dependency graph coordinated with a Compiler-Informed Block Tree.

Here is how Vue 3 actually tracks state, updates the DOM, and eliminates the re-render cascade.

1. The Reactivity Engine: Proxies, track(), and trigger()

In Vue 2, reactivity was implemented using Object.defineProperty(). The engine recursively traversed every property of your data object on initialization and converted them into getters and setters.

This approach suffered from notorious limitations:

  • Adding a new property (obj.newKey = 123) went undetected, requiring Vue.set().
  • Deleting a property went undetected, requiring Vue.delete().
  • Direct array index mutations (arr[0] = 'new') were unobservable without overriding prototype methods.
  • Deeply nested objects incurred heavy upfront performance costs during initialization.

Vue 3 replaced Object.defineProperty() entirely with modern JavaScript Proxy objects.

The Global Dependency Store (targetMap)

At the core of Vue 3 is a private, module-level data structure named targetMap.

targetMap is a nested multi-level registry that maps objects and their properties to the functions that depend on them:

targetMap (WeakMap)
 └── [target object] ──► depsMap (Map)
                          └── [property key] ──► dep (Set of ReactiveEffects)
  1. targetMap (WeakMap): Holds raw target objects as keys. Because it is a WeakMap, if your application discards the original object, the garbage collector cleans it up automatically, preventing memory leaks.
  2. depsMap (Map): Maps each specific property name of that object (e.g., 'count', 'username') to its dependency tracker.
  3. dep (Set): A Set containing all active ReactiveEffect instances (such as a component render function, a watch callback, or a computed value) that read that specific property.

How track() Registers Dependencies (The Getter Trap)

When you write:

const state = reactive({ count: 0 });

Vue wraps your raw object in a Proxy.

When a component renders, it executes inside a ReactiveEffect wrapper, setting a global pointer named activeEffect to point to that component's render function.

When your template evaluates state.count:

  1. The Proxy's get trap intercepts the property read.
  2. The proxy invokes Vue's internal track(target, 'count') function.
  3. track() checks: Is there currently an activeEffect running?
  4. If yes, it fetches or creates the dep Set for target.count inside targetMap and adds activeEffect to the Set.

You never declare dependency arrays because JavaScript's runtime call stack declares them for you. Any property read while activeEffect is running is automatically recorded as an exact subscriber.

How trigger() Fires Updates (The Setter Trap)

When you execute:

state.count = 42;
  1. The Proxy's set trap intercepts the mutation.
  2. The proxy assigns the new value to the raw underlying object using Reflect.set().
  3. It invokes Vue's internal trigger(target, 'count') function.
  4. trigger() looks up targetMap.get(target).get('count').
  5. It retrieves the Set of subscribed effects and schedules them for execution.

Only the exact components and computed properties subscribed to state.count are scheduled to run. Unrelated components are completely untouched.

2. The Compiler-Informed Virtual DOM: Block Trees and Patch Flags

Virtual DOMs earned a reputation for being heavy and resource-intensive because traditional implementations (like React's standard reconciler) operate on brute-force tree diffing.

In a traditional Virtual DOM:

  • When state changes, the component function executes again.
  • It allocates a brand-new tree of Virtual DOM nodes (VNodes) in memory.
  • The reconciler recursively compares every old VNode with every new VNode, checking tags, props, and children, even if 95% of those nodes are purely static HTML that can never change.

Vue 3 solved this through an architectural breakthrough: the Compiler-Informed Virtual DOM.

The Static Analysis Advantage

Because Vue templates have a deterministic structure, the Vue compiler analyzes your template at build time to identify which parts are dynamic and which parts are static.

Consider this template:

<div class="user-card">
  <header>
    <h1>User Profile</h1>
    <span class="badge">Verified</span>
  </header>
  <p class="bio">{{ user.bio }}</p>
  <button :class="{ active: isActive }">Follow</button>
</div>

In a traditional framework, updating user.bio requires diffing the <div class="user-card">, the <header>, the <h1>, the <span>, and the <button>.

The Vue 3 compiler does something radically different:

1. Static Hoisting

The <header> containing <h1>User Profile</h1> and <span class="badge"> contains zero dynamic bindings.

The compiler pulls those VNodes completely outside the component render function. They are created once when your application loads and reused across every future render. Their memory allocation during updates is zero.

2. Patch Flags (Bitwise Optimization)

For dynamic elements, the compiler attaches a numeric PatchFlag representing precisely what can change:

// Compiled output snippet
_createVNode("p", { class: "bio" }, _toDisplayString(_ctx.user.bio), 1 /* TEXT */)
_createVNode("button", { class: _normalizeClass({ active: _ctx.isActive }) }, "Follow", 2 /* CLASS */)

The number 1 is a bitmask for TEXT. The number 2 is a bitmask for CLASS.

When diffing the <p> tag, Vue performs a single bitwise check (patchFlag & PatchFlags.TEXT). If true, it updates node.textContent directly, skipping any checks for attributes, event listeners, or styles.

3. The Block Tree (dynamicChildren)

The root <div> is compiled into a Block.

A Block maintains a flat array called dynamicChildren. Instead of traversing the nested DOM tree recursively, the Block collects only the dynamic elements:

Block (div.user-card)
 └── dynamicChildren: [
       VNode (p.bio, PatchFlag: 1),
       VNode (button, PatchFlag: 2)
     ]

When user.bio updates, the diffing algorithm does not traverse the tree. It iterates over a flat array of two items!

The diffing cost becomes proportional to the number of dynamic bindings on the page, rather than the total size of your HTML tree.

3. ref() vs reactive(): The Destructuring Trap

One of the most frequent points of confusion for developers adopting Vue 3 is choosing between ref() and reactive().

Both create reactive state, but their underlying implementation mechanisms differ fundamentally.

The Mechanism of ref()

JavaScript primitive types (number, string, boolean, null, undefined) are passed by value, not by reference. You cannot wrap a primitive in a JavaScript Proxy.

To make primitives reactive, Vue introduces the RefImpl class:

class RefImpl {
  private _value;
  public dep = new Set();

  constructor(val) {
    this._value = val;
  }

  get value() {
    trackRefValue(this);
    return this._value;
  }

  set value(newVal) {
    this._value = newVal;
    triggerRefValue(this);
  }
}

A ref() is simply an object with a single property: .value.

Reading .value triggers the getter and tracks dependencies. Mutating .value triggers the setter and notifies subscribers.

Because it is wrapped in an object container, you can pass a ref across composable functions, return it from stores, and pass it as function arguments without losing reactivity.

The Mechanism of reactive()

reactive() accepts an object and wraps it directly in a Proxy.

It feels more natural to write because you do not need to append .value in your script code:

const user = reactive({
  name: "Emma",
  age: 26,
});

user.age++; // Natural syntax

The Destructuring Trap

Here is where thousands of developers run into unexpected silent failures:

// A common fatal mistake
const user = reactive({ name: "Emma", age: 26 });

// Destructuring breaks reactivity!
const { name, age } = user;

Why does destructuring destroy reactivity?

Remember: user is a Proxy intercepting property access on the user object.

When you write const { age } = user, JavaScript evaluates user.age, retrieves the raw primitive number 26, and assigns it to a new local variable named age.

The variable age is now just the plain number 26. It is completely disconnected from the Proxy. When the original user.age mutates later, age remains 26. The Proxy's getter and setter traps are never invoked.

The Solution: toRefs()

If you need to destructure a reactive object, you must convert its properties into individual ref objects using toRefs():

import { reactive, toRefs } from 'vue';

const user = reactive({ name: "Emma", age: 26 });

// toRefs wraps each property in a custom getter/setter proxy pointing back to user
const { name, age } = toRefs(user);

age.value++; // Reactivity is fully preserved!

4. The Batching Engine: Scheduler and nextTick()

What happens if you update a reactive variable fifty times inside a loop?

const count = ref(0);

function runStressTest() {
  for (let i = 0; i < 50; i++) {
    count.value++;
  }
}

Does Vue re-render the DOM fifty times in rapid succession, thrashing the browser layout engine?

No. Vue updates the DOM asynchronously using an internal Scheduler.

The Microtask Queue

When a reactive state change invokes trigger():

  1. Vue does not execute the component's render function immediately.
  2. It passes the render job to queueJob(job).
  3. The scheduler checks if this specific component's render job is already queued. If it is already in the queue, it ignores the duplicate call.
  4. The scheduler flushes the entire job queue in a single batch on the browser's next Microtask tick using Promise.resolve().then(flushJobs).

Regardless of how many times you mutate reactive state synchronously during a function execution, the component's render function runs exactly once.

Accessing Updated DOM via nextTick()

Because DOM updates are queued on a microtask, reading the physical DOM immediately after mutating state returns the old layout:

count.value = 5;
console.log(document.querySelector('.counter').textContent); // Still prints old value!

To wait until the scheduler has completed its microtask flush and committed the updates to the physical DOM, Vue provides nextTick():

import { nextTick } from 'vue';

count.value = 5;
await nextTick();
console.log(document.querySelector('.counter').textContent); // Now prints "5"

nextTick() simply attaches a callback to the exact same microtask promise chain, guaranteeing that your inspection logic runs immediately after the DOM update commits.

5. The Evolution: Vue 2, Vue 3, and Vapor Mode

Frontend framework design is moving away from heavyweight runtime Virtual DOM reconciliation toward compile-time direct DOM operations.

We have seen this trend through frameworks like Svelte and SolidJS.

Vue is uniquely positioned in this landscape because of its architectural progression across three distinct eras:

Era 1: Vue 2 (Runtime Virtual DOM + Object.defineProperty)

  • Relied on ES5 getters and setters.
  • Full-tree recursive Virtual DOM diffing.
  • Required manual workarounds for array mutations and dynamic properties.

Era 2: Vue 3 (Proxy Reactivity + Compiler-Informed Block Trees)

  • Native ES6 Proxies for complete reactivity coverage.
  • Build-time static hoisting, PatchFlags, and Block Trees.
  • Up to 300% faster VDOM reconciliation than traditional brute-force diffing engines.

Era 3: Vue Vapor Mode (Opt-In Direct DOM Compilation)

  • The next major leap in Vue's architecture.
  • For opted-in components, Vapor Mode completely eliminates the Virtual DOM.
  • The template compiler translates your template into fine-grained direct DOM creation and update calls tied directly to reactivity signals: 
// Conceptual Vapor Mode compilation output
import { renderEffect, setText } from 'vue/vapor';

const n0 = document.createElement('h1');
renderEffect(() => {
  setText(n0, count.value);
});

When count.value updates in Vapor Mode:

  • Zero VNodes are allocated in memory.
  • Zero diffing algorithms run.
  • The signal directly triggers setText(n0, count.value) to mutate the physical DOM node in place.

Best of all, Vapor Mode uses the exact same Single-File Component syntax (<template>, <script setup>). You do not need to learn a new templating language or rewrite existing components to benefit from zero-VDOM performance.

6. Three Common Vue Reactivity Traps

Understanding Vue's internal architecture immediately arms you against the three most frustrating pitfalls developers encounter:

Trap 1: Storing Heavy External Objects in reactive()

If you store non-primitive third-party objects (such as a Three.js scene, a Monaco Editor instance, a Chart.js canvas, or a Mapbox map) inside a standard reactive() or ref():

// DANGEROUS: Destroys performance
const editorInstance = ref(monaco.editor.create(...));

Vue will recursively wrap the thousands of internal properties, prototypes, and event listeners of that third-party library in reactive Proxies. This creates massive memory overhead and frequently causes third-party libraries to crash when their internal this contexts are proxied.

The Fix: Use shallowRef() or markRaw():

import { shallowRef } from 'vue';

// Safe: Only the .value pointer is reactive; inner properties are untouched
const editorInstance = shallowRef(monaco.editor.create(...));

Trap 2: Infinite Watch Loops

Because Vue tracks dependencies automatically during execution, creating circular reads and writes inside watchEffect() will crash your application:

// CRASHES: Maximum recursive update cycle exceeded
watchEffect(() => {
  total.value = items.value.length;
  // If reading total somewhere triggers items to update, an infinite loop ensues
});

The Fix: Prefer explicit computed() for derived state, and reserve watchEffect() strictly for side effects (such as making API calls or updating local storage).

Trap 3: Direct Mutation of Props

In Vue, data flow is strictly unidirectional. Passing a reactive object as a prop and mutating it directly in a child component bypasses parent state tracking and leads to unpredictable rendering inconsistencies.

The Fix: Emit events using defineEmits() or use v-model with defineModel() to maintain clear ownership over state mutations.

The Mental Shift

The difference between struggling with frontend performance and building scalable interfaces comes down to your mental model:

Stop thinking of reactive components as functions that need to re-execute repeatedly from top to bottom.

Vue 3 is an event-driven signal graph paired with an intelligent compiler.

  • State is a Proxy network, registering dependencies automatically on access.
  • Templates are Block Trees, diffing only the slots marked with PatchFlags.
  • DOM updates are batched asynchronously through microtask queues.
  • And with Vapor Mode, the Virtual DOM step disappears entirely, connecting state directly to DOM nodes.

Once you understand this architecture, the need for complex memoization hooks disappears, re-render cascades vanish, and building reactive user interfaces becomes natural, predictable, and exceptionally fast.

How has Vue's fine-grained reactivity model influenced how you design your frontend state? Have you experienced the performance shift between traditional re-render engines and Proxy-based tracking, or experimented with early Vapor Mode builds? Share your thoughts and architecture experiences in the comments below.

articles.title: Claude Code Output Validation Hooks in 2026: Linting Agent-Written Code Before It Touches Your Repo
articles.description: Deterministic validation hooks for AI-generated code. Stop type errors, security holes, and test failures before Claude commits them to your repository.
articles.body_html:
Claude Code Output Validation Hooks in 2026: Linting Agent-Written Code Before It Touches Your Repo

This article was written with the assistance of AI, under human supervision and review.

AI code agents produce output at a pace that makes manual review impractical. A Claude Code session can edit fifty files before the first test runs. The code lands in the repository clean or broken depending on whether validation happened before the commit. Most teams discover this after the damage shows up in CI.

The problem sits between the agent's tool execution and the repository state. Claude writes code that passes its internal checks but fails the toolchain's stricter rules. Type errors appear that TypeScript would have caught. Tests break that were passing ten minutes earlier. Security scanners flag patterns that a pre-commit hook would have blocked.

Claude Code workflow without validation showing compiler staying silent until CI fails

Validation hooks solve this by running checks at deterministic points in the agent's execution flow. A PreToolUse hook blocks a dangerous shell command before it runs. A PostToolUse hook lints every file edit and sends errors back to Claude for correction. A Stop hook verifies that tests pass before the turn ends.

Claude Code workflow with validation hooks showing checks passing before code reaches the repository

The validation happens in the same environment that runs the code. The agent sees the exact error message the compiler produces and fixes it in the next turn. The repository receives only code that already passed the checks.

Key Takeaways

  • Validation hooks intercept AI tool calls at specific execution points (before, after, or on session events) and run deterministic checks that return pass/fail decisions.
  • Exit code 2 blocks the action and returns stderr to Claude as feedback; exit 0 applies any JSON output fields but does not auto-approve.
  • PostToolUse hooks with formatters and linters are the most widely adopted pattern because they fix trivial errors automatically.
  • Agent-type hooks spawn subagents that can read files and run commands to verify conditions that require inspecting actual state rather than just evaluating input data.
  • Production workflows layer multiple hooks (linting, security scanning, test execution) with additionalContext injection to enforce repository policy deterministically.

PreToolUse vs PostToolUse: Choosing the Right Hook Point

Claude Code fires hook events at different stages of execution. The choice between PreToolUse and PostToolUse determines whether validation prevents an action or corrects it afterward.

A PreToolUse hook runs before the tool executes. The hook receives the tool name and input as JSON. Exiting with code 2 blocks the tool call and sends stderr back to Claude as the reason. This works for preventing destructive operations that cannot be undone.

Hook execution flow showing PreToolUse blocking risky operations and PostToolUse validating results

A PostToolUse hook runs after the tool finishes. The hook sees the tool output and can verify that the operation produced valid results. Exiting with code 2 here does not undo the tool call. Instead it signals that the output failed validation and Claude should try again.

The PreToolUse pattern prevents errors. The PostToolUse pattern detects and corrects them. Most production setups use both. Security checks run pre-execution to block dangerous patterns. Linters and formatters run post-execution to clean up style issues.

A Stop hook fires when Claude tries to end its turn. Exiting with code 2 sends Claude back to work with stderr as the reason it cannot finish yet. This enforces that work meets completion criteria before the turn ends.

The timing decision depends on what can be fixed automatically. Formatters and linters produce errors that Claude can resolve by re-editing the file. Those belong in PostToolUse hooks. Destructive operations like dropping database tables cannot be fixed after execution. Those require PreToolUse blocks.

Building a Pre-Commit Linting Hook That Blocks Bad Edits

The most effective validation hook runs TypeScript's compiler in --noEmit mode after every file edit. The hook exits with code 2 if type errors exist, which blocks the turn from ending and sends the full compiler output back to Claude.

Developers place this hook at .claude/settings.json in the repository root so it applies to every team member who works in the project, as documented at https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks. Workspace trust controls when the hook starts running on each machine.

{
  "hooks": {
    "Stop": [
      {
        "type": "command",
        "command": "pnpm tsc --noEmit 1>&2 || exit 2"
      }
    ]
  }
}

The 1>&2 redirection sends TypeScript's output to stderr because Claude Code reads stderr as the block reason when a hook exits with code 2. Without the redirect, the compiler errors go to stdout and Claude never sees them.

The hook runs every time Claude tries to stop. If the compiler finds errors, the exit code 2 prevents the turn from ending. Claude receives the type errors and continues working until tsc passes.

Claude Code validation hooks running TypeScript compiler checks

This pattern extends to any tool that reports errors on stderr and uses exit codes. ESLint with --max-warnings 0 blocks on linting violations. Prettier with --check blocks when formatting is inconsistent.

{
  "hooks": {
    "Stop": [
      {
        "type": "command",
        "command": "pnpm tsc --noEmit 1>&2 || exit 2"
      },
      {
        "type": "command",
        "command": "pnpm eslint . --max-warnings 0 1>&2 || exit 2"
      }
    ]
  }
}

Hooks in the same event array run in parallel. Both the typecheck and the linter execute at the same time. If either exits with code 2, the turn stays blocked until both pass.

The default block cap is eight consecutive stops with exit code 2 and no tool calls between them. After eight blocks, Claude Code overrides the next block and ends the turn anyway. Teams that need a higher cap set the CLAUDE_CODE_STOP_HOOK_BLOCK_CAP environment variable, documented at https://code.claude.com/docs/en/env-vars.

PostToolUse Feedback Loops: Teaching Claude to Fix Its Own Mistakes

PostToolUse hooks run after a tool finishes and receive the tool's output as part of the hook input. Exit code 2 in a PostToolUse hook does not block the original tool call because the tool already executed. Instead it signals that validation failed and Claude should continue the turn to address the errors.

PostToolUse feedback loop showing Claude editing, hook validating, and Claude fixing errors until validation passes

The hook script receives JSON on stdin that includes the tool name, input, and output. A PostToolUse hook for file edits parses this input to extract the edited file path and runs a linter against it.

#!/usr/bin/env node

const input = JSON.parse(require('fs').readFileSync(0, 'utf-8'));

if (input.tool_name === 'Write') {
  const filePath = input.tool_input.path;
  const { execSync } = require('child_process');

  try {
    execSync(`eslint ${filePath} --max-warnings 0`, {
      stdio: 'inherit',
      encoding: 'utf-8'
    });
  } catch (error) {
    process.stderr.write(`Linting failed for ${filePath}\n`);
    process.exit(2);
  }
}

process.exit(0);

The script checks whether the tool that just ran was Write. If so, it lints the file. A linting failure causes the script to exit with code 2 and write the error to stderr. Claude sees this feedback and edits the file again to fix the violations.

The feedback loop continues until the linter passes. Each iteration gives Claude the exact error message and line number. The agent applies the fix and the hook validates again. The turn ends only when no errors remain.

This pattern handles any validation that can be expressed as a deterministic check. Formatters, type checkers, and test runners all fit. The hook runs the check, and Claude iterates until it passes. The pattern works better than prompting Claude to "make sure to lint" because the hook enforces the requirement regardless of how Claude interprets the instruction.

Teams extend this approach to security scanning by running tools like semgrep or gitleaks in PostToolUse hooks. A finding triggers exit code 2 with the scanner's output on stderr. Claude sees which pattern triggered the alert and rewrites the code to avoid it.

Security Scanners and Test Runners as Validation Hooks

Security scanning belongs in PreToolUse hooks for shell commands and PostToolUse hooks for file edits. A PreToolUse hook on the Bash tool receives the command as part of the hook input and can block execution if the command matches a dangerous pattern.

{
  "hooks": {
    "PreToolUse": [
      {
        "type": "command",
        "command": "node .claude/hooks/security-check.js"
      }
    ]
  }
}

The security check script parses stdin to extract the command and matches it against a deny list.

#!/usr/bin/env node

const input = JSON.parse(require('fs').readFileSync(0, 'utf-8'));

if (input.tool_name === 'Bash') {
  const command = input.tool_input.command;
  const dangerous = [
    /rm\s+-rf\s+\//,
    /drop\s+table/i,
    /chmod\s+777/,
    /curl.*\|\s*bash/
  ];

  for (const pattern of dangerous) {
    if (pattern.test(command)) {
      process.stderr.write(
        `Blocked dangerous command: ${command}\n`
      );
      process.exit(2);
    }
  }
}

process.exit(0);

The hook exits with code 2 if the command matches any pattern. Claude receives the stderr message and knows the command was blocked. The agent adjusts its approach without executing the dangerous operation.

Test runners fit better in Stop hooks than in PostToolUse hooks because a single edit can break tests in unrelated files. Running tests after every file write creates unnecessary execution overhead. Running them once when Claude declares the work complete gives a single validation point.

{
  "hooks": {
    "Stop": [
      {
        "type": "command",
        "command": "pnpm test --run 1>&2 || exit 2",
        "timeout": 60
      }
    ]
  }
}

The timeout field gives the test suite 60 seconds to complete. If tests fail, the stderr output returns to Claude with the failure details. The agent reads which tests broke and continues the turn to fix them.

Security scanning and test execution as validation hooks

Some teams run focused test suites in PostToolUse hooks when an edit touches specific directories. A hook script checks the edited file path and runs only the related test file if one exists.

#!/usr/bin/env node

const input = JSON.parse(require('fs').readFileSync(0, 'utf-8'));

if (input.tool_name === 'Write') {
  const filePath = input.tool_input.path;
  const testPath = filePath.replace(/\.ts$/, '.test.ts');

  const fs = require('fs');
  if (fs.existsSync(testPath)) {
    const { execSync } = require('child_process');
    try {
      execSync(`pnpm test ${testPath} --run`, {
        stdio: 'inherit'
      });
    } catch (error) {
      process.stderr.write(`Tests failed for ${testPath}\n`);
      process.exit(2);
    }
  }
}

process.exit(0);

This approach gives fast feedback on test failures without running the entire suite after every edit. The full suite still runs in the Stop hook to catch cross-file regressions.

Command vs Prompt vs Agent Hook Types: When to Use Each

Claude Code supports three primary hook types that differ in how they make validation decisions. Command hooks run shell scripts, prompt hooks send a question to a Claude model for single-turn evaluation, and agent hooks spawn subagents that can use tools to investigate before deciding.

Comparison of command, prompt, and agent hook types showing execution patterns and decision mechanisms

Command hooks (type: "command") execute a shell command or script that receives the hook event data on stdin and communicates results through exit codes and stdout. The script has full access to the repository and can run any validation tool. This type handles most validation needs.

Prompt hooks (type: "prompt") send the hook input to a Claude model along with a prompt that asks for a decision. The model returns a JSON object with ok and reason fields. Prompt hooks work when the validation logic is too complex for a static script but does not require inspecting files. The official documentation at https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks shows examples of prompt hooks that evaluate whether a commit message follows conventional commit format.

Agent hooks (type: "agent") spawn a subagent that can use tools like Read, Grep, and Glob to verify conditions before returning a decision. The agent receives a prompt and the hook input, investigates using up to 50 tool turns, and returns a structured ok/reason response. This type fits verification that requires inspecting actual file contents or running commands to determine state.

Hook type Decision mechanism Filesystem access When to use
Command Exit code and stdout Direct shell access Deterministic checks with existing tools
Prompt Single LLM call returning JSON None, evaluates input data only Complex logic that does not need file inspection
Agent Subagent with tools over 50 turns Read, Grep, Glob tools Verification requiring actual codebase state

Command hooks cost nothing beyond the compute time to run the validation tool. Prompt hooks consume tokens on every invocation. Agent hooks can consume significant tokens if they perform extensive file reads or searches. The claude-code-cost-control-production post covers budgeting strategies for hook token usage.

Most teams start with command hooks for linting, typechecking, and security scanning. Prompt hooks enter the workflow when validation requires understanding intent rather than matching patterns. Agent hooks appear in workflows that need to verify cross-file consistency or check that tests exist for new features.

The official documentation at https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks describes agent hooks as experimental with behavior and configuration subject to change. Production workflows that require stability prefer command hooks with explicit tool invocations over agent hooks that may behave differently across Claude Code versions.

Production Validation Patterns: Multi-Stage Hooks and additionalContext

Production repositories layer multiple validation hooks that run at different execution points and inject context that guides Claude toward correct patterns. The layering creates defense in depth where each hook enforces a different aspect of repository policy.

Multi-stage validation flow showing security check, linting, testing, and context injection

A typical production configuration includes PreToolUse hooks that block dangerous operations, PostToolUse hooks that validate file edits, Stop hooks that enforce completion criteria, and SubagentStart hooks that inject security guidelines into background tasks.

The additionalContext field in hook output adds text to Claude's context. A SubagentStart hook can inject repository-specific rules that apply only when a subagent runs, as documented at https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks.

{
  "hooks": {
    "SubagentStart": [
      {
        "type": "command",
        "command": "node .claude/hooks/inject-security-context.js"
      }
    ]
  }
}

The injection script reads security guidelines from a file and returns them in the hookSpecificOutput field.

#!/usr/bin/env node

const fs = require('fs');
const guidelines = fs.readFileSync(
  '.claude/security-guidelines.md',
  'utf-8'
);

const output = {
  hookSpecificOutput: {
    hookEventName: 'SubagentStart',
    additionalContext: guidelines
  }
};

process.stdout.write(JSON.stringify(output));
process.exit(0);

The subagent receives these guidelines in its initial context before its first prompt. This pattern keeps security rules in a single source file that applies automatically to all subagent work.

Hook precedence determines which settings file wins when the same hook appears in multiple locations. Managed settings override project settings, which override user settings. The claude-code-structured-output-zod post covers settings precedence in detail.

Teams that enforce validation hooks organization-wide place them in managed settings files that individual repositories cannot override. A managed Stop hook that requires passing tests applies to every project regardless of local configuration.

Production teams set onFailure: "block" on critical hooks to ensure that hook failures prevent the action even when the hook exits with a non-standard error code. This field appears in the hook handler object alongside type and command.

{
  "hooks": {
    "PreToolUse": [
      {
        "type": "command",
        "command": "node .claude/hooks/security-check.js",
        "onFailure": "block"
      }
    ]
  }
}

With onFailure set to "block", a hook that crashes or times out blocks the tool call instead of allowing it through. This setting matters for security hooks where a failure to validate should err on the side of blocking rather than permitting.

The multi-stage pattern combines fast feedback from PostToolUse hooks with comprehensive validation from Stop hooks. Linters and formatters run immediately after edits so Claude sees errors while the file is still in working memory. The full test suite runs once at the end to catch cross-file issues.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can validation hooks slow down Claude Code sessions significantly?

Hooks add latency proportional to the validation tool's runtime. A TypeScript typecheck that takes five seconds blocks the turn for five seconds. Fast linters like ESLint add under one second. Hooks run in parallel when multiple handlers exist for the same event, so a typecheck and a linter running together take the time of the slower tool, not the sum. The timeout field limits how long Claude Code waits before considering the hook failed.

What happens when a hook exits with code 2 but prints valid JSON to stdout?

Claude Code reads the JSON fields even when the hook blocks with exit code 2. Decision fields like permissionDecision: "block" apply, but the block from the exit code stands regardless. The JSON can add a structured reason or inject context, but it cannot override the block. The official documentation at https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks includes a table showing which fields apply on each exit code.

Do hooks configured in a repository apply to every developer who clones it?

Hooks in .claude/settings.json apply to everyone who works in the project after they accept the workspace trust dialog for that folder. Deny rules apply immediately. Allow rules and hooks wait for trust acceptance. Each developer's local machine respects the CLAUDE_CODE_STOP_HOOK_BLOCK_CAP setting, so teams that need higher caps document the required environment variable in the repository README.

Can agent-type hooks access environment variables and credentials?

Agent hooks spawn subagents that run in the same environment as the main session. Environment variables available to Claude Code are visible to the subagent. Credentials stored in environment variables or accessible via the system's credential store work in agent hooks the same way they work in command hooks. The subagent's tool set determines what it can access, and agent definitions can restrict tools to Read, Grep, and Glob to prevent modification.

How do hooks interact with Claude's prompt cache to avoid redundant context loading?

SubagentStart hooks that inject additionalContext place that content in the subagent's context before its first prompt. Claude Code reuses this context across requests via prompt caching as documented at https://code.claude.com/docs/en/prompt-caching. When the subagent's context undergoes auto-compaction and discards the injected copy, the next SubagentStart hook run injects it again, maintaining the guideline presence without breaking the cache.

Making Validation Hooks Repository Policy

Validation hooks enforce what prompts and documentation only suggest. A CLAUDE.md file that says "always run tests" depends on Claude interpreting and following that instruction. A Stop hook that exits with code 2 when tests fail makes the requirement deterministic.

The shift from guidance to policy changes how teams use AI coding tools in production. Repositories with comprehensive hook coverage allow less experienced developers to work with Claude because the hooks prevent the common mistakes that would otherwise require senior review. The claude-code-ci-agentic-review-test-auto-fix post shows how validation hooks integrate with CI to create a complete quality gate.

Hooks belong in the repository's .claude/settings.json file where they version-control alongside the code. Teams that adopt hooks as policy commit them to the main branch and document them in the project README. Developers who join the project inherit the validation rules when they accept workspace trust for the repository.

Organizations that enforce hooks across all repositories place them in managed settings. The hooks run whether or not individual projects configure them locally. This approach makes security scanning and compliance checks organization-wide policy rather than per-project configuration.

Validation hooks turn AI code generation from a supervised activity into a governed process. The agent operates within deterministic boundaries that hold regardless of how it reasons about the task.

Sources

  • Best practices for Claude Code - Claude Code Docs
  • Automate actions with hooks - Claude Code Docs

articles.title: How a Privacy-First Online Image Editor Works Without Uploading Your Photos (WebAssembly + On-Device AI)
articles.description: Most online image editors follow the same pattern. You pick a file, the browser uploads it, a server...
articles.body_html:
Most online image editors follow the same pattern. You pick a file, the browser uploads it, a server processes it, and a result comes back. It is simple to build, and it quietly means every photo you edit passes through someone else's infrastructure.

Browsers no longer need that arrangement. With WebAssembly, the Canvas API, and models that run on the client, the work of a photo editor, background remover, and image converter can happen on the device in front of you.

Akhouri Systems built APIC, a free browser-based editor, around that constraint. This article documents how a privacy-first online image editor is put together when nothing is uploaded, which trade-offs come with that design, and what users can reasonably expect from it.

Why "no upload" is an architecture decision, not a slogan

Privacy claims are cheap. Architecture is harder to fake.

When image processing happens on a server, privacy depends on policy: retention windows, access controls, and trust. When processing happens on the device, the image never leaves the browser tab, so there is nothing to retain and nothing to leak in transit.

That changes a few things for anyone building or choosing an online photo editor:

  • Sensitive images stay local. ID photos, product prototypes, client work, family pictures.
  • There is no upload queue. Speed depends on the user's hardware, not on server load.
  • Large files are no longer a bandwidth problem. A 40 MB photo does not need to travel anywhere.
  • Offline use becomes possible. After the first load, much of the tooling does not need a connection.

The cost is that the client has to do real work. The rest of this article is about how that work gets done.

The building blocks of a browser-based image editor

1. Canvas for live editing

Filters, brightness, contrast, saturation, blur, rotation, and flipping are all operations on pixel data, and the Canvas API handles them well. Because the work is local, sliders update the preview live with no round trip.

For more demanding color work, the same approach scales up. APIC's advanced panel includes a live histogram with shadow and highlight clipping indicators, RGB curves, an 8-band HSL mixer, three-way color grading, clarity, and grain. It can also export a 33×33×33 3D LUT as a .cube file, so a grade built in the browser can be reused in tools such as DaVinci Resolve, Premiere, or Photoshop.

One honest limitation: spatial effects like clarity, sharpening, vignette, and grain are not purely color transforms, so they cannot be baked into a LUT. The export covers the color-only parts of the grade.

2. WebAssembly for the heavy lifting

JavaScript alone is not the right tool for neural-network inference on a full-resolution photo. WebAssembly gives near-native execution inside the browser sandbox, which is what makes on-device AI practical. Every AI feature below runs this way.

3. Model caching so the cost is paid once

On-device AI has a real first-run cost: the model has to be downloaded. A well-behaved implementation downloads it once, caches it in the browser, and reuses it afterward.

For background removal, APIC offers three tiers so users can match the model to their device:

Tier First download Best for
Light about 5 MB Phones and quick cut-outs
Fast about 44 MB Everyday use
Maximum about 176 MB Highest accuracy, multi-pass, desktop-class hardware

After the first run, the model loads from cache, and nothing is sent to a server at any point. If a download fails, the app retries automatically and surfaces a retry button rather than failing silently.

On-device AI background removal

Background removal is a segmentation problem: classify every pixel as subject or not, then turn that mask into transparency. Doing this locally means the full-resolution original stays in memory on the user's device.

Two details matter for quality:

  • Edge refinement. Raw masks tend to leave hard or jagged boundaries. A refinement pass smooths them.
  • Color-fringe removal. Pixels at the edge often carry color from the old background. Removing that spill is the difference between a cut-out that looks pasted on and one that looks natural.

For output, keep transparency by exporting to PNG or WebP. JPEG has no alpha channel, so it will flatten the result.

Removing objects with on-device inpainting

Object removal is a different problem from background removal. You paint over what you want gone, such as a stray person, a sign, or a blemish, and a model fills the region so it blends with its surroundings.

APIC uses two engines, which illustrates a useful design pattern, graceful degradation:

  • MI-GAN (about 28 MB) is lightweight enough to run on phones.
  • LaMa, a large Fourier-convolution inpainting network (about 208 MB), gives the most accurate fills for big or complex areas, and is intended for desktop-class devices.

If a model cannot load, the tool steps down automatically: Ultra, then MI-GAN, then a quick patch fill. Only the area around the brush is processed, and the fill is color-matched and re-grained to match the original photo, which avoids the telltale "too clean" patch.

A practical tip that applies to any inpainting tool: paint slightly outside the object, so shadows and reflections are covered too.

Compressing an image to an exact file size

A common real-world task is hitting an upload limit: "under 200 KB" for a form, "under 1 MB" for a CMS. Guessing a quality slider is tedious.

A better approach is to search across quality levels and keep the highest one that fits the target. APIC's compress image online tool works this way. If the target is impossible at any quality, it reduces the dimensions as a fallback and reports the actual resulting size rather than pretending it hit the number.

Resizing without the muddy look

A single large downscale is a classic source of soft, blurry results. Resampling in several half-size steps preserves more detail, and every pixel is recomputed at full quality. The tool leaves the image uncropped and unstretched unless you deliberately change the aspect ratio. You can specify exact pixels or a percentage, with an aspect-ratio lock.

Converting formats: PNG, JPG, WebP, BMP, ICO, PDF

Format conversion is where most people start. The practical rules of thumb:

  • PNG: lossless, supports transparency. Best after background removal.
  • JPEG: small files, no transparency. Best for photos.
  • WebP: small files and transparency. A strong default for the web.
  • BMP: uncompressed.
  • ICO: app and favicon icons.
  • PDF: a single-page document from an image.

All six conversions run locally, so converting a private document scan does not involve a third party.

Social media sizes without the guesswork

Every platform has its own dimensions for profile pictures, banners, covers, posts, and stories, and they change. APIC's Social tab holds exact-size presets for 15 networks, including Instagram, YouTube, Facebook, X, TikTok, LinkedIn, Pinterest, Snapchat, Threads, Bluesky, Discord, Twitch, and Spotify.

Two features make this more useful than a list of numbers: safe-zone guides that show where a platform crops or covers your image, and ZIP export so you can download every size for a network at once.

Batch processing and an offline desktop version

Single-image tools only go so far. A batch studio takes many images through background removal, resizing, compression, and conversion in one pass and returns one ZIP, again processed entirely on the device.

For people who want no browser involved at all, there is also a Windows desktop build that runs fully offline with the edit, convert, and compress tools.

A note on accounts and what data is involved

Being specific here matters, because "no upload" can be misread. The editing tools work without an account. Signing in with Google is optional, and it uses your name, email, and photo for the account. The images themselves are not uploaded.
We request you to signing in APIC even when it is optional because it will help us to send you guys update emails.

Frequently asked questions

What is a privacy-first online image editor?
It is an editor that processes images on your own device instead of sending them to a server. Editing, conversion, compression, resizing, and AI features all run in the browser.

Can AI background removal run without uploading the photo?
Yes. A segmentation model can run in the browser through WebAssembly. The model downloads once, is cached, and processes the image locally.

Is there a free online photo editor that keeps images on-device?
APIC is one. It is free, has no paid tiers, and runs its tools locally.

How do I compress an image to a specific size in KB?
Use a compressor that searches for the highest quality under your target size, such as the Compress tool in APIC.

Which format keeps a transparent background?
PNG and WebP. JPEG does not support transparency.

Does it work on phones?
Yes. Lighter model tiers exist specifically for phones, with heavier ones recommended for desktop hardware.

Where to try it

If you want to see these techniques in practice, APIC is a free online photo editor, background remover, and image converter that runs in your browser, with no uploads of your images.

We are interested in how other engineers approach on-device processing. Which tasks have you moved from the server to the client, and what held you back? Share your experience in the comments.

About Akhouri Systems: we build software with privacy and performance as design constraints. Follow our dev.to organization for more engineering write-ups.

WE BUILD WHAT OTHERS FORGOT TO FIX

articles.title: PB&J: The Story of the Three People Behind DEV
articles.description: Let me tell you a story about a sandwich 🥪   Open the About page on DEV and you will find...
articles.body_html:
Let me tell you a story about a sandwich 🥪

Open the About page on DEV and you will find this sentence:

Ben ( @ben ) is the B. Peter ( @peter ) is the P. Jess ( @jess ) is the J. A peanut butter and jelly sandwich, made out of three people.

I read that line and had one of those "wait, how did this actually happen?" moments. I knew DEV started as a Twitter account. I knew it got big. I knew it was open source. But I had no idea how three people ended up running it together, who did what, or how the whole thing started in the first place.

So I went and read everything I could find. Podcast transcripts. AMAs. Old progress reports. Funding announcements. A college newspaper article from 2009 (yes, really). And what I found was a better story than I expected, with a missing date, a mystery typo, a Twitter account with 108,000 followers, and a plot twist in February 2026.

This post is that story, told in order, so you do not have to piece it together like I did.

The rules I am following


Before we start, a few promises, because this kind of article is easy to get wrong.
  • I did not talk to any of them. Everything here comes from things the founders and companies made public. When someone told a story about themselves, I say "Ben said" or "Jess wrote." I have not checked their personal stories against anyone else, and I say so when it matters.
  • When I am guessing, I will say "I am guessing." A few dates have to be worked out from other numbers. Those are marked as my math, not as official facts.
  • When nobody has said something, I will not invent it. There are real gaps, like deal prices and exact titles. I will point at the gap and move on.

Who is who (so you do not get lost)

Here is the cast, so you can come back to this if you get confused:

Ben Halpern started the Twitter account that became DEV. He is the funny one, the one who writes most of the announcements, and the one most people think of first.

Peter Kim Frank (sometimes just "Peter Frank") is Ben's earlier business partner. He is the one on the business side, and he has been running online projects since high school.

Jess Lee met Ben a bit later, joined the project in 2016, and runs operations. Jess uses they/them pronouns, which Jess shared in a post in March 2026, so that is what I use here. When I quote older interviews that say "she," I leave them as they were.

And two words people mix up constantly:

DEV is the community, the website at dev.to.

Forem is the open-source software DEV runs on (and the company that grew around it). DEV is the first Forem. We will get to why that matters.

Okay. Ready? Let's go back to the beginning. Or at least, as far back as the record goes.

Table of Contents

  • Chapter 1: A guy with a second Twitter account 🐦
  • Chapter 2: The business partner who started young
  • Chapter 3: The person who did not know what a startup was
  • Chapter 4: From a joke account to an actual website
  • Chapter 5: The decision, and the date that cannot be right 🕵️
  • Chapter 6: The year everything grew 17 times
  • Chapter 7: The day the code went public 🔓
  • Chapter 8: Money arrives, and the office disappears
  • Chapter 9: DEV gets a big sibling called Forem 🌍
  • Interlude: how DEV actually felt to run
  • Who does what, in plain English
  • Chapter 10: February 18, 2026 🚀
  • Where the three are now
  • Epilogue: the ten-year promise

Chapter 1: A guy with a second Twitter account 🐦

Our story starts with Ben, and Ben starts with a website he built at about 13.

In a Learn to Code With Me interview, Ben said he grew up fascinated with HTML and built websites as a hobby. His first real application, he told Developer Tea, was a fantasy sports site. He has also said he has been an entrepreneur in some form "since I was 12." (That one is from the Changelog interview.)

Then the plot gets less straight. He took some computer science in college, dropped out of that track, and graduated with a marketing degree. He interned somewhere and did not enjoy it. So he thought about comedy writing, spent a summer in New York living with his brother and trying to meet people in TV, and found there was not much of a path.

Meanwhile he had stopped believing programming was for him. A professor had discouraged him, and he has admitted to imposter syndrome. Then around 2012, a friend in a college cafeteria pointed him at Ruby on Rails while Ben was thinking about an app idea. That was it. He got back into programming "for real," he said, and he loved it.

He also overdid it. He has talked about 17 and 18 hour coding days, and about getting shingles twice from overwork. So when you read the rest of this story and think "these people worked a lot," keep that in mind. At least one of them has told you how much.

Where does the Twitter account come in?

Here is the part I like.

Ben's own profile says he is "a Canadian software developer who thinks he's funny." In his 2017 interview on Developer Tea, he explained that he made a second Twitter account, The Practical Dev, so he could post about programming without annoying the friends who followed his personal one.

Notice what that is. It is not a business plan. It is a guy trying not to spam his friends.

At first the account shared programming articles. Then he added his own opinions and jokes, and that is when it "really started taking off." He also said his marketing degree helped him understand how to grow it, so the degree he thought he wasted came in handy.

He told Learn to Code With Me that jokes are only about 5 percent of what the account posts. Which is funny, given what people remember it for.

The Changelog hosts asked him about the O'Reilly-style parody book covers. Ben called them "the first major chapter" of the story. If you have ever seen a fake programming book cover with an animal and an absurd title, that style of joke is part of what made the account spread.

When did this start?

Ben does not give a birthday for the account in the interviews I read. But the founders' first progress report, from November 2017, says it had been 1,174 days since the account started. If you count back from November 1, 2017, that lands around August 15, 2014.

That is my math, not an official date. I will do the same trick with other dates in a minute.

By April 2017, when Ben spoke to Developer Tea, the account had about 108,000 followers. In an earlier interview he said "just under 100,000." Each tweet, he said, sent a few thousand people to dev.to.

So hold that picture: a joke account, three years old, with a big and loyal audience, and a guy who has just realized the audience could be a community.

Right. Now meet the second person.

↑ Back to contents

Chapter 2: The business partner who started young

If you want to understand Peter, start with a college newspaper from 2009.

The Wesleyan Argus ran a story in February 2009 about a freshman in the class of 2012, Peter Frank, who was running a website called CollegeACB from his dorm room. ACB stands for anonymous confession board. It was a network of roughly 500 boards for different schools, and the Wesleyan one was the busiest.

Here is what the article says, and I am only repeating it:

  • CollegeACB had been started about a year earlier by two other students. Peter took it over about three months before the article, after they said they wanted a successor.
  • He had already been running a small company, Sumdae LLC, since his sophomore year of high school in 2005. It was built on registering domain names.

Chapter 4: From a joke account to an actual website

So how does a Twitter account turn into a website?

Slowly, and with a few accidents.

Ben told Developer Tea that he first registered practicaldev.com, and later switched to the shorter dev.to. According to the November 2017 progress report, the dev.to domain was bought about 550 days before the post, which lands around April 30, 2016. (My arithmetic again.)

Ben also said that around this time he decided to take the project seriously and build a real programming platform, while keeping most of his creativity pointed at the Twitter account. That sounds right to me. The account was the thing people loved, and the site had to earn its place next to it.

His goal, as he put it on the Changelog, was to fix the things he had been making fun of: career chaos, inconsistent learning resources, and a lack of tools and places for developers to gather. In other words, the jokes were the symptoms and the site was the treatment.

The first article was an interview with DHH

This is my favorite detail in the whole story.

Ben told the Changelog that the first thing published on dev.to was an interview with DHH, the creator of Rails, timed around the Rails 5 release. How did a guy with a joke account land an interview with one of the most famous names in the Ruby world? Ben said he emailed him, asked nicely, and made it easy to say yes. That is the whole trick.

He lined up more interviews with other open-source people after that. The original idea was a high-touch, interview-driven site. Then, he said, audience feedback pushed it in a different direction: a place where anyone could write about anything software-related, with an enforced code of conduct.

If you have used DEV, you know which version won.

The login button nobody could find

Here is a detail that made me laugh. Ben said the login feature was hidden in the footer at first. Hidden. And people found it anyway and logged in in large numbers, which surprised him.

A few other early choices are worth knowing, because they explain why DEV felt the way it did:

Sign-up needed an existing Twitter or GitHub account.

Ben called that a low barrier for most developers. It also gave the team some history to look at, since a brand new account that mirrors a banned one can be flagged as spam or harassment. If you had neither account, he said, they worked with you.

Writers could cross-post.

Jess said an early feature let creators import posts through RSS while keeping their canonical URL, so people could bring their blog posts with them without losing credit.

The team reached out to writers by hand.

And the Twitter account amplified quality content from writers who were not famous, which Jess says helped DEV grow.

The technical choices were deliberately dull.

Ben picked Rails and called it "boring and old" on the Changelog, which he meant as a compliment. In his 2021 Indie Hackers AMA, he said the choice of "solid, stable technology" was the best early decision they made. He also said he had been using Node at his day job and wanted an environment he liked more.

One more quote I like from Developer Tea:

Ben was making the case that a person explaining a tool in their own words is often more useful than the project's official docs. That is basically DEV's entire pitch in one sentence.

The worry that almost stopped it

Now for the quiet tension in this chapter.

Ben told the Changelog he was protective of the project. He worried that turning it into a business could ruin it. He wanted everything on the site to be "additive," not extractive.

What changed his mind? A conversation with Saron Yitbarek, the founder of CodeNewbie, who had just left her job to run CodeNewbie full-time. Seeing that, Ben said, helped him believe the project could be a real business.

And then he made a promise: he committed to giving the project ten years. In his 2021 Indie Hackers AMA, he repeated that as advice for anyone building open-source companies: commit to a ten-year horizon, even through the slow years.

Hold on to that ten-year promise. We will come back to it at the end.

How big was it, at the very start?

We have exactly one number from the early days, and it comes from the progress report. The team ended October 2016 with 69,259 sessions for the month.

That is not nothing, but it is small. A year later, the same report would say something very different. We will get there. First, we need to answer the question that has been hanging over this whole story.

How did three people become a company?

In the Dec 2017 AMA, he put it more simply: when dev.to "could be bigger than a two-person side project," that is when they brought Peter on. And, with a joke, he said, "Having three partners is great for breaking ties in arguments."

Wait. January 2016?

Here is where the detective work starts.

The progress report says the three agreed to combine "in January 2016." I read that line, then read the post's own numbers, and something did not add up.

Let me lay it out, because this is the kind of thing you can only trust if you can check it yourself:

  1. Jess had not joined yet in January 2016. By the report's day counts, Jess joined 485 days before November 1, 2017. That is about July 2016. So Jess could not have been preparing to go full-time six months before even starting.
  2. Ten months does not match 2016. The report says the merged team had been together for "about ten months." Ten months before November 2017 is roughly January 2017.
  3. The report says they were dreaming of it a year earlier. It also says that in October 2016 they were "dreaming of" working on dev.to full-time. That only makes sense if the decision came after October 2016.

So my reading is that "2016" is a typo for 2017. And I am fairly sure, because more sources lean the same way:

  • In the AMA Peter posted on December 20, 2017, he says he has worked on dev.to with Ben and Jess "since last January."
  • Peter's DEV profile says he joined on January 3, 2017.
  • In the same thread, Ben says they brought Peter on when dev.to "could be bigger than a two-person side project earlier this year." (Earlier this year, as in 2017.)
  • Jess, in the 2021 interview, says the team went full-time in 2017.

I want to be honest about what this is. It is an inference from the report's internal numbers and the founders' other statements. I did not find anyone correcting the original post. But I would be surprised if the answer were anything other than January 2017.

A coincidence I cannot explain

While I was working on this, I found something interesting. DEV has a Product Hunt page with a launch date of January 2, 2017. The ranking of number one for the day is credited to January 3.

So the Product Hunt launch, Peter's DEV join date, and the "January" decision all happen in the same few days.

I want to be very clear: I have no evidence that these are connected. It may just be a coincidence of timing. I also cannot fully explain why the page shows two dates for the launch. Time zones and the way Product Hunt displays launches might explain a one-day gap, but that is a guess, and the upvote counts on the page were ambiguous, so I am leaving them out. The founders do not say the launch caused anything. I will not say it for them.

What the report does not tell us

This is one of the places where the record goes quiet, so let me list what is missing, because it is a lot:

  • Who suggested the merger.
  • How equity was split, or what anyone was paid.
  • How titles were handed out.
  • Who came up with "PBJ" and why it stuck.

I looked for these elsewhere and found nothing. That does not mean the answers do not exist. It means they have not been made public, as far as I can tell.
