One line from that thread keeps coming back to me, because it is a trade-off many founders would recognize. You "can't do any of this in an authoritarian way," he said, and you "have to frustrate some people in order to stick to your personal values." And on decentralization, he said it has to be made invisible through good UX, because most people move toward usable, delightful experiences.

What a "Forem" looked like in practice

Jess's 2021 interview gives some real-world examples.

  • Forem also powers the CodeNewbie Community.
  • Companies like Microsoft Azure and AWS now publish on DEV through organization accounts. Jess called that a "plan for opportunism" moment, a principle that guided their career.
  • New Relic launched "The Relicans" on Forem and chose the hosted version instead of self-hosting.
  • The company produces two podcasts: DevDiscuss (Jess and Ben) and DevNews (Saron Yitbarek and Josh Puetz).
  • Jess leads Nevertheless She Coded, a campaign tied to International Women's Day on March 8. In 2021 it was in its fifth year.

The one sentence that clears this up

So here is the simplest way to hold it in your head:


DEV is a place. Forem is the software that makes places like it.

DEV is the first and biggest Forem. When one source says "the co-founders of DEV" and another says "the co-founders of Forem," they mean the same three people at different points in the company's history.

And what happened to Forem as a business after 2021? I could not find reliable public numbers on customers, instance counts or revenue. So I will not make any up.

↑ Back to contents

Interlude: how DEV actually felt to run

Before the big news, let me step out of the timeline for a moment, because a few things the founders said explain why DEV felt different from other places. This is the "how," and it helps make the "what happened next" make sense.

The community was the point

When the Changelog hosts asked Ben for the secret sauce, he said it was merging "fundamental human community needs with practical software development needs." He described DEV as something like Medium for developers, with portfolio features like showing your GitHub projects, and, he said, no recruiter spam. Members could host posts on their own blogs and cross-post.

He told one small story that stuck with me. A member had shut down a language project he had worked on for years, and the community showed up to support him. That is not the kind of thing you plan for in a product spec.

Moderation, in their own words

DEV's approach to moderation comes up in almost every interview, so it is worth laying out.

Ben said DEV's main difference from Twitter was that it moderates at all. He called the platform pro free speech "in every way that's practical," but said other platforms are naive about human behavior and how some groups are more vulnerable than others. He also said Twitter did not treat harassment as a problem until the outside world called it out.

The tools he described:

  • A code of conduct that the team enforces.
  • Crowdsourced reports that can escalate quickly to admins.
  • Private messaging and small chat rooms that act as "break-out rooms" away from big public threads.
  • Account history checks, so a brand-new account mirroring a banned one can be flagged.

He also noted that harassment often arrives after a post gets shared on Hacker News or Reddit. And he said the team wrote down the DEV voice in documents, with guidance like "Say this, not this," because he handled most of the communication himself and the voice had to scale.

Jess described the same philosophy in 2021. Moderation should be values-driven and human-led, not outsourced, and people who cross the line get banned. A friendly, welcoming tone lowers the barrier for newer developers. And "repeat questions are totally valid," Jess said, because the answers change as technology changes.

That is how two founders describe it. I did not find an independent audit of how well it worked in practice.

The tech, kept boring on purpose

On the engineering side, Ben's description on the Changelog is a masterclass in not overcomplicating things.

  • About 90 percent of traffic is served from the CDN, he said, so most page loads do not touch Rails at all.
  • Pages are served without personal information. Anything specific to you loads in a quick asynchronous call and is cached in local storage.
  • The CDN is Fastly, and he praised its instant purge, with cache clears taking roughly 100 to 200 milliseconds.
  • Algolia handles search, so a user in a place like Tokyo gets fast responses from nearby nodes.
  • Ben described using Varnish Configuration Language on the edge, which is a less common approach, and he gave a RailsConf talk about it.
  • Building for edge caching from the start mattered, he said. Retrofitting it later would have been "ten times tougher."

In 2021, he told Indie Hackers that Postgres is "the only technology in the stack that is really precious." He also said the team did not get too enamored with static site generators.

As always, treat those numbers as what the team said at the time. They may not match today.

Not everyone is a fan

A ShiftMag piece on the MLH deal collects community concerns: that DEV's content quality has slipped, with repetitive beginner posts, search-driven writing and AI-generated articles crowding out deeper work. Those are outside opinions, not measurements, and the piece notes some of the complaints predate the current AI wave.

I mention this because a fair story about a community should include the people who are not thrilled with it.

↑ Back to contents

Who does what, in plain English

By now you might be wondering how three people with such different skills actually split the work. The founders have described it themselves, so here is that, with dates attached, because titles change.

Founder How the role was described As of Where it came from
Ben Halpern Co-CEO: long-term vision, product decisions, community leadership Nov 2019 Series A announcement
Peter Kim Frank Co-CEO: partnerships, growth, new opportunities Nov 2019 Same announcement
Jess Lee COO: internal operations, hiring plans, team organization, compensation committee Nov 2019 Same announcement
All three "Forem's co-founders" who lead DEV, no individual titles Current About page dev.to/about

I also found an April 2021 archived copy of the About page that still listed Ben and Peter as co-CEOs and Jess as COO. The current page uses only the group description. So I do not claim any current title for any of them.

The self-descriptions fit those titles nicely:

  • Ben calls himself abstract, chaotic and disorganized.
  • Jess is the organized, disciplined one, per Ben. In 2021, Jess also described an open-source community manager, Christina Gorton, who brings community requests to the engineers.
  • Peter calls himself the least technical, and handles strategy, operations and much of the business and legal side.

You can also see the split in public, though that only tells you about public output, not about who worked hardest. Ben writes most of the announcements and product posts under his own name. Jess wrote the progress report, the open-source thank-you and the remote-work post. And Peter's DEV profile is quieter, with more personal side projects and the occasional post for The DEV Team.

↑ Back to contents

Chapter 10: February 18, 2026 🚀

For a long time, the story of DEV is about growth, and openness, and community. Then in February 2026, it gets a new chapter.

On February 18, 2026, Major League Hacking, known for its student hackathons, announced that it had acquired DEV. MLH's own post, Major League Hacking acquires DEV, says it plainly: "Major League Hacking has acquired DEV (dev.to)." The founders posted their own version the same day, signed "PBJ."

A New Chapter: DEV is Joining Forces with Major League Hacking (MLH)
Ben Halpern
Ben Halpern
for The DEV Team
Feb 18

A New Chapter: DEV is Joining Forces with Major League Hacking (MLH)

#news #devto #hackathon #discuss
445 reactions Comments 125 comments
6 min read

A press release carried the same news. ShiftMag wrote its reaction piece two days later.

What the companies confirmed

I am going to keep this section very clean, because it is where rumors love to grow.

DEV is now part of MLH.

DEV's post says "DEV is officially part of the MLH organization." The wording differs between the two sides ("joining forces" in DEV's post, "acquired" in MLH's), and DEV's own post does not use the word acquisition, but MLH's post and the press release do.

Size.

MLH describes DEV as having more than 3 million developers and MLH as reaching more than 1.5 million across nearly 100 countries, for roughly 5 million together. Those are MLH's figures.

The team stays.

DEV's post says "The original team isn't going anywhere" and that CodeNewbie remains a core part of DEV. It promises a revamped Trusted Moderator program and the return of some past community initiatives, which it calls "immediate, community-first improvements," and not sales initiatives.

Forem continues.

The post says MLH and DEV will remain stewards of Forem, that the partnership will clarify the difference between DEV and Forem, and that Forem will be able to operate more independently. It also admits the team does not have the Forem arrangement "entirely worked out," with news promised in "the coming months." MLH's post says something similar: it is working toward a structure that supports Forem's independence.

Ben has a new role.

He wrote that he was "already hard at work in my new role at MLH." The post does not say what the role is.

A livestream.

A Q&A with Ben, Jess, Peter and MLH's leaders was set for February 19, 2026. I did not watch it, so anything said there is outside this article.

What nobody has said (yet)

I looked hard for these and could not find any of them:

  • The price, the structure (cash, stock, both), the closing date, or a valuation. If you see a number for the deal, it is not sourced.
  • Titles, equity or pay for Jess and Peter after the deal, or Ben's exact role.
  • Who owns and governs Forem now.
  • Any change to DEV's domain, pricing, data handling or staffing, beyond the "original team" line.

The community's first reaction

The ShiftMag piece calls it too early to judge. It collects worries (low-effort content, a site that could turn into a marketing channel for hackathon projects) and some optimism that MLH could help if it curates strong engineering writing. Those are the opinions of the people quoted. I am not adding a verdict of my own.

How Jess described it

The most personal account I found is from Jess. In a post titled A year of change and persistence, dated March 31 (no year on the page, but the WeCoded 2026 banner makes 2026 the obvious reading), Jess called the acquisition "a moment of immense pride that also marked a profound transition."

A Year of Change and Persistence
WeCoded 2026: Echoes of Experience 💜
Jess Lee
Jess Lee
Mar 31

A Year of Change and Persistence

#devchallenge #wecoded #career #dei
114 reactions Comments 33 comments
4 min read

They described what changed. For years, Jess, Peter and Ben ran the company as a trio, and their identities were closely tied to it. After the acquisition, Jess went from holding final responsibility for decisions to being one voice in a larger organization, which means "leading through influence rather than direct authority."

The post also covers things beyond the deal: Jess's decision to use they/them pronouns, the climate for women and underrepresented people in tech, a visit to an MLH hackathon for women in computing, and a line I think is worth repeating, that developers "are the architects of the interfaces the world lives in." It is worth reading in full if you care about the people behind DEV and not just the deal.

↑ Back to contents

Where the three are now

This is the part most likely to go stale, so every line has the date I last checked it. I checked the public pages below on November 10, 2026. DEV leaves the year off recent posts, so where I give a year for a post, I inferred it from the page's own last-updated date.

Ben. His DEV profile still says "Co-founder of DEV" and Community Curator. Recent posts include the Meme Monday series and a series called Daily Context, with the latest in October 2026 (profile last updated October 21). Ben said in February that he was already in a new role at MLH. Neither the post nor the profile names it, so I do not either.

Jess. Jess's profile lists them as Founder-in-Residence at Major League Hacking and co-founder at DEV. I did not find a description of what the Founder-in-Residence role involves.

Peter. His profile says he works "across all things partnerships, sales, biz dev at DEV and MLH." He is still posting: a welcome thread and a post for The DEV Team in 2025, and personal projects through 2026, the latest I saw dated October 13.

Ben Halpern

A Canadian software developer who thinks he’s funny.

Jess Lee

Building DEV with everyone here. What do we have if not community?

Peter Kim Frank

Working across all things partnerships, sales, biz dev at DEV and MLH 🤝️

The three together. The About page, last updated November 9, 2026 according to its metadata, still says DEV is led by Forem's co-founders and that DEV "has joined forces with Major League Hacking." So as of that date, all three are presented publicly as still connected to DEV and MLH. What I cannot tell you is who reports to whom, who holds which title, or whether anyone is in an operating or advisory role.

↑ Back to contents

Epilogue: the ten-year promise

Let me end where I told you we would end.

Back in 2018, Ben told the Changelog he had committed to giving the project ten years. In 2021, he said the same thing to Indie Hackers as advice for open-source founders: commit to a ten-year horizon, even through slow years. If you start counting from when dev.to began in 2016, or from when the three went full-time in 2017, ten years lands in 2026 or 2027.

And that is exactly where the story is now. DEV is part of MLH. Ben is still publicly connected to it, and says he is hard at work in a new role. That is my observation, not something any of them said, and I will not stretch it into a prediction.

What the story shows

Here is what I take away, and I tried to tie each point to something the sources actually show.

  1. The audience came first. The Twitter account began around August 2014 and the dev.to domain arrived roughly twenty months later. By the time the site had 69,259 sessions in October 2016, there was already a crowd to invite.
  2. They combined instead of competing for Ben's attention. Per Jess's report, Ben's conflict between a CTO job and dev.to got resolved by putting three people and their resources together.
  3. Titles came late. The founders said in 2019 that they had barely discussed titles before the Series A.
  4. Open source was a choice, and the community showed up. Contributors made real changes, and some got hired.
  5. Funding stayed modest for a long time. Friends and family in 2017, about $950,000 in 2018, an $11.5 million Series A in 2019, with the three keeping a majority of the board.
  6. The revenue they described stayed small and close to the community. Job listings, sponsors, memberships, and later Forem services.

And a thing I want to say plainly: so many separate pieces had to line up for a Twitter account to turn into a company. An audience. A partner willing to take on a conflict of interest. A third co-founder ready to go full-time. And investors who liked an open-source plan. Each of those is documented. What happened in all the years in between is the part only the founders can fully tell, and I did not talk to them.

The timeline, on one page

If you got lost anywhere above, here is everything with a date, in order. "Approximate" means I worked it out from a source's numbers.

Date What happened
About 2013 Ben and Peter begin working together, after meeting on Reddit (from Ben's and Peter's comments)
About Aug 2014 The Practical Dev Twitter account starts (approximate, from the 2017 report)
Dec 27, 2015 Join date shown on Ben's DEV profile, earlier than the domain date below; Ben first used practicaldev.com, which may explain it (my guess)
About Apr 2016 dev.to domain bought (approximate)
About Jul 2016 Jess joins the project (approximate)
Oct 2016 69,259 sessions for the month
Jan 2017 Product Hunt launch (Jan 2 or 3), Peter joins (Jan 3), the three likely combine efforts (my reading of the report)
Apr 2017 Ben cites about 108,000 Twitter followers
Nov 1, 2017 First monthly progress report, 1,203,378 October sessions
Dec 20, 2017 Peter's AMA on DEV
Jan 2018 Sustaining memberships announced
Aug 8, 2018 Codebase goes open source
Oct 2018 Roughly $950k raised (as described later)
Aug 8, 2019 One year of open source
Oct 10, 2019 Team goes fully distributed
Nov 7, 2019 $11.5M Series A led by Mayfield
May 28, 2020 Forem named
Jul 20, 2021 Forem self-host officially supported
Feb 18, 2026 MLH announces it has acquired DEV

The things I still do not know
  • Who came up with "PBJ," and when.
  • Whether "January 2016" in the 2017 report was a typo for 2017. I think so, for the reasons above, but I have no confirmation from the authors.
  • The terms of the 2018 round, the Series A valuation, and any figure for the MLH deal.
  • What Ben, Jess and Peter do at MLH, and how Forem will be structured.
  • Whether the community's worries about content quality play out once MLH's plans take shape. ShiftMag says it is too early to tell, and I agree.

Your turn 🙂


If you have been on DEV a while, when did you first notice the "PBJ" sign-off, and what did you think it meant? And if you were writing a note to the next team that takes this on, what would you tell them to protect?

Tell me in the comments.

articles.title: How Tracing Contours Cut My rMQR SVG Path by 67%
articles.description: Whenever I needed vector artwork to survive resizing, rotation, or a trip to the print shop, I had a...
articles.body_html:
Whenever I needed vector artwork to survive resizing, rotation, or a trip to the print shop, I had a familiar routine. Open Illustrator, select the pieces, click Unite in Pathfinder, and get on with the job.

Then I caught myself doing that to an rMQR Code generated by my own JavaScript library.

The generator had already worked out exactly which modules were dark. It exported an SVG. And there I was, opening Illustrator to join the pieces it had just drawn. What was I doing?

In my earlier posts, I was trying to save space in the Kanji lookup table and then in the encoded text. This time, the matrix was already finished. I wanted to draw it with less SVG and stop reaching for Pathfinder.

A dot here, a fence over there

The obvious way to draw a QR Code is one square per dark module. It is easy to generate and easy to check. It also means that a solid block of dark modules is described as a pile of little squares, each with its own position and edges.

I tried the usual ways of making the markup smaller. Move the fill color to the root element. Define a square once and reference it with <use>. Eventually I settled on one <path> with a little rectangular subpath for each dark module.

Then I started joining neighbors. If five dark modules sit next to each other in a row, draw one rectangle five modules wide. Do the same down the columns, compare the two strings, and keep the shorter one.

That helped, but the rectangles still met along internal edges. In some of my export and rendering workflows, I could see hairline seams after scaling or transforming artwork built from touching shapes. Sometimes the squares looked like dots. Sometimes the longer strips looked like a picket fence. The geometry said the pieces met. The rendered result occasionally disagreed.

My usual workaround was to make the pieces a tiny bit bigger so they overlapped. The idea felt familiar from print. In offset printing, trapping creates small overlaps to compensate for misregistration. In my SVG, I was borrowing the overlap trick to hide a seam. Adobe’s guide to trapping

It worked well enough that I kept doing it. Then came that next trip to Illustrator. I already had the grid in JavaScript, including the answer to whether every pair of neighbors belonged to the same dark region. Why was I asking a vector editor to figure that out again?

Four ways to draw the same grid

I used the same 43 × 13 rMQR matrix for all four versions. It has 283 dark modules. All three rectangle passes start at the bottom right. The per-module and horizontal passes go row by row, while the vertical pass goes column by column.

Method Subpaths Characters in d
One square per module 283 3,676
Merge vertical runs 152 1,978
Merge horizontal runs 159 2,073
Trace the contours 17 1,195

The counts cover the d attribute alone, before compression. All four methods use z to close the final side. The 17 contour subpaths include the cutouts.

Tracing reduced the path string by about 67% compared with individual squares and 40% compared with the shorter grouped path. For this grid, that was the vertical pass.

What those paths actually draw

All four paths below draw the same solid 3 × 2 block, from (0, 0) to (3, 2). Each starts at the bottom-right corner, (3, 2), and follows the same clockwise direction.

One square per module Each of the six dark modules gets its own rectangle.

M3,2h-1v-1h1zM2,2h-1v-1h1zM1,2h-1v-1h1zM3,1h-1v-1h1zM2,1h-1v-1h1zM1,1h-1v-1h1z

Vertical runs The two dark modules in each column form one rectangle.

M3,2h-1v-2h1zM2,2h-1v-2h1zM1,2h-1v-2h1z

Horizontal runs The three dark modules in each row form one rectangle.

M3,2h-3v-1h3zM3,1h-3v-1h3z

Contours The boundary of the whole block forms one closed rectangle.

m3,2h-3v-2h3z

The fill is identical in every case. The difference is how many edges we ask SVG to draw.

Left to right: six squares, three vertical runs, two horizontal runs, one contour.

Parts × modules per part: 6 × 1 = 3 × 2 = 2 × 3 = 1 × 6 = 6 modules.

The difference shows up when a shape extends in both directions. A solid 3 × 2 block takes six squares, two horizontal strips, or three vertical strips. Its outline is one rectangle. The grid already tells us where that outline is.

Keep the edges that matter

For each dark module, contourPath checks its four neighbors. A side belongs to the boundary if it faces a light module or the outside of the matrix. When two dark modules touch, their shared side contributes nothing to the outline.

Left to right: two modules with directed edges; their shared side highlighted; the remaining outer boundary. The opposing edges on the shared side are removed.

I store each surviving edge at its starting vertex on the grid. The four directions fit in a bit mask. The numbers beside the arrows in the diagram are their bit values.

0001  =  1  |  right
0010  =  2  |  down
0100  =  4  |  left
1000  =  8  |  up

A vertex can have more than one outgoing edge, so several bits can be set at once.

At the shared vertex, two edges point out:

0100 | 0001   = 0101
left | right
   4 | 1      = 5

Each edge points in the direction that keeps the dark area on its right. That little rule determines which way the walk goes around the outside and which way it goes around a cutout.

Follow the edges into closed paths

Starting at a vertex with an unused edge, the walk takes that edge, clears its bit, and pushes the next vertex onto a stack. When it reaches a vertex with no outgoing edges left, it pops back along the stack and records the route in reverse.

The stack earns its keep when two dark squares meet at a corner. There can be more than one way out of that vertex. The walk can return to it and take the remaining branch, visiting the same vertex twice in one closed route. When that route is complete, the outer loop looks for another unused edge elsewhere in the grid.

When writing the SVG, I keep the turns. Five steps to the right become h5. Three steps up become v-3. The closing z brings the path back to its starting vertex.

1. At the shared vertex, choose the right edge.
   Clear bit 1: 0101 -> 0100

2. The top and right edges have been followed.
   Choose the bottom edge, pointing left.

3. The right loop is complete.
   At the shared vertex again, choose the left edge.
   Clear bit 4: 0100 -> 0000

The orange point is the shared vertex. Red marks the selected edge, green the edges already followed, and blue the unused edges. Continuing around the left loop joins both loops into one closed route.

A hole is a contour too

Take a 3 × 3 block of dark modules and remove the center. The walk finds an outside boundary and a smaller boundary around the light module.

Following the dark-on-the-right rule takes the outside boundary clockwise and the inside boundary counterclockwise. Both go into the same SVG path. Under SVG’s default nonzero fill rule, their winding contributions cancel inside the hole, so the background shows through. SVG fill rules

Left:  8 dark modules, 1 empty center.
Right: the same shape, traced as two contours.

Outer boundary: clockwise.
Inner boundary: counterclockwise.

Inside the ring: one winding contribution.
Inside the hole: opposite contributions cancel.

In the exported SVG, the foreground is a single filled path.

Try it on your own rMQR Code

Set vrb: 1 to get a square per dark module, or use the default to get the traced path. Both start from the same encoded matrix, so you can compare the SVGs without changing the message or the symbol.

Open the live demo, expand Inside rMQR Code, and turn on Explore SVG contours to see the routes and cutouts.

articles.title: We Keep Hearing About AI Productivity. The QA Group Chat Told a Different Story.
articles.description: An anonymous poll, a debate about multimodal testing, and some uncomfortable questions about who...
articles.body_html:
An anonymous poll, a debate about multimodal testing, and some uncomfortable questions about who benefits from the AI rush.

Recently, I published an article on DEV.to about our company's AI testing practices and the organizational changes that followed.

It was selected for DEV's weekly Top 7 Featured Posts and included in the official DEV newsletter.

The comments were more interesting than I expected. Readers from different backgrounds started sharing their own experiences. They talked about outdated PRDs, agents reporting the same bug repeatedly, isolated test environments, and the mess that automation can expose when people have been quietly filling in the gaps.

One reader from the manufacturing industry even compared our experience with his factory's automated material-tracking project. Different industry, same problem: once you automate a process, all the messy handoffs that people used to handle manually become much harder to hide.

I was still thinking about those discussions when something else caught my attention.

It happened in a QA community group I'm part of.

1. Sixteen People Said They Weren't Employed


The group has around 500 members. Someone started an anonymous poll asking a simple question:

Are you currently employed?

When I checked the results, 76 people had voted.

Status People Percentage
Employed 60 78.9%
Not currently employed 16 21.1%

Sixteen people.

To be clear, this isn't an unemployment survey of the software testing industry. The poll was anonymous, and we have no idea why those 16 people weren't working. They could have been laid off, resigned, or simply be between jobs. Only 76 out of roughly 500 group members participated, so there's no reason to treat this as an industry-wide statistic.

Still, the number got my attention.

I also have a former colleague who works in software testing. They've been out of work for six months and still haven't found another job.

That's no longer just a number in an anonymous poll. It's someone I know and have worked with.

I don't know all the details of their job search, and I wouldn't automatically blame AI for their situation. But six months without finding another role is difficult to ignore.

The group chat quickly filled up with comments.

All we're seeing is layoffs. Nobody's hiring.

Almost 50. Who's going to hire me now?

Is there still a future in this field?

Some people suggested changing careers. Others said it was time to prepare for what's coming.

One comment summed up the mood rather well:

With all this AI-driven productivity improvement, it's getting harder and harder to keep up.

Then, almost as quickly as the conversation started, it turned to AI testing.

2. Can AI Really Compare an App Screen with Its Design?


Someone asked whether AI-powered test automation could compare an actual app screen against its UI design, checking element sizes, colors, positions, and other visual details.

The suggestions came quickly.

Some people proposed OCR to extract information from the design and the actual screen. Others suggested multimodal models. There were also concerns about maintenance: what happens when the UI changes slightly? Do we have to rebuild the whole thing?

Someone joked:

How well will it actually work? Who knows?

I joined the discussion.

My answer was that it's technically possible, but the AI needs enough context and sufficiently detailed instructions. Just throwing a demo page at a model and expecting it to understand everything won't get you very far.

I also pointed out that using a top-tier multimodal model for this kind of work can consume a lot of tokens.

Then came my questions:

Is management paying for the tokens?

And:

If not, they can go to hell.

I made the point one more time:

You can use a top-tier multimodal model, sure. But the token consumption can be huge. If management isn't paying for it, to hell with that.

Yes, I really said that. 😆

The joke aside, I meant it.

There's a difference between proving that something can be done and proving that it's worth doing.

OCR, DOM inspection, image comparison, and multimodal models can all help with UI verification. The right approach depends on what you're trying to check. Not every visual problem needs an expensive model.

But once you start taking screenshots, sending them for analysis, comparing results, and repeating the process across multiple runs, the bill can grow quickly.

Before adopting a solution like this, I'd want to know how many real issues it catches, how many false positives it produces, how much it costs to run, and how much effort is needed to maintain it when the UI changes.

If a company expects testers to use AI but leaves them to pay for their own tokens, something is wrong.

I've seen people in that group joking about collecting free credits from different platforms every morning before starting work.

It's funny, but think about it: employees are being told to embrace AI and improve productivity, while some are trying to keep their experiments running on whatever free credits they can find.

If a company wants AI-driven productivity, AI usage needs to be part of the company's budget.

3. AI Writes the Code, AI Tests It. What Could Possibly Go Wrong?


Another part of the conversation made me laugh.

Someone described an almost completely automated development process:

Describe a requirement, call the product skill, generate a demo and PRD, call the technical skill, generate the technical documentation, architecture, interfaces, and framework. Write the code, generate the tests with AI, run everything, and ship it. Done. A pile of bugs goes live.

That last sentence says a lot.

Someone else complained:

The boss uses AI to generate a demo, decides the idea is viable, and then expects everyone to build it.

Another person added:

Management expects us to deliver exactly that.

And someone joked:

Sounds like all we need is the boss. Everyone else can leave.

I've seen why this attitude develops. A demo can look convincing, and AI can generate a surprising amount of code in a very short time. It's easy to look at that output and assume the hard part is already done.

But a working demo isn't a validated product.

A generated PRD isn't proof that the requirements have been properly discussed. Generated code and generated tests don't automatically share the same understanding of what the system is supposed to do.

I ran into a version of this problem in our own testing work.

In one knowledge-base project, AI found 36 potential defects, while manual testing found 11. After review, 30 defects were confirmed as valid. AI had contributed 21 of them.

Those numbers were encouraging, but something else caught my attention.

Some of the reported issues weren't actually implementation bugs. Product and development had already agreed on changes, but nobody had updated the PRD.

The AI was following the document. The people were following an agreement that existed only in conversations.

In the past, testers often bridged that gap through experience and informal communication. They knew who to ask and which version of the requirements the team was actually following.

The AI didn't have that context.

It did exactly what it had been asked to do, and the result was a test report full of issues that looked legitimate but weren't necessarily bugs.

That's one of the things I find interesting about AI testing. It doesn't just test the software. It can expose how disconnected the people building that software actually are.

4. Why Is Every Company Suddenly Chasing AI?


As the group conversation continued, people started discussing the industry rather than individual jobs.

One member argued that many Chinese companies keep a close eye on what's happening in the US, where much of the current technology leadership comes from. One member said Chinese companies keep a close eye on what's happening in the US, and estimated that the gap between the two markets was at least six months.

That's their estimate, not a figure I've independently verified. But the broader observation is worth discussing.

A lot of companies seem afraid of being left behind.

One company adopts AI for coding, so others feel they need it too. Another introduces AI testing, and suddenly everyone wants an AI testing strategy. When large technology companies start talking about full-stack AI transformation, smaller companies feel pressure to follow.

Someone in the group put it bluntly:

Everyone just copies what's already working elsewhere. AI cuts costs and improves efficiency. What boss wouldn't like that?

Fair point.

But how many companies have actually worked out where AI fits into their business, rather than adopting it simply because competitors are doing so?

Another member brought up education and talent development. For years, the emphasis had been on catching up and getting new technology into production quickly. Now, they argued, the demand is shifting toward people who can innovate, lead, and break new ground.

Whether that shift is happening quickly enough is another question. But the contrast is interesting: following someone else's lead and creating something new require very different skills.

There was also a comment about management thinking:

Most companies are run by professional managers focused on making it through this year. How can you expect them to think long-term?

I understand the frustration behind that.

When a company is under pressure, cost reductions and headcount cuts are easy to measure. Building new capabilities, developing people, and investing in ideas that might pay off several years later are much harder to justify.

AI fits very neatly into the first category. Its potential for the second is real, but much harder to guarantee.

5. Is AI Productivity Becoming a Sales Pitch of Its Own?


One group member raised a more cynical possibility:

Everyone is selling tokens. They need to create the impression that AI improves productivity and that companies will fall behind if they don't use it. That pushes everyone to adopt AI. And with the market already in bad shape, companies can use AI as another reason to cut jobs.

I wouldn't go as far as saying that the entire AI productivity story is manufactured. I use these tools myself, and I've seen what they can do in testing, code analysis, and bug discovery.

But there are commercial incentives here that are worth recognizing.

AI providers want companies to use their models. Companies want to lower costs. Employees are being told that they need to become more productive with AI.

Those interests can reinforce one another, even when nobody has fully worked out the business case.

A company might adopt AI because it doesn't want to fall behind, rather than because it has identified a clear problem that AI can solve.

And once AI is in place, the conversation can quickly shift from what the technology can improve to how many people the company can do without.

One person in the group pointed out another part of the problem: the IT industry went through years of aggressive hiring. Large numbers of people entered the market, and companies expanded their teams rapidly.

Now the market looks very different.

From that perspective, AI isn't necessarily the original cause of the employment pressure. It may be the trigger that makes an existing imbalance more visible.

I think that's an important distinction.

We shouldn't assume every job reduction is caused by AI. Market conditions, years of hiring, changing business models, and company decisions all matter.

But AI gives companies another way to reorganize work, and that can accelerate changes that were already underway.

6. We Keep Pushing Harder. Where Does It End?


One line from the group chat stuck with me:

We keep trying to outdo everyone else, until we end up working ourselves out of a job.

Someone else described the result as a possible vicious cycle.

The IT industry has always moved quickly. One group member joked that if you stop learning for a year or two, you'll fall behind. And people in their thirties and forties are still pushing themselves to learn new things constantly.

I know what that feels like.

New frameworks, new models, new agents, new tools. Before you've finished getting comfortable with one, three more have appeared.

Companies want employees to become more productive. Employees want to stay competitive. AI providers want more adoption. And companies watch their competitors to make sure they're not falling behind.

Everyone has a reason to run faster.

But here's the question: what happens when every company tries to do more with fewer people, while the number of available jobs doesn't grow at the same pace?

We could end up in a strange situation where every company becomes more efficient, but the people working in the industry feel less secure.

We might work so hard trying to beat everyone else that we end up making the whole situation worse for ourselves.

7. Embrace AI, or Get Fired Now. Embrace AI, and Get Fired Later.


There was one more line in the group chat that deserves to be repeated:

If you don't embrace AI, you'll get fired immediately. If you do embrace AI, you'll just get fired later.

It's a joke, but not a particularly comfortable one.

Companies tell employees to learn AI, use AI, and improve productivity. Employees do their best to keep up.

But what happens after they become more productive?

Some worry that they'll end up automating their own jobs. Others are concerned that age and a changing job market will make it harder to find another role if they lose the current one.

People in the group were already suggesting that others should change careers or start preparing for something different.

I don't think learning AI is pointless. And I certainly don't think refusing to use it will protect anyone's job.

But embracing AI doesn't guarantee job security either.

Learning AI can make you more capable. It can't guarantee that a company will continue to need you.

Those are two different things.

Individuals can improve their skills, but they can't control the job market, company budgets, or every organizational decision.

I don't think it's fair to put the entire burden of career survival on whether someone is willing to learn the latest AI tool.

Final Thoughts

I don't want to use the 21.1% from this poll to claim that the testing industry is experiencing mass unemployment.

It was an anonymous poll in a group of around 500 people. Only 76 participated, and 16 said they weren't currently employed. We don't know why.

It isn't an industry-wide survey.

But I think the conversation is worth remembering.

People were worried about losing their jobs, then spent time discussing how AI could help them perform more advanced testing.

They were worried about being replaced by AI, while exploring how multimodal models could improve their automation.

They were concerned about token costs, while looking for free credits from different platforms.

They questioned whether AI was really improving productivity, while worrying that their companies might fall behind if they didn't adopt it.

And I have a former colleague who has been out of work for six months and still hasn't found another job. That makes the conversation feel a lot less theoretical.

I'm embracing AI too. I'm building AI testing workflows, experimenting with agents and models, and changing some of my own assumptions about what automation can do.

I see the possibilities. I'm not interested in pretending otherwise.

But I also don't think productivity gains automatically solve business problems, create new markets, or guarantee better opportunities for employees.

We can build faster, generate more code, run more tests, and produce more output than before.

The harder question is what all that extra productivity is actually going to achieve, and who gets to benefit from it.

There's a Chinese idiom I keep coming back to: 管中窥豹 — looking at a leopard through a narrow tube. You can see a few markings, but never the whole animal.


That's what this poll and the group chat offer: a glimpse, not a complete picture of the QA industry. Seventy-six votes cannot tell us how widespread the problem is, and one group conversation cannot explain what's happening across every company.

But it does reveal a few things worth paying attention to: job anxiety, pressure to adopt AI, arguments over token costs, and uncertainty about who actually benefits when productivity goes up.

We may not be seeing the whole leopard. But what we can see is worth taking seriously.

If we're all becoming more productive, why are so many people becoming less confident about their future?
