articles.title: Part 5: The Control That Protected an Empty Bucket
articles.description: This is Part 5 of a series building an HL7 v2 to FHIR R4 interoperability service in public. The...
articles.body_html:
This is Part 5 of a series building an HL7 v2 to FHIR R4 interoperability service in public. The repository is ND-codes/nhs-interop-platform, and the code as it stood for this article is tagged part-5.

Part 4 was about an alert that watched a metric that nothing exported. This part is about the same failure in documentation. I had written a security document with a threat table, a Caldicott mapping, a UK GDPR table and a DSPT mapping, all in the present tense, all with an evidence column. Then I checked every row against the code.

The problem with a control table

A security document is read differently from other documentation. Nobody reads a threat table for inspiration. They read it to find out what is true, usually because they have to decide whether to trust the system or sign something about it.

That makes the format itself a risk. Mine put aspiration and fact in the same table, in the same tense, with the same kind of evidence citation beside each. There was no way to tell, from the inside, which rows described code and which described intent. An assessor reading it would have believed all of it.

Ten of those rows did not hold. The most instructive one was not a missing control. It was a control that was built properly and protected nothing.

The control that protected an empty bucket

The GDPR table cited an S3 lifecycle rule as the storage-limitation control for patient data. That rule is real. It is in infra/terraform/s3.tf, it moves objects to infrequent access at 30 days and Glacier at 90, and it expires them at 2555 days, which is the seven-year NHS records retention. The bucket it governs is versioned, encrypted with a customer-managed key, has public access blocked and has Object Lock configured. If you were auditing the Terraform, you
would tick that row and move on.

Nothing writes to it.

No service in the repository imports boto3, or any other S3 client. The only mention of S3 anywhere in the application code is in the transform service's own docstring, which says the dead-letter path is "S3 in prod". That was an intention someone wrote down once, and it then got cited in a compliance table as though it described the system.

In every configuration that actually runs, the dead-letter path is local. Under Docker Compose it is a named volume at /tmp/dlq. In Kubernetes it is an
emptyDir mounted at /tmp.

Both of those matter more than they look.

An emptyDir does not survive the pod. A restart or a reschedule discards it. So in the deployed configuration, the dead-letter path loses exactly the messages it exists to preserve, precisely when it is most likely to be restarted, which is during the outage that filled it. Meanwhile, the runbook told the on-call engineer to "inspect the DLQ bucket" and said messages "will replay once the write path recovers". There is no bucket to inspect, and nothing replays.

The Docker Compose case was worse and is the one that got caught first. The named volume was root-owned while the container runs as uid 10001, so every dead-letter write failed with PermissionError, and the message was lost silently. That was found by running make break-fhir, the failure demonstration script from Part 4, in its first week of existence.

And the dead-letter path is the most sensitive store in the stack. A
dead-lettered message is the complete raw HL7 message: every PID field,
including the ones the mapper deliberately drops before building the Bundle. The FHIR store holds less patient data than the dead-letter path does. It had no retention rule of any kind.

So the real compliance position was a well-built seven-year retention control protecting an empty bucket, while the patient data sat in an ephemeral volume with no retention, no durability, and a runbook pointing the wrong way.

The NHS number in four log lines

The second finding is smaller and more common.

The pds-client service logged the NHS number at INFO on every lookup, every cache hit, every stub response and every upstream error. Four call sites.

What makes it easy to miss is the serialisation. The log format string is "%(asctime)s %(levelname)s %(name)s %(message)s", which does not mention the identifier at all. The call looks harmless:

logger.info("PDS cache hit", extra={"nhs_number": nhs_number})

python-json-logger serialises everything passed in extra, whether or not
the format string names it. The line that reaches stdout is:

{"asctime": "2026-11-09 14:07:46,693", "levelname": "INFO",
 "name": "pds-client", "message": "PDS cache hit",
 "nhs_number": "9000000009"}

The NHS number is the strongest patient identifier in English healthcare, and it was going to stdout, which in the Helm deployment means a log store with different retention and different access control from the patient record itself. The document, meanwhile, cited Caldicott principle 3 and told the reader that only the minimum necessary data was used. The National Data Guardian's wording for principle 2 is that confidential information "should not
be included unless it is necessary for the specified purpose(s)".

It was also going somewhere worse. The outbound call to the PDS sandbox set the correlation header from the patient:

resp = await http.get(url, headers={"X-Request-ID": nhs_number})

A request id is echoed in upstream error responses and recorded by every intermediary that handles the request. That leaks considerably further than our own log store.

The fix turned out to be a deletion rather than an addition, and the reason is the interesting part. The transform service already sends X-Trace-Id on every call to pds-client. The handler signature was async def lookup(nhs_number: str), which reads no headers, so the trace id was being sent and thrown away. With the correlation identifier discarded, the NHS number was the only thing left to log. Accepting the header makes the patient identifier unnecessary:

async def lookup(
    nhs_number: str,
    x_trace_id: str | None = Header(default=None),
) -> dict:
    trace_id = x_trace_id or str(uuid.uuid4())

I did consider logging a hash instead, and decided against it. An NHS number is ten digits with a constrained check digit, so an unsalted hash of one is recoverable by brute force almost immediately. A salted hash would work, but it needs the salt managed as a secret, and it would only be earning back correlation that the trace id already provides.

The test that had to look at the bytes

The obvious way to test this is caplog. It is the wrong way.

caplog inspects the log record. The defect lives in serialisation: the record carries nhs_number as an attribute, and the question is whether it reaches stdout. A caplog assertion can pass while the leak continues.

So the tests attach the service's real JsonFormatter to a StringIO and assert on the output:

handler.setFormatter(
    jsonlogger.JsonFormatter("%(asctime)s %(levelname)s %(name)s %(message)s")
)
main.logger.addHandler(handler)
...
assert NHS_NUMBER not in captured_log.getvalue()

That is a substring assertion over the exact bytes the container would write, across the cache path, the stub path, the upstream error path and the open breaker path. It does not care how the identifier got there, as long as the test makes that path fail the way it fails for real. It will catch the next person who adds a fifth log line, including me. Further down is the case where my first version of this test didn't.

All ten of those tests fail against the previous version of the service and pass against the current one. That is the only check I trust on work like this.

Eight runbook links that never resolved

Each of the eight alert rules carried a runbook annotation, like this one:

runbook: "docs/runbook.md#pds-circuit"

None of them resolved. There are no anchor tags anywhere in the runbook, and GitHub generates a heading's anchor from its text, so the real target for that section is #2-pdscircuitopen. An on-call engineer clicking an alert link landed at the top of the file.

I did not work this out from the slug rules. I fetched the rendered file from GitHub and read the anchors out of the DOM, which gave the actual list rather than my recollection of the algorithm:

#1-transformlatencyhigh   #2-pdscircuitopen   #3-dlqratehigh
#4-transformerrorratehigh #5-ingestnotraffic  #6-fieldsdroppedratehigh
#7-invalidnhsnumbers      #8-patientwriteswithoutidentity

Three of those eight dead links were mine. I added them in Part 4 by copying the convention the existing five used, and the convention had never worked. The sections even carried a line reading Anchor: #fields-dropped, which was decoration. It declared an anchor rather than creating one.

The annotations now point at the generated anchors, every section states its own link, and the alert rule tests assert the exact annotation string, so a renumbering that breaks a link breaks a test. That trade-off is written down in the runbook, because tying a link to a section number is not obviously right.

The tag that existed only in a comment

The data sensitivity section claimed DataClass = patient-identifiable was applied to every AWS resource through Terraform default tags. The provider block containing those tags was commented out. The string DataClass appeared exactly once in the whole Terraform directory, inside that comment.

This matters more than cost allocation. The data classification tag is what an access review or an assessment uses to find the resources holding patient data. A tag that exists only in a comment finds nothing.

It is now in the live provider block. Two small honesty notes came out of writing it. The claim can only be "every taggable resource", because several resources here take no tags argument at all, including aws_kms_alias and the S3 bucket sub-resources. And the block syntax was checked against HashiCorp's own tutorial rather than written from memory: default_tags is a block with a nested tags map and no equals sign. Part 2 went out with a Terraform CI job that used an invalid Trivy flag, because the flag was recalled instead of looked up, and that is a cheap mistake to stop repeating.

The one boundary that takes arbitrary input

POST /hl7 reads its body with await request.body() and no limit. The document claimed Pydantic validation at every HTTP boundary, which is true everywhere except the one place it matters, because an HL7 v2 message is not JSON and has no model.

It now reads the stream in chunks and stops at 256 KiB. The limit is checked against Content-Length first because that is cheap, and then enforced while reading anyway, because Content-Length is a claim the client makes and a chunked request need not send one. There is a test for each of those, plus one that an exactly-at-the-limit body is still accepted, which is where this kind of check is usually wrong.

What I did not fix

POST /hl7 still has no authentication. Anything that can reach the service can submit a message that becomes a Patient record. The mitigations that exist are that the subnets are tagged for an internal load balancer and that NetworkPolicy restricts pod-to-pod traffic, and neither of those is authentication.

I thought about adding a shared-secret header and decided not to, two days before publishing. A trust would use mutual TLS or the Spine Secure Proxy, and shipping an API key check would have produced exactly the thing this article is about: a row in a table saying authentication is implemented, describing something nobody would actually deploy. It is in the "Claimed, not built" section, and it is a roadmap issue.

The dead-letter path still has no durability. It has a 72-hour retention window, pruning on write and on startup, an exported age, an alert and a runbook entry. It does not survive a pod restart. Fixing that means writing to the bucket that already has the right controls, which needs an AWS account.

And pruning on write and startup has a hole I should name: a stack that
dead-letters nothing and never restarts keeps its oldest message past the window. The alert on hl7_dlq_oldest_seconds is there because that case should be visible rather than silent. The actual fix is to move retention to the storage layer, where it runs whether or not the application does.

Where AI helps here, and where it doesn't

I built this project with Claude Code, and this week gave a clean reading on both halves of that.

The sweep is where it earns its place. Reading every row of a control table, finding the file each row cites, and checking whether the thing is actually there is tedious, mechanical work that gets skipped precisely because it is tedious. Most of these ten findings came out of that pass, and I would not have done it by hand two days before publishing.

The failure mode is sharper, and this part of the series has now shown it twice.

Part 4 shipped a fix for an alert that could never fire. The fix did not work either. The breaker was applied as a decorator to a coroutine function, so pybreaker counted the returned coroutine object as a success and the real failure raised later, on await, outside the breaker. The breaker never opened, which means the gauge that had just been added and the alert that had just been
made fireable still could not fire.

The test for it passed. It drove the breaker with a synchronous function, so it proved the gauge worked rather than proving the breaker worked, which is the same shape of error as the original bug, one layer down. I only found it by starting the stack and watching the breaker refuse to open. The commit is
b43f462.

This week the identical defect turned up in pds-client, and it was only found because I now knew to look for it. The same fix applies:

with breaker.calling():
    resp = await http.get(url, headers={"X-Request-ID": trace_id})

calling() is the right API here rather than call_async, because
call_async is implemented with tornado.gen.coroutine and this service runs on asyncio. That came from reading the installed pybreaker source rather than assuming.

The runbook anchors are the same failure in a smaller form: a broken convention reproduced faithfully three times, because reproducing a convention does not involve testing it.

And while writing this part up, I nearly shipped two more. Before merging, I had Claude Code review the finished week, and this time the review ran the code instead of reading it.

The first find was that the NHS number still reached the logs. The test for the upstream error path raised a connection error, which is the one httpx exception whose message carries no URL. A real 500 or 429 from PDS raises HTTPStatusError, httpx builds that message from the request URL, and the URL ends in the NHS number.

Both services logged str(exc), so the leak was open while the test guarding it passed. They now log the error type, status code and trace id, and the test makes PDS answer with a real 500.

The second was worse, because it was Part 4's bug again. The new retention alert fires when the oldest dead-lettered message passes 80 hours, and the gauge it reads was only updated when pruning ran. Pruning deletes anything past 72 hours, so the gauge could never get past 72, and then froze until the next write.

The promtool test fed the rule a made-up 290,000 seconds and the rule fired. That proved the rule and said nothing about the metric, which is the breaker test from Part 4 all over again. The gauge is now read from disk at scrape time, and a new test ages a file past the threshold with nothing else happening.

The pattern across both weeks is that an assistant is reliable at applying a shape and unreliable at noticing the shape is wrong, and that tests written in the same pass as the fix inherit the same blind spot. Every time, what caught it was running the system. That is an argument for the failure demonstration scripts from Part 4 rather than against the tooling, and it is why make break-fhir found the root-owned volume in its first week.

Worth stealing

Separate what is built from what is intended, structurally, not with a
qualifier. One table for implemented controls, one section headed "Claimed, not built". A hedged row still reads as a yes.

Make the evidence column name a file that exists and, for a document, an anchor you have checked. Four of my rows cited .gitlab-ci.yml, a pipeline that cannot run because the repository is on GitHub. That file is deleted now rather than left to be cited again.

Point a control at a test where you can. A row that names a test is the only kind of security documentation that stays true without somebody remembering to update it.

Test the serialised output, not the record, whenever the question is what leaves the process. The same applies to metric labels, error responses and anything that gets rendered on the way out.

Check which store actually holds the data before you write a retention
control. The bucket with the seven-year rule held nothing.

Give a retention rule a metric. A rule nothing measures is a sentence in a document.

What I'd do differently

I would have written the security document last. Writing it early, from the architecture rather than from the code, is precisely how it filled up with things that were true of the design and not of the system.

I would have audited it when the repository moved from GitLab to GitHub. That move invalidated four evidence citations in one commit and nobody checked.

And I would have treated the first "in prod" in a docstring as a flag. Both of this week's worst findings trace back to a sentence describing an intended future, which later got read as a description of the present.

Sources

  • The Caldicott Principles, National Data Guardian, GOV.UK
  • Data Security and Protection Toolkit, NHS England
  • Configure default tags for AWS resources, HashiCorp
  • The calling() context manager and the Tornado implementation of call_async were read from the installed pybreaker 1.2.0 source
  • The runbook anchor list was read from the rendered file on GitHub, not derived from the slug rules

Next

Part 6 is the ten-minute walkthrough: running the stack from nothing, and the
questions an interviewer actually asks about it.

Have you ever audited a control table against a codebase, and what did you find
that was worse than an empty bucket?

This is a personal project. It is not affiliated with or endorsed by NHS England or any NHS organisation. It uses the public PDS FHIR sandbox and synthetic test data only. Views are my own.

articles.title: DuckDB 2.0's quack server lets ten writers share one file for under 2ms a query
articles.description: DuckDB 2.0 ships a built-in server so several processes can finally write to one database file. Ten concurrent clients landed 1,000 inserts with no errors, at a cost of roughly 1.7ms extra per query and a frozen local catalog while connected.
articles.body_html:
Try to open a DuckDB file from two processes at once and you get this:

_duckdb.IOException: IO Error: Could not set lock on file "server.duckdb":
Conflicting lock is held in /usr/bin/python3.11 (PID 1355).

That has been true since the beginning. DuckDB is an in-process database: one file, one writer, full stop. DuckDB 2.0, which went GA on 21 October 2026, ships an extension called quack that turns a running DuckDB process into a small network server other DuckDB processes can connect to. I wanted to know whether that actually gets you past the lock, what it costs per query, and what it still refuses to do.

I ran DuckDB 2.0.0 through the Python client (pip install duckdb==2.0.0), started a server on a table with a million rows, and hit it from separate Python processes acting as independent clients.

Setting it up

The server side loads the extension and calls quack_serve:

con = duckdb.connect('server.duckdb')
con.execute("INSTALL quack; LOAD quack;")
con.execute("CREATE TABLE t AS SELECT range AS i, 'row_'||range AS s FROM range(1000000)")
con.execute("CALL quack_serve('quack:localhost:9494', token='testtoken123')")

A client attaches to it as a remote database and routes its whole session there with CONNECT:

con = duckdb.connect()
con.execute("INSTALL quack; LOAD quack;")
con.execute("ATTACH 'quack:localhost:9494' AS srv (TOKEN 'testtoken123')")
con.execute("CONNECT srv")
con.execute("SELECT count(*) FROM t").fetchall()  # [(1000000,)]
con.execute("DISCONNECT")

CONNECT takes about 3ms the first time and the client then talks to the server for every query until it disconnects.

The lock is still there, and that's the point

Opening server.duckdb directly from a second process while the server holds it still fails with the exact error above. Quack doesn't touch DuckDB's file-locking model at all. What it does is give you a second door into the one process that is allowed to hold the write lock, so that ten processes can write through that one door instead of fighting over the file.

I also checked whether the lock problem was ever really about reads. It isn't: with no writer active, two processes can open the same file with read_only=True at the same time and both query it fine. That already worked before 2.0. Quack's actual contribution is concurrent writes, not concurrent reads, which is a narrower claim than "multiple processes can now use one DuckDB file" might suggest.

Writes that used to be impossible

I ran 10 client processes, each opening its own connection through CONNECT and firing 100 single-row inserts, 1,000 inserts in total.

Setup Errors Rows landed Distinct (client, seq) pairs
2 processes, direct file open 1 (lock error, immediate) 0 —
10 clients via quack CONNECT 0 1,000 1,000

Every insert landed, nothing was lost or duplicated, and the server-side count matched the client-side count exactly across three repeats of this test. That is the headline: a workload that used to be impossible to run from more than one process at a time now runs correctly from ten.

Concurrency doesn't scale the way I expected

I measured throughput for the same 1,000 inserts split across 1, 5, 10 and 20 concurrent clients, three full sweeps:

Clients Run 1 Run 2 Run 3
1 (serial) 401/s 380/s 348/s
5 692/s 735/s 655/s
10 542/s 570/s 508/s
20 362/s 332/s 342/s

Throughput peaks at 5 concurrent clients, then falls off. At 20 clients it drops back to roughly the same number as a single client running everything serially, sometimes below it. I didn't expect that, so I reran the whole sweep twice more to make sure it wasn't a fluke. It wasn't. DuckDB still executes writes against one file one at a time internally; quack's connection handling adds its own overhead on top, and past a handful of clients that overhead eats whatever the server-side queueing gains you. If your workload is many short-lived writers, five seems to be roughly where this particular setup stopped paying off and started costing more than it saved.

What a query costs going through the wire

Even on loopback, going through the server instead of talking to the file in-process adds a tax on every query, measured over 200 runs:

Query In-process Via quack CONNECT
SELECT 1 (median) 0.25ms 1.92ms
SELECT sum(i), count(*) FROM t (median, 1M rows) 0.77ms 2.42ms
SELECT * FROM t (full 1M rows fetched) 0.334s 0.391s

For small queries the absolute numbers are tiny but the ratio is large, about 7–8x for a trivial query. For a query that returns a lot of data, the gap narrows to roughly 17%, which is closer to what you'd expect from serialising a result set over HTTP instead of handing back memory directly.

Your local tables disappear while you're connected

This one surprised me. I created a local table, then ran CONNECT to the server:

CatalogException: Catalog Error: Table with name local_only does not exist!
Did you mean "pg_collation"?

I tried qualifying it explicitly with the schema name DuckDB normally uses for the default database:

CatalogException: Catalog Error: Table with name "memory.local_only" does not
exist because schema "memory" does not exist.

Both failed. While CONNECT-ed, the local catalog isn't just deprioritised, it's gone from view entirely, and there's no prefix that gets it back. DISCONNECT returns it immediately. If your plan was to pull a remote aggregate and join it against a local staging table in the same session, that plan doesn't work; you have to disconnect, or keep the remote session in a second connection object.

What it refuses, in its own words

A wrong token fails immediately at ATTACH, before CONNECT is even called:

_duckdb.InvalidInputException: Invalid Input Error: Authentication failed

Trying to bind the server to anything other than localhost without opting in fails the same way:

Invalid Input Error: Only localhost is allowed as a Quack RPC hostname by
default, set allow_other_hostname=true to override. We strongly recommend
reverse-proxying the Quack RPC when making it publicly available.

Both of those matched what the docs say, which was reassuring given how much else I had to work out by trial and error.

Watching it from the server side

quack_active_connections() sounds like a live connection list. It's closer to a short query log: it kept rows for finished queries, with status active or finished, the query text, a connection id and a timestamp, even after those queries completed. Useful for seeing what clients just ran, less useful as a "who is connected right now" view, since finished work stays visible until something ages it out.

What it costs to run

The server process holding the million-row table idled at about 120MB RSS. Under ten concurrent clients hammering it with small queries, that rose to roughly 132MB and settled back down to about 125MB once the load finished. For a table this size, the server itself isn't the expensive part.

One more thing worth knowing: killing the server process with kill -9 released the file lock immediately. A fresh direct connection to the same file afterwards worked on the first try, with all million rows intact. No stale lock file, no recovery step.

What I got wrong on the way

My first attempt at the client side used ATTACH 'quack://localhost:9494' AS srv, modelled on an ordinary URL. DuckDB took that literally as a filesystem path and failed with "Cannot open file", which looked like a connection problem and sent me checking the server log for several minutes before I noticed the double slash. The actual scheme has no slashes: quack:localhost:9494, the same shape DuckDB already uses for postgres: and mysql: connection strings. Once I matched that, everything else worked first time.

Run it yourself 

python3 -m venv venv && ./venv/bin/pip install duckdb==2.0.0

Server:

import duckdb, time
con = duckdb.connect('server.duckdb')
con.execute("INSTALL quack; LOAD quack;")
con.execute("CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS t AS SELECT range AS i, 'row_'||range AS s FROM range(1000000)")
print(con.execute("CALL quack_serve('quack:localhost:9494', token='testtoken123')").fetchall())
while True:
    time.sleep(1)

Concurrent writers, run while the server above is up:

import duckdb, threading, time

def make_client():
    con = duckdb.connect()
    con.execute("INSTALL quack; LOAD quack;")
    con.execute("ATTACH 'quack:localhost:9494' AS srv (TOKEN 'testtoken123')")
    con.execute("CONNECT srv")
    return con

setup = make_client()
setup.execute("CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS writes (client_id INTEGER, seq INTEGER)")
setup.execute("DISCONNECT")

def worker(client_id):
    con = make_client()
    for seq in range(100):
        con.execute(f"INSERT INTO writes VALUES ({client_id}, {seq})")
    con.execute("DISCONNECT")

t0 = time.perf_counter()
threads = [threading.Thread(target=worker, args=(i,)) for i in range(10)]
for th in threads: th.start()
for th in threads: th.join()
print("elapsed", time.perf_counter() - t0)

What I'd do with this

If you have a single-node analytics workload where more than one process occasionally needs to write to the same DuckDB file, quack solves a real problem that had no good answer before. I wouldn't reach for it to serve many short, latency-sensitive clients: the per-query tax is real, and my own numbers show throughput getting worse, not better, past a handful of concurrent writers. I'd also budget for the catalog isolation explicitly, since it changes how you'd structure a session that needs both local and remote tables. Test your own concurrency sweet spot before picking a client pool size; mine was 5, and I have no reason to think that number generalises to a different machine or workload.

articles.title: Behind the scenes, two months later: How we ship Google Agent Skills like products
articles.description: In my previous post, I took you behind the scenes of Google Agent Skills, covering how the project...
articles.body_html:
In my previous post, I took you behind the scenes of Google Agent Skills, covering how the project started, how we maintain quality at scale, and how we handle governance. In this post, I'll share what we've built since then: the automated quality gates every change must pass, the AI review agent that inspects skill quality, and the lessons we learned along the way. You can adopt the same gates and review rules in your own skill repository.

Since my last post, the Google Agent Skills repository has passed 21,000 GitHub stars, up from 15,000. It now hosts over 170 skills from teams across Google, and we distribute them across multiple AI platforms.

Building agent skills for a single developer or a small project is straightforward. You write a SKILL.md file, define a few instructions, test it manually, and it works. At our scale, manual workflows stop being effective. Unvetted edits can introduce subtle bugs, and it becomes difficult to catch issues before they reach users.

The core philosophy: Ship skills like products

One key lesson from my previous post: a skill is a living product, not a one-off document. In practice, that means we ship every skill update like a product release.

It's tempting to treat a skill as documentation. But documentation explains concepts to a human reader, while a skill steers an AI agent's reasoning loop, tool selection, and execution path. A misplaced phrase in a skill can cause an agent to invoke invalid command flags, enter an infinite loop, or waste tokens.

That makes every instruction edit a behavioral change. You wouldn't ship a product update without testing it, and the same goes for a skill. This principle drives three core requirements:

  • Strict semantic versioning: Every behavioral change requires an explicit version bump.
  • Deterministic automated validation: Linters and validators check every proposed change before a human or AI reviewer sees it.
  • Mandatory evaluation evidence: Every change includes an evaluation report. It compares the skill against its previous version, or against an agent without the skill if the skill is new.

Automated conformance gates: The pull request pipeline

In my previous post, I briefly listed the checks every skill passes on check-in: linters, link checkers, and AI-assisted checklists. Here's what's inside them, plus two gates I haven't covered before: semantic versioning and evaluation suite validation.

When an author submits a change to our internal skills repository, an automated continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipeline triggers immediately. A skill must pass six automated gates and human approval before it's exported to GitHub:

  • Structural conformance: Directory layout, allowed files, taxonomy
  • Skill linters: Frontmatter, folder naming, Markdown rules
  • Semantic versioning: Version bump for every behavioral change
  • Evaluation suite: Valid eval suite and a fresh eval report
  • Link validation: Relative links are valid
  • AI review agent: Skill quality and design standards
  • Human approval: Final approval from a human reviewer (subject matter expert)

Structural conformance and skill linters

Our automated validation suite inspects every pull request for structural and syntactical correctness. Some of the rules include:

  • Folder name and metadata name must match
  • SKILL.md and description length limits are enforced
  • All required fields in the frontmatter metadata are present
  • Only a curated list of files and directories is allowed within a skill directory
  • All Markdown files follow formatting rules
  • The main README.md and the machine-readable index.json registry are up to date

Semantic versioning

Every skill declares a semantic version in its SKILL.md frontmatter metadata:

---
name: spanner-basics
metadata:
  version: "1.1.1"
  category: Databases
description: "..."
---

First, our automated checks verify that the version is a quoted string. YAML parses unquoted values such as 2.0 as numbers, which causes unexpected parsing errors in tools that expect a string.

Second, the validator checks the version transition itself. New skills must start at 1.0.0, and any change to an existing skill's instructions, scripts, or references requires a version bump or the pull request is blocked. Standard reset rules apply: bumping MAJOR (for example, 1.4.2 to 2.0.0) resets MINOR and PATCH to 0, and bumping MINOR (for example, 1.4.2 to 1.5.0) resets PATCH to 0.

Why enforce strict versioning if the agent only reads the Markdown instructions? The version number is for the developer and their package tooling, not for the model at runtime. Skills don't auto-update in the background, which means there's no network check or latency overhead each time an agent invokes a skill. Instead, explicit versions let developers compare their locally installed skills against the upstream catalog and decide when to pull changes — for example, by running npx skills update. This also supports workflows where teams want to lock a critical skill to a known-good version to guarantee reproducible agent behavior across their projects.

Evaluation suite validation

Our continuous evaluations (evals) compare agent performance with and without each skill. Those results are only as reliable as the evaluation suites behind them. If a suite contains broken file references or compound expectations, test results become noisy and untrustworthy.

Our validator parses each evaluation suite and the pull request description, then checks several strict invariants:

  • Resolution of file-based prompts: When a test prompt references a file (such as @file:test_prompt.txt), the validator confirms that the target file exists and isn't empty.
  • Atomic expectations: Each expectation must check exactly one criterion. The validator blocks compound expectations until authors split them. Lesson 2 later in this post shows why.
  • Duplicate detection: The validator flags duplicate test prompts and conflicting expectations within the same evaluation suite.
  • Mandatory evaluation report: Every pull request that modifies a skill must link to an evaluation report in its description.
  • Eval staleness check: Authors usually iterate on a pull request as reviewers leave feedback. The validator confirms that the linked report ran against the latest commit.

Link validation

Over 170 skills link to documentation for fast-evolving Google products, and those pages can move long after a skill passes review. Rather than waiting for users to report broken links, we validate links at two stages. Before merge, pull request checks verify all relative links, such as files in references/.

Then, every Monday, a GitHub Actions workflow runs lychee across all external links in the public repository and routes any broken links to skill owners for remediation.

AI review agent

Linters and schema validators catch syntactic errors, but they can't evaluate overall quality. They can't tell you if an instruction is confusing, if a reference guide is too verbose, or if a task should have been a bash script instead of a large language model (LLM) instruction.

To solve this, we integrated an AI review agent into our review pipeline. When a change affects a skill, the AI reviewer inspects it using a dedicated review skill. Yes, we use a skill to review skills.

Here are the core rules the AI reviewer evaluates. You can adopt these rules in your own skill development workflows.

1. Skill suitability and the deterministic trap

The first question our AI reviewer asks is simple: Does this task belong in an instruction?

We often see authors fall into the "deterministic trap." They write rigid, numbered sequences of command-line interface (CLI) commands directly into Markdown text.

LLMs are probabilistic engines. If an operation requires a strict sequence of commands where a variation can cause an error, embedding those commands in the instruction text invites hallucinations.

Our AI reviewer enforces a clear boundary between deterministic and probabilistic logic. Rigid CLI sequences, JSON parsers, and deployment steps must live in executable scripts under scripts/. Markdown instructions are reserved for tasks that require judgment, such as choosing an architecture, diagnosing error logs, or synthesizing code.

This rule complements the Model Context Protocol (MCP) guidance I shared last time: prefer remote MCP tools whenever possible. When you must fall back to CLI or API calls, wrap them in a script instead of spelling them out in the instructions.

2. The L1/L2/L3 modular architecture

Context windows are valuable. Loading a 2,000-line skill into an agent consumes context and degrades reasoning.

Our AI reviewer enforces a three-tier information hierarchy that follows the progressive disclosure model of Agent Skills:

  • Level 1 (Metadata): The YAML frontmatter (name, description). The agent uses this concise summary for discovery and routing.
  • Level 2 (Core instructions): The main SKILL.md file. The body must stay compact (under 500 lines). It provides workflow overviews, decision trees, and guardrails.
  • Level 3 (Reference docs): Detailed API references, schemas, and other reference tables live in a references/ directory.

Our AI reviewer enforces two distinct rules for Level 3: flat directory structure and single-hop indirection. Keeping references/ flat (no subdirectories) is a repository convention that discourages sprawling documentation trees and makes file discovery simpler. More importantly for runtime performance, the reviewer blocks chained references, where SKILL.md links to a reference file that links to yet another file. Each hop requires an extra tool call, adding latency and cost, and our evaluations showed that agents frequently stop before following a second level of chained references.

3. Non-interactive script design

When skills bundle helper scripts in scripts/, we expect agents to execute them directly in terminal sandboxes.

Our AI reviewer flags any script that blocks on interactive prompts. Every script must accept inputs through command-line flags or environment variables, provide --help documentation, and include a --dry-run or confirmation flag for destructive operations. Scripts also need to separate output cleanly, writing structured data (usually JSON) to standard output and actionable error messages to standard error.

Example AI review checklist snippet

The review skill also checks frontmatter for spec compliance and discovery, and turns the L1/L2/L3 architecture into concrete structure rules. Here's an excerpt from those criteria:

### Front Matter & Discovery

-   **Spec Compliance**: YAML front matter MUST strictly follow the Agent Skills
    Reference Specification (https://agentskills.io/specification). Use `>-`
    (folded strip-chomping) format for multi-line descriptions.
-   **Name Constraints**: The `name` field must be **64 characters or less**,
    correspond to the product name, use kebab-case (`[a-z0-9-]`), and avoid
    vague names (`helper`, `utils`, `tools`, `data`). The `name` field must
    match the directory name where it's located (i.e. `skills/cloud/gcloud`
    directory should contain a front matter with `name: gcloud`).
-   **Description Quality**: The `description` field must follow the
    [Description Guide](references/description_guide.md).

### Content Structure & Authoring Quality

-   **L1/L2/L3 Architecture**: Enforce modular structure. The main `SKILL.md`
    body must stay under 500 lines. Move deep domain reference material to
    `references/` (see [Skill Structure](references/skill_structure.md)).
-   **Flat References Directory**: `references/` must be a flat directory (one
    level deep, no nested subdirectories). References > 100 lines must include a
    Table of Contents with line hints (see
    [Skill Structure](references/skill_structure.md)).
-   **Avoid Deeply-Nested References**: Avoid deeply-nested references (e.g.,
    `SKILL.md` -> `references/guides.md` -> `assets/output.tmpl`). Keep
    reference structures shallow (one level of indirection from `SKILL.md`)
    because agents might not load such link targets fully.

Human approval

After passing all automated checks, every pull request must receive approval from a human reviewer. The reviewer is typically the skill's subject matter expert and, for new skills, a member of the Central Skills team.

Lessons learned from repository history

Six months of commit history and pull request discussions reveal several practical takeaways.

1. Scope CI checks carefully

Early in the project, we configured automated pull request checks with coarse directory globs.

One check required an approved bug tracking ticket on every change. Because the glob matched too broadly, engineers making a one-line typo fix were blocked for missing a tracking ticket. Meanwhile, newly added skills in deeper subdirectories went uninspected.

Takeaway: Match automated check rules to specific file operations, such as added versus modified files, and verify exact path depths. Treat minor edits to existing skills differently from new skills.

2. Atomic expectations

When we started writing evaluation suites, we saw authors write compound expectations, such as:

# Bad: Compound expectation
- "The agent must create a Cloud Storage bucket in us-central1, enable
  uniform bucket-level access, and apply lifecycle rules."

If the agent configured the region and lifecycle rules but missed the uniform access flag, the LLM-as-a-judge scorer returned inconsistent ratings.

Migrating to atomic expectations resolved this issue:

# Good: Atomic expectations
- "The agent specifies us-central1 for the bucket location."
- "The agent enables uniform bucket-level access on the created bucket."
- "The agent defines a lifecycle configuration rule deleting objects
  older than 30 days."

Takeaway: Check exactly one criterion per expectation. Atomic expectations make evaluation results clear, reliable, and debuggable.

3. Documentation drift happens fast

In a multi-contributor repository, documentation tables drift within days if maintained manually.

Takeaway: If you publish an index or catalog, never rely on contributors to update it manually. Instead, write a generator script and enforce it with a CI unit test. That's the origin of the README.md and index.json check in our linters. Our index.json even opens with a warning: "This file is generated. Do not edit it by hand."

4. Gate expensive LLM checks behind fast deterministic ones

Running full evaluation suites and an AI review agent on every change can get expensive fast, both in token usage and CI runtime — especially when authors push frequent small commits during review.

In our pipeline, fast deterministic checks run first. Structural conformance, skill linters, and semantic versioning act as blocking gates: if any of them fail, the pipeline stops immediately and won't trigger the AI reviewer or evaluation checks until those issues are fixed.

Takeaway: Stage your pipeline so cheap, deterministic checks block broken changes before LLM-powered gates run. When building a similar system, consider adding further cost guardrails, such as manual triggers for heavy checks (for example, a /run-evals pull request comment) or only triggering automatic re-runs when the diff exceeds a specific threshold.

Conclusion

Building a scalable Agent Skills repository requires more than good prompt engineering. It requires solid developer infrastructure:

  • Ship skills like products: version, validate, and evaluate every change.
  • Enforce semantic versioning and atomic expectations with automated CI gates.
  • Use an AI reviewer to catch design anti-patterns, such as the deterministic trap.
  • Check links before merge and on a weekly schedule.

Links and further reading

To get started with Google Agent Skills, check out:

  • Google Agent Skills repo: github.com/google/skills
  • Previous post: Behind the scenes: How we build, test, and scale Google Agent Skills
  • Launch announcement: Level Up Your Agents: Announcing Google's Official Skills Repository
  • Skills tutorial: Introduction: What Are Google Cloud Agent Skills?

What's next?

If you found this post helpful:

  • Share this post with your friends on social media.
  • Connect with me via LinkedIn, X, or Bluesky.

Thanks for reading!

articles.title: Is LiteLLM Rust Really 7x Faster? A Closer Look at the Numbers
articles.description: Benchmark headlines are easy to share and hard to check.  In July, LiteLLM published benchmarks for...
articles.body_html:
Benchmark headlines are easy to share and hard to check.

In July, LiteLLM published benchmarks for its new Rust AI gateway. The headline numbers were big: roughly 7x lower overhead and 9x less memory than Bifrost, plus about 4.5x more requests per dollar. For anyone choosing an LLM gateway, numbers like that make the decision sound easy.

The Bifrost team then went through LiteLLM's raw CSV and JSON files and published a response: Debunking LiteLLM Rust Benchmarking, Part 1. Their conclusion is that the raw data tells a much less dramatic story than the headlines.

I've written before about why I switched from LiteLLM to Bifrost for production systems, so I was curious. In this article, I'll walk through what LiteLLM claimed, what the raw numbers actually show, where each side has a fair point, and how you can check the results yourself.

I'll cite the numbers as published and point out the caveats on both sides.

What LiteLLM Claimed About Its Rust Gateway

LiteLLM's benchmark post, published in July 2026, compared four gateways: the LiteLLM Rust beta, LiteLLM Python v1, Bifrost v1.6.4, and Portkey OSS. All of them pointed at the same local mock provider, so the numbers reflect each gateway's own overhead rather than real model latency.

The headline results looked like this:

Metric LiteLLM Rust Bifrost Portkey LiteLLM Python
p99 added latency ~0.7 ms 4.5 ms 2.3 ms 257.7 ms
Peak memory 21.8 MB 199.1 MB 90.4 MB 329.5 MB
Est. cost per 1M requests ~$0.000175 $0.001008 $0.001042 $0.015354
Requests per dollar-hour ~283,833 63,246 n/a n/a

From those, LiteLLM's site and blog drew four big claims:

  • ~7x lower overhead than Bifrost
  • ~9x less memory than Bifrost
  • 3.5x lower overhead than "the next AI gateway"
  • ~4.5x more requests per dollar than Bifrost

To be fair to LiteLLM, its own post includes some caveats. It says the benchmark is vendor-run, that streaming and the full feature set are still landing, and that readers should treat the differences as order-of-magnitude.

What Bifrost's Team Found in the Raw Data

Instead of running a new benchmark first, the Bifrost team went back to LiteLLM's own published files in the ai-gateway-bench repo and checked whether the headlines matched the data. Here are the main issues they raised.

1. The "7x" overhead number doesn't appear in the sweep

The 4.5 ms Bifrost overhead figure used for the "7x" claim doesn't show up in any row of LiteLLM's latency sweep. In the sweep itself, Bifrost and LiteLLM Rust trade places depending on concurrency (more on that below).

2. The "3.5x" claim is against Portkey, not Bifrost

The homepage line about "3.5x lower overhead than the next AI gateway" compares against Portkey (2.29 ms vs 0.66 ms). Easy to miss, and easy to misread as a Bifrost comparison.

3. "Memory at rest" is actually peak memory

The chart is labeled "memory at rest" and "idle," but the underlying column is peak_rss_mb. LiteLLM's files also contain three different memory pairs, and the headline uses the widest one (199.1 MB vs 21.8 MB). The other pairs are 144 MB vs 26.1 MB, and 282 to 298 MB vs 35 to 36 MB.

4. The configs weren't like-for-like

LiteLLM says logging, spend tracking, and persistence were disabled for every gateway. But according to the Bifrost team's reading, the Bifrost config in the repo doesn't actually set enable_logging to false, and Bifrost's logging plugin is enabled by default in gateway mode. So Bifrost was carrying logging overhead (including SQLite memory) that the Rust gateway wasn't. The Bifrost team notes this reading is based on newer code and not yet confirmed on v1.6.4.

5. An old Bifrost version

The benchmark used Bifrost v1.6.4. Since then, Bifrost has shipped v1.6.5 to v1.6.11 and v2.0.0 to v2.4.0, and the Bifrost changelog now lists v2.5.1. The Bifrost team says 2.x substantially reduced memory use, though this post doesn't measure that yet.

6. Missing setup details and single runs

The hardware, core counts, worker counts, and mock latency aren't published, so "identical hardware" can't be verified. Each result also appears to be a single run with no error bars, and the Bifrost team says rankings flip between files.

7. A partial Rust port

The Bifrost post points out that LiteLLM's Rust migration is still in progress. By source bytes, the repo is 3.11% Rust, and LiteLLM's own tracker reports 24% of major APIs built as of v1.107.0-rc.2. In the Bifrost team's words, the benchmark measures "a narrower Rust beta, not the full LiteLLM product rewritten in Rust."

Smaller issues

  • The throughput table shows a dash for Bifrost, which hides a gap of only 0.1% to 2.5%.
  • A footnote says "single client," but the sweep runs from 1 to 64 concurrent requests.
  • A "~21% CPU" figure doesn't appear in any Rust CPU file; the highest is 15.9%.
  • A concurrency-256 run exists in the results folder but was left out of the sweep.

The Numbers: What LiteLLM's Own Data Shows

These figures come straight from LiteLLM's own results/latency_vs_concurrency.csv in the ai-gateway-bench repo. I checked every value below against it. They match the figures in the Bifrost post, and every run had zero errors.

Added p99 latency over a direct call (ms)

Concurrency LiteLLM Rust Bifrost LiteLLM Python
1 +0.89 +0.75 +9.79
4 +0.61 +0.63 +26.95
16 +0.33 +0.89 +251.34
64 +40.28 +28.68 +546.04

The two trade places: Bifrost is lower at concurrency 1 and 64, LiteLLM Rust at 4 and 16. At concurrency 4, the gap is just 0.02 ms. That is a long way from "7x."

Throughput (requests per second)

Concurrency Direct LiteLLM Rust Bifrost LiteLLM Python
1 46.2 45.2 44.8 34.4
4 184.5 181.2 180.2 92.7
16 735.6 721.8 722.7 158.4
64 2,855.7 2,722.2 2,719.1 179.8

At the highest tested concurrency, Rust and Bifrost are separated by about 0.1%. For practical purposes, that's a tie.

Memory, CPU, and Concurrency 256: What the Files Show

One caveat before the numbers: they come from a setup where Bifrost was likely running with logging on and Rust wasn’t, on a Bifrost version that’s several releases old.

The Bifrost post reports these results openly, and I think they’re worth repeating:

  • Memory and CPU. Rust uses less in every file. Its highest memory reading (~36 MB) is below Bifrost's lowest (~144 MB). Mean CPU was 0.66% for Rust vs 2.59% for Bifrost.
  • Concurrency 256. In this single exploratory run, Rust had lower p50 (55.5 ms vs 89.3 ms) and lower p99 (2,667.8 ms vs 5,421.3 ms). Even the direct baseline went past the benchmark's threshold here, so the Bifrost team treats it as exploratory, not a capacity result.

The "requests per dollar" figure is a model

The 4.5x requests-per-dollar figure and the cost per 1M requests are calculated, not measured end to end. They're based on an assumed 4 vCPU / 16 GB instance and the CPU and memory numbers above. So if the memory comparison isn't like-for-like, the cost comparison inherits the same problem.

How to Run the LiteLLM Rust Benchmark Yourself

The best way to settle a benchmark argument is to run it on your own hardware. LiteLLM's benchmark lives in the BerriAI/ai-gateway-bench repo, and its blog outlines the basic flow:

# 1. Clone the repo and set up the environment
git clone https://github.com/BerriAI/ai-gateway-bench.git
cd ai-gateway-bench
python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt

# 2. Start the mock upstream provider
cargo run --release -p mock-upstream

# 3. Start each gateway pointed at the mock
#    (follow gateways/<name>/README.md for each one)

# 4. Run a scenario, then regenerate the charts
python analyze/make_chart.py

If you run it, these are the changes that make the comparison fair, based on the gaps the Bifrost team found:

  1. Use a current Bifrost build, not v1.6.4. The Bifrost setup docs show how to start the latest version with NPX or Docker.
  2. Match the configs. Turn logging off on every gateway, or turn it on for all of them. Don't compare one with logging against one without.
  3. Run each scenario several times and report the spread, not a single run.
  4. Write down your setup: machine type, CPU cores, worker counts, mock latency, and concurrency for every run.
  5. Label memory honestly. Report idle memory and peak memory separately.
  6. Keep every concurrency level you tested, including the ones where results get messy.

That's also exactly what the Bifrost team says it will do in Part 2: same benchmarks, current build, logging on and off, repeated trials, and full hardware disclosure.

How to Read Any LLM Gateway Benchmark

This back-and-forth is a useful reminder that a benchmark is only as good as its setup. Whatever gateway you're evaluating, these are the questions I'd ask before trusting a chart:

  • Is the raw data published? If you can't see the CSVs, you can't check the headline.
  • Do the headline numbers appear in the data? A "7x" claim should trace back to a specific row.
  • Were the configs equivalent? Logging, caching, plugins, and persistence all change results.
  • Which versions were tested? Gateways move fast, and an old build can be months behind.
  • What hardware was used? "Identical hardware" means little without the machine type.
  • How many runs? One run per scenario can't tell signal from noise.
  • Is it measured or modeled? Cost-per-request figures are often calculations built on other numbers.
  • Who ran it? Vendor benchmarks, including Bifrost's own, deserve the same scrutiny.

And most importantly: benchmark the features you'll actually use. A gateway with logging, budgets, fallbacks, and caching turned on behaves very differently from a stripped-down proxy forwarding requests to a mock.

Final Thoughts

LiteLLM's Rust gateway is a real step forward from LiteLLM Python. The jump from hundreds of milliseconds of added latency to under a millisecond is impressive, and its memory and CPU footprint is genuinely small.

But the headline comparisons against Bifrost don't hold up well against LiteLLM's own raw data. On latency, the two trade places depending on concurrency. On throughput, they're within about 0.1% at the top tested load. The bigger memory and cost gaps come from a setup that compared an old Bifrost version, likely with logging on, against a Rust beta with logging off.

So instead of "7x" and "9x," the honest summary is closer to this: on the tested setup, Bifrost and LiteLLM Rust perform about the same on latency and throughput, and Rust uses less memory and CPU in a configuration that wasn't like-for-like.

I'm looking forward to Part 2, where the Bifrost team plans to rerun everything with a current build and full disclosure. Until then, the best advice is the simplest one: don't pick a gateway from a headline. Run the benchmark on your own workload, with the features you'll actually use.

If you want to try Bifrost yourself, it's open source and you can find it at getmaxim.ai/bifrost.

articles.description: NVIDIA's GPU Is Closed Hardware With a Compiler Inside It. Here's What Reverse Engineering...
articles.body_html:
NVIDIA's GPU Is Closed Hardware With a Compiler Inside It. Here's What Reverse Engineering Actually Found.

NVIDIA documents PTX and keeps SASS, the machine code your kernels actually run as, undocumented. Everything below that line was learned the hard way, by timing hand-written instructions on real silicon. This covers what that work found, who did it, and which results I'd trust.

The Compiler Is Part of the Hardware

The best single paper here is Analyzing Modern NVIDIA GPU Cores from UPC Barcelona. Its method is simple. Write short sequences of hand-written SASS, wrap them in reads of the GPU clock counter, and use the elapsed cycles to confirm or refute a hypothesis. The authors used CuAssembler for this, the latest in a line of third-party assemblers that began with MaxAS.

The central finding is that modern NVIDIA hardware doesn't check most hazards itself. It relies on the compiler to encode dependencies in control bits on every instruction. Three mechanisms do the work:

  • Stall counter. For fixed-latency producers, the compiler sets a per-warp counter, and the hardware doesn't check RAW hazards for these instructions at all. A wrong value gives a wrong answer, not a stall.
  • Dependence counters. For variable-latency work like memory loads, each warp has six counters (SB0–SB5), each counting up to 63, with a 6-bit mask per instruction saying which to wait on. One counter can be released at register read (for WAR hazards) and another at write-back, which matters because source operands are often read hundreds of cycles before the result lands.
  • Reuse bit. The register file cache is software-managed through a per-operand reuse bit.

Two findings contradict what academic simulators assumed. There is no operand collector stage, since variable operand-fetch time would make fixed instruction latencies impossible. And the scheduler policy is "Compiler Guided Greedy Then Youngest", where the compiler's control bits steer a greedy-then-youngest warp selector.

The bank-conflict experiment is a good example of the method. Two back-to-back FFMAs took five cycles with odd source registers, six with one even, and seven with two even. That timing exposes a two-bank register file with one read port per bank.

The cost argument is where it gets interesting. Per the paper, the control-bit scheme needs 41 bits per warp, about 0.09% of an SM's register file, versus 5.32% for a scoreboard design with 63 consumers per entry. The authors' simulator model reached 13.98% mean error against an RTX A6000, 18.24 points better than Accel-Sim's baseline. They compare it to AMD, where a waitcnt instruction requires an explicit extra instruction rather than control bits.

Limits to keep in mind: the scheduler behavior is confirmed only for warps within one CTA, and the authors say they couldn't find a read policy matching every case. It's validated on Ampere and Turing, and the Hopper and Blackwell generations extend it with new tensor instructions.

Who Has Mapped the Rest

Mesa's NVK external hardware docs are the best index of public NVIDIA reverse engineering. They credit Kuter Dinel's nv_isa_solver with Hopper and Ada instruction encodings, point to nv-shader-tools for disassembly and fuzzing, and list envytools for Maxwell and earlier. They also describe tooling for dumping command sequences from the proprietary driver (envyhooks) and disassembling them (nv_push_dump).

That work feeds a real driver. Per the nouveau status page, NVK became a conformant Vulkan 1.4 implementation in December 2024, and was enabled for Blackwell and Kepler starting with Mesa 25.2.

The Driver Split Almost Nobody Mentions

The open-gpu-kernel-modules release changed what's reversible. NVIDIA started shipping open kernel modules with the R515 driver branch. Behind them sits a firmware boundary: the GPU System Processor is a RISC-V coprocessor, and NVIDIA's Resource Manager is split into a host CPU portion and a GSP portion. That has two consequences:

  1. Nouveau on RTX 40-series and later requires the GSP firmware blobs.
  2. There was no stable ABI for the GSP firmware at that point, so each driver version brought revised firmware. Treat the ABI point as dated, since it describes 2023.

The reverse-engineering target therefore moved. You can read the host side of the RM interface, but the firmware stays closed.

A Clean-Room CUDA Stack, With Footnotes

The most striking recent claim is a preprint on a clean-room toolchain for the GB10 (DGX Spark), with code in the CUDA++ repo. Its reported approach has three parts:

  • A roughly 900-line driver client written against the open kernel module's public headers, reproducing the object, memory, channel and submission sequence libcuda performs over ioctl.
  • Instruction encodings recovered from three sources: NVIDIA's compiler as an offline oracle on probe kernels, the open-source Mesa NAK compiler, and the chip itself, with arithmetic models fitted until output matched bit for bit.
  • Launches assembled in the order Mesa's NVK uses, with the launch descriptor (QMD) built directly.

The headline result: a 35-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model served with zero CUDA libraries mapped in the process, its output identical to a host reference. Read the caveats before repeating that. It's a single-author Zenodo preprint, not peer reviewed, and the author says it was built by one engineer directing AI coding agents. The paper states its own boundaries: NVIDIA's open kernel module remains in the path, and GSP firmware stays NVIDIA's because the chip verifies its signature. So this is a replacement for the user-space stack, not for the whole trust chain.

Blackwell: Measured Versus Marketed

Two microbenchmark papers cover Blackwell, and they differ in how much to trust them. The GB203 study reports that low-precision mma.sync PTX instructions translate to new SASS opcodes (QMMA and OMMA) on Blackwell, where Hopper consistently uses HMMA.

The B200 study describes the architectural shift in more detail. Per the paper, Blackwell replaces warp-synchronous MMA with tcgen05.mma, a single-thread instruction, with operands from shared memory or a new Tensor Memory (TMEM). TMEM is 256 KB per SM, laid out as 128 lanes by 512 columns of 32-bit cells, managed in software through the tcgen05 instruction family. Its PTX-to-SASS table maps FP4 to OMMA and FP6/FP8 to QMMA, and FP64 is not supported by tcgen05.mma.

I'd verify its numbers before quoting them. The paper says it couldn't share code under double-blind review, uses hedged phrasing such as "consistent with a spatial array design" for its microarchitecture inferences, and says dual-die behavior across the NV-HBI link remains future work. A reasonable way to use it: take the instruction mappings and TMEM structure as leads, and re-measure any latency or throughput figure on your own hardware.

What Reverse Engineering Can't Tell You

It shows structure, not intent. Microbenchmarks recover latencies, port counts and policies, and they say nothing about why NVIDIA chose them. They also age fast, since each generation changes tensor instructions while the control-bit scheme carries forward. As a cross-check, the UPC authors note NVIDIA's own diagrams show significant changes limited mostly to tensor cores, ray tracing units and minor features.

The practical rule for this space: trust a claim only if it traces to a timing experiment, an open driver header, or a disassembly you can reproduce.

articles.body_html:
The 90% AI Code Quota: Why Big Tech Is Manufacturing Fragile Codebases

Imagine being a senior software engineer at Meta, and the baseline requirement to survive performance reviews and avoid layoffs is: having an LLM generate at least 90% of your code.

This isn't dystopian fiction. It was just publicly documented by senior engineer Evan X. Merz, who was laid off from Meta in May. In his recent retrospective, Merz revealed that pumping out 90%+ AI-generated code was the table stakes for maintaining a decent performance rating. Engineers who focused on architectural durability, deep testing, and systemic code quality were pushed out. At his new Big Tech employer, that expectation has reportedly escalated to 100%.

The result? Management dashboards celebrate historic commit spikes and "10X productivity," while production environments crumble beneath an unmaintainable house of cards.

The Four Fatal Flaws of AI-Generated Codebases

Merz's breakdown highlights four critical architectural points of failure that are now quietly infecting enterprise software across the industry:

1. Shallow, Synthetic Test Suites

Modern LLMs optimize for line-level test coverage metrics rather than behavioral edge cases. They happily generate hundreds of lines testing trivial getters and setters, while end-to-end tests merely re-validate happy paths already covered in the codebase. Coverage metrics read 95% green, but the application explodes under the first non-trivial edge case in production.

2. Over-Engineered Accidental Complexity

LLMs dogmatically enforce patterns like DRY to an absurd extreme. Instead of writing a straightforward, readable routine, an agent will splinter a simple task into three separate helper abstractions and generic indirection layers. This rigidity makes production debugging a nightmare for human engineers.

3. Total Loss of Systemic Comprehension

As organizations mandate that engineers outsource thinking to AI models, human developers stop understanding the core data structures and underlying algorithmic flows. When engineers no longer understand their own architecture, code reviews become ceremonial rubber-stamping.

4. The Speed Trap of Unreviewed Pull Requests

When code is generated in seconds, the velocity of pull requests overwhelms human review capacity. Senior engineers skim PRs in seconds. Merz observed top engineers approving pull requests where simple CSS states were replaced by 30 lines of brittle JavaScript mouseover event listeners. Nobody paused to ask, "What are we actually building?"

Velocity Is Not Productivity

Writing 1,000 lines of code you don't understand is not speed—it is taking out a high-interest payday loan on technical debt.

AI models are blind to any architecture that doesn't fit within their immediate context window. Handing a developer who doesn't understand underlying systems an AI code generator doesn't build a cathedral; it just helps them drill through load-bearing walls faster.

When production inevitably crashes, the managers who celebrated commit velocity won't find a single engineer who knows how the machine works.
