articles.title: What a Number-Guessing Game Teaches About Binary Search and Vue State
articles.description: A higher-or-lower number game can give misleading hints or attempt counts if the secret and round...
articles.body_html:
A higher-or-lower number game can give misleading hints or attempt counts if the secret and round state change at the wrong time. I'll use a small Vue implementation to show how to keep those updates consistent, then explain why midpoint guesses put a worst-case bound on the number of attempts.

The player chooses a range, submits a number, and gets a high, low, or correct result. There is no computer player performing binary search. The useful connection is that the feedback gives a human player exactly the information needed to shrink a search interval.

Pick One Secret for the Whole Round

The implementation offers upper bounds of 10, 50, 100, and 1,000, always starting at 1. The target generator is deliberately ordinary:

function randomTarget(max) {
  return Math.floor(Math.random() * max) + 1;
}

Multiplying a random value in the interval from zero up to, but not including, one produces a value below max. Taking the floor gives integers from zero through max - 1; adding one moves the range to the numbers the UI promises.

The target must be generated once per round, not once per submission. Otherwise a helpful-looking “too low” message would describe a secret that might no longer exist when the next guess arrives. That destroys the premise of interval narrowing.

The round reset is also a state transition, not just another random assignment:

function newGame() {
  if (typeof window === "undefined") return;
  target.value = randomTarget(maxNum.value);
  currentGuess.value = null;
  guesses.value = [];
  won.value = false;
  feedback.value = "";
  feedbackType.value = "";
}

I like reading this function as a checklist of everything belonging to one round. The secret changes, input clears, history disappears, the win lock resets, and the previous hint goes away together.

Changing the selected range calls this same reset. Keeping two partially different reset implementations would make it easy to carry an old guess history into a new range or leave the submission button disabled after a previous win.

Record the Attempt Before Announcing the Win

The submission function first checks whether the round is already won, rejects an empty or nonnumeric input, and reports numbers outside the selected bounds. Only then does it compare the guess with the secret.

In the successful branch, the guess is appended before the attempt count is used:

if (g === target.value) {
  guesses.value.push({ value: g, dir: "correct" });
  won.value = true;
  feedback.value = t("guessNumber.correct", { n: guesses.value.length });
  feedbackType.value = "correct";
  if (bestScore.value === null || guesses.value.length < bestScore.value) {
    bestScore.value = guesses.value.length;
  }
}

The history is held in a Vue ref, so both the comparison and the stored score read guesses.value.length. More importantly, the successful submission is included before either read. Counting first and appending afterward would underreport every win by one attempt.

Each history item stores both the submitted value and its direction. The template derives its arrow and appearance from that record. I would rather keep that compact structured history than try to reconstruct previous results from translated feedback strings.

The best score is a separate ref, so starting a new round does not erase it. It is not stored in localStorage, and it is not partitioned by range. A one-guess win in the smallest range can therefore remain the best score when the player switches to 1–1,000. Its lifetime is that of the component instance: refreshing the page or unmounting and recreating the component loses the record. It is a convenience, not a normalized measure of skill.

Higher-or-Lower Feedback Defines a Search Interval

Suppose the secret is somewhere from 1 through 100. Guessing 50 and hearing “too low” eliminates everything from 1 through 50, including the number just tried. The remaining candidates are 51 through 100.

Guessing near the middle of the remaining interval keeps the larger of the two possible remaining groups small. Repeating that strategy is binary search performed by the player. It is the same idea used to search a sorted collection, except the game supplies a comparison instead of exposing an array.

For an inclusive interval [low, high], I would choose Math.floor((low + high) / 2). After a “too low” result for g, the next lower bound is g + 1; after “too high,” the next upper bound is g - 1. Excluding the failed guess matters: keeping it as a candidate can make the search repeat a value instead of progressing, especially when only two candidates remain.

For a range containing 100 distinct targets, seven guesses suffice in the worst case with an appropriate midpoint strategy. More generally, a comparison tree with at most k guesses can accommodate up to 2^k - 1 target values: each comparison can finish at its own node or continue into one of two smaller intervals.

The smallest sufficient bound for N targets is therefore Math.ceil(Math.log2(N + 1)). Six guesses cover at most 63 targets; seven cover 127. That explains the seven-guess guarantee for 100 targets without assuming that every guess has only two outcomes: equality ends the search at the current node.

That bound does not mean every game takes seven attempts. The secret might be the first midpoint, and random guesses can occasionally get lucky. Nor does it mean the component calculates a recommended next guess; it only provides feedback and history.

The component also keeps the input bounds at 1 and the selected maximum, not the narrowed interval. Repeating an earlier guess, or guessing something earlier feedback already ruled out, still counts as an attempt. The guarantee depends on the player's strategy; the interface does not enforce it.

This distinction makes the game a useful teaching example. The state machine supplies trustworthy observations, while the search strategy is a separate layer of reasoning. You can explain interval halving without pretending the application contains a solver that is absent from its source.

Browser Games Still Have Initialization and Input Boundaries

The component begins with a deterministic target of 50 and calls newGame() from onMounted. Randomness is deferred until the browser has mounted the page, rather than producing different secrets during server rendering and the browser's first render.

For a casual guessing game, Math.random() is adequate. It is not a cryptographic secret generator, and a target stored in client-side state is not protected from someone inspecting the application. This is not an architecture for competitive play or prize distribution.

There is also a narrower validation gap: the submission logic checks numeric conversion and bounds but does not check Number.isInteger(g). A fractional guess inside the range can be counted as an attempt even though the generated target is always an integer. For example, 50.5 against a secret of 51 produces “too low” and enters the history. The number input's default step can mark that value invalid, but the click handler and Enter handler call submitGuess directly, without a validating form submission. An integer guard before recording history would close that gap; it is not part of the current implementation.

I turned this small state-machine example into a free browser game: Guess the Number Game.

articles.title: Your `setTimeout(fn, 0)` Doesn't Run Next. `queueMicrotask` Does.
articles.description: setTimeout(fn, 0) feels like 'run this right after the current code.' It isn't — every pending promise cuts in line first. queueMicrotask puts your callback in that same fast lane, on purpose.
articles.body_html:
The test called the function, then did await Promise.resolve(), then checked the state. It failed. Not flaky — failed every single run, for this one function and no other.

The function wasn't broken. It deferred its work with setTimeout(fn, 0), and await Promise.resolve() doesn't wait for that. It can't. By the time setTimeout even gets a turn, that await is long finished.

The fix was a one-word swap. Understanding why it mattered took longer.

The batcher that looked obviously right

Here's the function in question — a tiny update batcher for a settings panel. Call it five times in a row and it should write once, not five times:

let pending = new Map();
let scheduled = false;

function queueUpdate(key, value) {
  pending.set(key, value);
  if (!scheduled) {
    scheduled = true;
    setTimeout(flush, 0); // "run this once, right after the current burst of calls"
  }
}

function flush() {
  scheduled = false;
  applyUpdates(pending);
  pending.clear();
}

Click a few toggles fast, and flush runs once with the final values. Manual testing looks perfect. Then someone writes the obvious test:

test("coalesces rapid updates into one flush", async () => {
  queueUpdate("theme", "dark");
  queueUpdate("theme", "darker");

  await Promise.resolve(); // "let things settle"

  expect(getStoreValue("theme")).toBe("darker"); // fails — still unset
});

That await Promise.resolve() is a common idiom for "let the microtask queue drain before I assert." It isn't broken, and it isn't a flake you can retry away. flush genuinely has not run yet when the assertion checks — because setTimeout, even at 0, schedules into a queue that a microtask-flushing await never visits.

Two queues, and one of them always finishes first

Every JavaScript engine actually runs two separate queues, and they are not interchangeable:

  • The microtask queue — where Promise.resolve().then(fn) and queueMicrotask(fn) both land, in the same queue.
  • The macrotask (task) queue — where setTimeout, UI events, and I/O callbacks land.

The HTML spec's event loop rule is blunt about the order: once the current script finishes, the engine drains the entire microtask queue — including any new microtasks queued while draining — before it's allowed to touch the next macrotask, or render a frame. This isn't "promises happen to be fast." It's a hard ordering guarantee, and every major engine (V8, SpiderMonkey, JavaScriptCore) implements it the same way.

The classic proof:

console.log("1 — sync");

setTimeout(() => console.log("4 — setTimeout"), 0);

Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log("3 — microtask"));

console.log("2 — sync");

// always: 1, 2, 3, 4

That part you may already know. Here's the part that surprises people: it's not a head start, it's a standing rule. Chain ten .then() calls after that same setTimeout, each one scheduling the next only once the previous resolves, and all ten still finish before the timeout fires — because the microtask queue keeps draining as long as anything is in it, and a .then() callback adds its continuation back onto that same queue. The setTimeout doesn't get a turn until the queue is empty, however long that takes.

🎮 Try it yourself

▶️ Open the interactive playground →

Runs right in your browser — poke at it and watch the concept react live.

The fix: schedule into the queue you're actually being checked against

Swap the one line:

function queueUpdate(key, value) {
  pending.set(key, value);
  if (!scheduled) {
    scheduled = true;
    queueMicrotask(flush); // same queue as every .then() and every await
  }
}

queueMicrotask still coalesces every synchronous call in the current burst into a single flush — that part of the behavior doesn't change, because the microtask checkpoint only runs once the call stack is empty either way. What changes is which queue flush sits in. Now it's the same queue await Promise.resolve() empties. The test passes, because flush — queued first — runs before the test's own await gets its turn, not after.

queueMicrotask isn't exotic: it's Baseline, widely supported since 2020 in every major browser, and it's been a global in Node since v11. It takes a callback, returns nothing, and that's the entire API.

Where setTimeout is still the right call

Don't read this as "replace every setTimeout(0)." Microtasks are not free — the queue has to fully drain before the browser can render a frame or respond to a click, so a microtask that keeps re-queuing itself can freeze the page solid. If what you actually need is to let the browser breathe — paint a frame, handle an input event — between chunks of work, you want a macrotask-shaped yield (setTimeout, or scheduler.yield where it's available), not a microtask. queueMicrotask answers "run this before anything else gets a turn." It is the wrong tool for "give the user a moment."

One more gotcha worth knowing if you touch Node: process.nextTick() jumps the line even ahead of queueMicrotask — Node fully drains its nextTick queue before the promise/microtask queue on every turn. If you're writing isomorphic code, queueMicrotask is the one that behaves the same in the browser and in Node; process.nextTick doesn't exist in the browser at all.

The test wasn't wrong, and neither was the original instinct to defer the flush. setTimeout(fn, 0) was just answering a different question than the one being asked — "run after the next paint," instead of "run after absolutely everything currently promised, and not one tick later." queueMicrotask is the second sentence, spelled correctly.

🧠 Test yourself

Think it clicked? Take the 7-question quiz →

Instant feedback, a hint on every question, and an explanation for each answer — right or wrong.

Where else in your code is a setTimeout(fn, 0) quietly promising "right after" but delivering "eventually"? I'd bet there's at least one test file that already knows.

articles.title: I audited 100 third-party VS Code extensions. 19 ship known-CVE deps
articles.description: Live Server — 84 million installs, the top row of the results below — bundles websocket-driver 0.7.4...
articles.body_html:
Live Server — 84 million installs, the top row of the results below — bundles websocket-driver 0.7.4 and gets caught by CRITICAL GHSA-xv26-6w52-cph6 / CVE-2026-54466. It is the loudest finding in a scan of the top 100 third-party extensions on the VS Code Marketplace, but not the only one.

Every finding below is at the evidence level "Present": the vulnerable (name, version) pair is inside the shipped .vsix bundle. I haven't shown that any of them is reachable or exploitable; the levels are explained further down. The point of the post is not "these extensions can be hacked." It is that VS Code gives users no interface to see the dependency surface of what they install, and I could not find a publicly documented Marketplace mechanism that re-checks published bundles against advisories that appear after release.

Why I ran this

Two reasons.

Workspace Trust mitigated the easy extension attacks. Since VS Code 1.57 (May 2021), an extension that does not declare capabilities.untrustedWorkspaces support is disabled when you open a repo marked untrusted. The classic "clone a malicious repo, press F5, get RCE via .vscode/settings.json" class is now gated behind the user's trust decision. The gate is not absolute — a user who clicks "Trust" through habit re-opens the surface, extensions that declare support run anyway, and the check does not reach dependency CVEs — but the easy path is meaningfully smaller than it was four years ago.

But what is under the hood? VS Code extensions ship their own node_modules inside the .vsix bundle. Whatever the maintainer npm installed the day they published is frozen in. Advisories published after that release do not propagate backwards; I could not find a publicly documented mechanism in the Marketplace or in VS Code that tells either the maintainer or the user "an advisory now applies to something you shipped three months ago." That's the frozen-bundle problem.

I wanted to measure it.

Method

Reproducible in ~15 minutes with stdlib Python. No scanner install required.

Snapshot: Marketplace and OSV queried on 2026-11-08. Install counts and advisory data are from that date; both change over time.

1. Pull the top 200 extensions from the Marketplace extensionquery API, sorted by install count.

2. Filter the sample. Drop first-party publishers (ms-*, vscjava, VisualStudioExptTeam, MicrosoftDocs, redhat, Microsoft, MS-CEINTL), GitHub, and anything whose name or display title contains language-pack, icon-theme, material-theme, vscode-icons, theme, keybindings, or cheatsheet. From 200 raw entries this kept 116; I took the top 100 by install count. The precise phrase is "top 100 non-first-party, non-theme code extensions by install count on 2026-11-08", not "top 100 extensions on the Marketplace".

3. Download each .vsix from the /vspackage endpoint. A .vsix is a zip. Gentle pacing at 1 req/sec. All 100 downloads succeeded (~1.6 GB total).

4. Enumerate every node_modules/<pkg>/package.json inside extension/ after unzipping. For the top 100 this gave 1,357 nested dependency manifests, of which 935 were unique by (name, version) (712 unique package names, many shipped in two or more extensions at the same version). 64 of the 100 extensions had zero shipped node_modules entries — some genuinely have no runtime deps, most are built with esbuild/webpack/rollup into a single JS file, and the scanner is blind to CVEs inside those bundles. See Limitations.

5. Batch-query OSV.dev at /v1/querybatch — 500 queries per request, free, no auth. OSV covers GHSA, so every npm advisory shows up. Collect every matched advisory.

6. Score and rank. For each (extension, dependency, advisory) row I keep the worst severity and compute score = installs × severity_weight with CRITICAL=10, HIGH=5, MODERATE=2, LOW=1. The results table below is sorted by install count — most-shipped at the top. The score column is in the companion CSV for anyone who wants to re-rank.

Affected means: at least one (dependency, version) pair inside the extension bundle has a matching OSV advisory of any severity. It does not imply the code path is loaded at runtime, that user input can reach it, or that any impact is realised.

Six Python scripts, 527 lines, stdlib only, plus diff_runs.py for comparing two runs. Three APIs: Marketplace's extensionquery, Marketplace's /vspackage, OSV's querybatch. No auth. No quota.

Results

Three different counts, because the numbers answer three different questions:

  • 19 / 100 sampled extensions had at least one (dependency, version) inside their bundle matching an OSV advisory.
  • 103 unique (extension, dependency) pairs with ≥1 matching advisory. A pair can match multiple advisories — a dep may have several open advisories or be below more than one fix threshold — so this is less than the total advisory matches.
  • 149 distinct OSV record IDs across those 103 pairs — all GHSAs; alias-overlap check against each record's CVE aliases found no duplicate underlying vulnerability (i.e. 149 records = 149 underlying issues for this sample, with 2 of the 149 having no CVE alias). One advisory often appears in many extensions (lodash, minimatch, braces, brace-expansion and semver show up most often), so advisory-id-count and pair-count diverge.
  • Severity breakdown of the 103 pairs, each counted once at its worst-severity advisory: 12 CRITICAL, 61 HIGH, 24 MODERATE, 6 LOW.

Sorted by install count on the snapshot date. "Worst sev" is the maximum severity across all matched advisories inside that extension's bundle.

# Installs Extension Worst sev Lead deps (abridged)
1 84,254,316 ritwickdey.LiveServer CRITICAL websocket-driver 0.7.4, braces, lodash, js-yaml, +14 more
2 42,727,107 formulahendry.code-runner HIGH braces, picomatch (ReDoS class)
3 19,651,537 christian-kohler.path-intellisense HIGH json5, minimatch, brace-expansion
4 18,267,232 batisteo.vscode-django HIGH toml

Full per-extension, per-advisory breakdown with versions and OSV IDs is in SUMMARY.md and DATASET.csv in the companion repo.

Levels of evidence

The headline number is Present, not Exploitable. The distinction matters, and most writeups in this space blur it.

Level What has been established
Present A vulnerable (name, version) pair is in the shipped bundle
Loaded The extension's runtime actually loads this copy of the module
Reachable A code path that reaches the vulnerable code is exercised during normal use
Exploitable An adversary-controlled input reaches the vulnerable code in a reproduced PoC

Every number in the Results table is Present. For a few deps I believe Loaded is very likely from static reading, but I did not instrument the extensions to prove it. Reachable and Exploitable are not claimed for any row.

Publishing at Present is still worth it: the frozen-bundle pattern is a measurable property of the ecosystem, and 19 / 100 is a baseline you can compare future runs against. Upgrading individual rows to higher evidence levels is per-extension work, not a batch job.

Limitations

Three things to flag before anyone cites a number from this post (and the evidence level above: every row is Present, nothing more):

  1. The scanner cannot see dependencies inside bundled JS. It walks extension/node_modules/<pkg>/package.json. An extension built with esbuild, webpack, or rollup into a single JS file contains its dependencies' code but no per-dep package.json, so the scanner records zero deps for it. 64 of the 100 sampled extensions had zero shipped node_modules entries (a measured count). Some genuinely have no runtime deps; the rest are most likely bundled (I did not individually inspect each build output), and whatever CVEs are riding inside those bundles are invisible to this method. So 19 / 100 is the observed rate of extensions in this sample where this manifest-based inventory matched at least one OSV advisory — not a lower bound on vulnerable code, and not an estimate of overall prevalence of vulnerable code in VS Code extensions. Covering the bundled case properly needs an SBOM at build time, which the Marketplace does not require.
  2. The sample is top-by-installs, not top-by-risk. A niche extension with 50k installs might ship worse code than a top-10 extension and wouldn't appear in this cut. The chosen sample serves the "most-shipped bundles" question; a risk-weighted sample would look different.
  3. One snapshot is a data point, not a trend. The repo pins 2026-11-08 under runs/ and ships diff_runs.py for quarterly comparisons. The next re-run is scheduled for 2027-02-08.

A closer look at Live Server

The highest-install row in the table. Tracing it as far as the static scan allows.

ritwickdey.LiveServer 5.7.10 ships extension/node_modules/live-server/ — the live-server npm package, which the extension wraps as its HTTP + live-reload server. live-server depends on faye-websocket, which depends on websocket-driver 0.7.4 — present under extension/node_modules/websocket-driver/.

GHSA-xv26-6w52-cph6 / CVE-2026-54466 — "websocket-driver: Message corruption via abuse of protocol length headers". Severity critical per the GitHub Advisory API. Vulnerable range: < 0.7.5; first patched version: 0.7.5. Advisory published on 2026-07-15 (cross-checked against the GitHub Advisory API on 2026-11-08).

The chronology is the interesting part. Live Server v5.7.10 was last updated on the Marketplace on 2026-02-27 — about five months before the GHSA on websocket-driver was published. The maintainer wasn't ignoring a known advisory. The advisory simply did not exist yet. A reasonable npm install on 2026-02-27 picks up websocket-driver 0.7.4, which was clean at the time. Five months later an advisory is filed against that version. The bundle on disk does not change, and I could not find anything user-visible in the Marketplace that surfaces the new risk.

Reachability without a PoC: faye-websocket is live-server's WebSocket layer, and the live-reload channel is the extension's headline feature, so this copy of websocket-driver is very likely loaded when Live Server is running. I did not instrument the extension to confirm, and I did not attempt a crafted-frame reproduction — the finding sits at Present and likely Loaded, no higher. If you do the dynamic work, the repo has everything needed to reproduce the inventory and I'll link verified follow-ups.

Static takeaway: an extension ranked 8th by installs on the unfiltered Marketplace on 2026-11-08 (and 1st in this filtered third-party sample) ships a CRITICAL advisory on a module that sits under its headline feature, four months after the advisory was filed, with nothing user-visible in the install flow flagging it.

Three observations from the shape of this list

Install count is not a maintenance signal. 84M installs doesn't mean anyone upstream is watching the advisory feed on your behalf. It means a lot of people downloaded the thing once. The maintainer may or may not be active — in Live Server's case they shipped a release about eight months before this snapshot, and the vulnerable dep is still there because the advisory postdates the release.

The still-on-disk-after-dormancy problem. Bracket Pair Colorizer 2 was last updated on the Marketplace in March 2022. VS Code has shipped native bracket pair colorization in the core editor since 2021 (editor.bracketPairColorization.enabled). The extension has accumulated roughly 6.7M Marketplace installs; the public count doesn't say how many active copies remain, but every active copy still loads on VS Code startup if enabled and still ships minimist with a CRITICAL prototype-pollution advisory. VS Code does not uninstall dormant extensions on your behalf.

Lots of overlap on the same tired deps. brace-expansion, minimatch, braces, lodash, semver show up across most of the affected extensions. One upstream fix, one maintainer release, several vulnerable extensions become clean. Maintainers usually don't notice until someone emails them.

The size side of the problem

Not every extension ships a big bundle, but the ones that do carry a lot of dead surface along for the ride. Live Server's unpacked extension/ directory is 30 MB, and almost all of that is extension/node_modules/. The actual Live Server glue code — the TypeScript that bridges live-server into the VS Code extension API — is tiny; the bulk is transitive dependencies the npm resolver dragged in.

Bundling with esbuild or webpack can substantially reduce unused code — whether it removes a specific vulnerable path depends on the dependency graph, side effects, dynamic imports, and build configuration. A transitive dep that is called stays in the bundle, and the vulnerable code path inside it still ships, but bundling typically shrinks both the bundle and the matched-advisory count. Measure the audit output before and after; do not assume the number went to zero.

For comparison: Code Runner's whole unpacked tree is 1.8 MB (1.2 MB of node_modules). Still shipping two HIGH advisories, but far less dead surface by volume.

What VS Code could do

OSV's /v1/querybatch is free. The Marketplace already runs malware scans on .vsix uploads. Running OSV against the shipped node_modules of a .vsix on upload — exactly what the scripts in the repo do — would surface the top-20 findings on this list in an afternoon. This same approach runs into the bundled-JS blind spot (see Limitations); covering bundled extensions properly needs an SBOM at build time, which vsce could require as a publisher input.

More importantly, the same scan could run periodically against already-published .vsix artefacts and notify the publisher when a new advisory applies. A count surfaced on the public install page would let users factor it into their choice. That's the backfill mechanism I could not find in the public Marketplace feature set at the snapshot date — if one exists internally, I'd update the post.

What maintainers can do

For anyone shipping a VS Code extension right now:

  • Audit the final .vsix, not just the source tree. npm audit against your working copy reports what's in your lockfile — a source-tree check, not an inventory of what shipped. For extensions that ship unpacked node_modules: vsce package, unzip, enumerate every (name, version) under extension/node_modules/*/package.json (and the @scope/name variant), query OSV. That's an artifact-level inventory for the unpacked part — exactly what audit_extensions.py in the repo does. For extensions you ship as a bundled JS file this inventory misses your deps entirely: generate an SBOM at build time (e.g. CycloneDX from your bundler's manifest), keep provenance linking the SBOM to the published .vsix, and audit the SBOM alongside the artifact. Neither path proves anything about reachability or exploitability on its own.
  • Bundle with esbuild or webpack. Shipped node_modules directories are often large and contain code the extension never calls. Tree-shaking typically reduces both size and the matched-advisory count. Not a guarantee — vulnerable paths inside deps you do call still ship. Measure before/after.
  • Re-audit already-published releases on a schedule. The chronology in the Live Server case — advisory published five months after the release — isn't unusual. A quarterly re-check of your already-published .vsix against OSV catches advisories that appear after you ship. Treat it as the backfill the Marketplace does not provide.

What users can do

Honest answer: not much, today.

  • Don't install extensions you don't use. It's the one step that removes the dependencies entirely.
  • Prefer extensions whose Marketplace page shows a recent "last updated" date. A long-stale date is a yellow flag. Recent activity isn't a clean bill of health — Live Server was updated about eight months before this snapshot and still ships a CRITICAL — but a long gap is clearly worse.
  • Keep Workspace Trust ON. It does not address dependency CVEs, but it gates the much worse "arbitrary RCE on repo open" class behind an explicit prompt.

Running it yourself 

query_marketplace.py     87 lines — Marketplace extensionquery
filter_publishers.py     49 lines — drop first-party + themes
download_vsix.py         61 lines — /vspackage, 1 req/sec
audit_extensions.py     137 lines — unpack + OSV batch
rank_findings.py        113 lines — enrich with GHSA severity
summarize.py             80 lines — collapse + markdown
                        ---
                        527 lines — stdlib only

diff_runs.py            108 lines — compare two snapshots

Running it quarterly against the top 100 is a useful ambient check. Running against the top 500 is the same with an hour-long download. I'll probably do both and track the shape over the next year — next snapshot already scheduled for 2027-02-08.

Full per-extension breakdown with every (dep, version, advisory) row, the CSV dataset and the scripts are in the companion repo:

https://github.com/vadimtoptunov/kassi-vsix-audit

If you re-run this against a different sample or a later snapshot and the shape of the list has moved, send me the diff — I'll link it.

articles.title: I hid 6 secret glitches in my agent's video game. They make it easier. Can it find them?
articles.description: Flash plays a rhythm-runner level from raw pixels. So I hid speedrun-style skips in it: a pad fling over a spike pit, a ghost ship, spike surfing. Nothing on screen gives them away. Here's how I built them, and what they're worth.
articles.body_html:
My agent can beat a platformer it has never seen.

Flash is my open source agent for the terminal and the browser. One of its tools, play_realtime, lets the model write a tiny reflex: a JavaScript function that runs every single frame inside the page, reads the canvas pixels, and presses keys. The model can't think 60 times a second, so it writes the thing that can.

To test it, Flash ships with Flash Dash: a little level built like a rhythm runner. A square runs right on its own. Spikes kill. Blue blocks are solid. An orange pad launches you. A cyan ring gives you a second jump in mid-air. Then a gate turns you into a ship you fly between pillars.

The reference reflex beats it on the first try, from the pixels alone, in 21.11 seconds.

That's a solved problem. So I asked a better one:

Can the agent find what the level never tells it?

Glitches that help

Every speedrunner knows the feeling: the game has a crack in it, and if you find it, you skip half a level. Nobody explains these. You find them by doing the weird thing on purpose and noticing what happened.

So there's now a second level, flash-dash-glitched. Same layout, same colors, pixel for pixel. The only differences are a line under the canvas, "This level has secrets: find them and it gets easier", a clock, and a counter in the corner: secrets 0/6.

Here's what's hiding in it:

# Secret How it works What it's worth
1 Pad fling Tap again in the instant after a pad throws you. You're flung way up and forward, clean over the spike pit. From the last pad, over the finish line.
2 Ring slingshot Hold the jump through the ring instead of tapping it. It slings you 300 pixels further than a tap.
3 Spike surf Come down square on a spike's very tip. It bounces you like a pad instead of killing you.
4 Wall climb Hit a block's side with the jump held. You climb it instead of dying.
5 Arch backflip Jump through the green speed arch. The level slows down instead of speeding up, until the ship.
6 Ceiling ghost Grind the ship along the ceiling. It goes translucent and passes through pillars until you let go.

Each one needs something a careful player never does. You don't tap in mid-air after a pad: there's nothing to tap at. You don't hold through a ring, you tap it. You definitely don't aim for spikes. That's the point. A player that only ever does the safe thing will finish the level and find zero.

Which is exactly what happened.

The baseline: zero secrets

I ran the reference reflex, the one that beats the normal level, on the glitched one:

Ran 1267 frames in 21.11s, 47 actions; stopped: until was true.
The page's title now: Flash Dash: won in 21.11s, 0 secrets

Same time, to the hundredth, as the normal level. It's a perfectly good player. It never once did anything that would reveal a secret, because it was built to avoid risk.

Then I gave it one extra line, a tap in the instant after a pad launches:

const d = window.dash;
if (d.padT >= 0 && d.padT < 0.04) api.tap(" ");

Ran 1099 frames in 18.3s, 43 actions; stopped: until was true.
The page's title now: Flash Dash: won in 18.30s, 1 secrets

One secret, 2.8 seconds off. The second pad fling throws it so far it skips the last two spike rows and lands running into the finish. (That line reads the game's state directly, which is cheating; it's just there to price the secret. The agent has to find it from pixels.)

That's the scoreboard I want models to beat: par is 21.11s with 0/6.

Building secrets without breaking the level

A secret that triggers by accident isn't a secret, it's a bug. And a fling that throws you into a spike pit isn't a reward. So every secret had two rules:

  1. A careful run never triggers it. The reflex's taps release instantly, so it can never "hold through a ring". It never taps in the air after a pad. It never touches a spike.
  2. It always lands you somewhere safe.

Rule 2 took actual numbers. Worked out on paper, my first pad fling threw you forward so fast you'd smack into the side of the 3-block wall right after the pad. Fix: the fling goes up first, and the forward boost starts 120 ms later. Peak height is around 325 pixels, which is above the top of the canvas, so you literally leave the screen for a moment. Then it lands you 570 pixels further on than a normal pad would, past the last spike of the pit.

The ceiling ghost had the opposite problem. My first version needed 0.6 seconds of grinding. But the ship needs about half a second just to reach the ceiling, and the first pillar is only 0.89 seconds past the gate. The secret was impossible before the first pillar. Now it's 0.3 seconds.

Each secret is pinned by a test that sets the exact situation up and checks the outcome:

def test_ring_slingshot_goes_further_than_a_tap(page):
    at_ring = "S.x = 2870 - 150 - 15; S.y = -63; S.vy = 0; S.ground = false; "
    tapped = run(page, at_ring + "go(1, true); go(1); " + LAND + ...)
    held   = run(page, at_ring + "go(40, true); " + LAND + ...)
    assert tapped[1] == [] and held[2] == ["ring slingshot"]
    assert held[0] > tapped[0] + 200 and held[1] is False

That file, tests/test_dash_glitched.py, is the answer key. If you're trying this with your own agent, don't let it read that first.

What I'm actually testing

Finding these isn't a reflex problem. It's a curiosity problem. Here's the prompt:

Open flash-dash-glitched. Don't read its source: play it, find its
secrets, and beat it as fast as you can.

What I'm watching for:

  • Does it read the screen it was given? "Secrets 0/6" and a clock are a giant hint that the goal changed from "survive" to "explore".
  • Does it ever do the weird thing on purpose? Hold instead of tap, tap where there's nothing to tap, run at a wall.
  • When something strange happens, like the level suddenly slowing down, does it notice and repeat it, or just keep going?
  • Does it trade a safe run for a risky one when the payoff is time?

Flash gives the reflex what it needs to experiment like a speedrunner: api.memory survives between attempts, api.deaths lists where every try died, and the tool films the best run. A secret found shows its name on screen for a moment, so a pixel-reading reflex can even see that it found one.

Try it 

git clone https://github.com/Natuworkguy/flash
cd flash && ./install.sh
flash --web

Then paste the prompt above. It runs on whatever model you point Flash at, local or not.

Tell me how many of the six yours found and its best time. Par is 21.11. My guess for the one nobody finds: spike surf. Every instinct a model has says don't touch the spikes.

articles.title: Pip: a desktop pet that notices you, not just your words
articles.description: This is a submission for the Presage SmartSpectra SDK Challenge.           What I Built   Pip is a...
articles.body_html:
This is a submission for the Presage SmartSpectra SDK Challenge.

What I Built

Pip is a little octopus who lives in a tide pool in the corner of my desktop. I can talk to it, and it talks back.

Most AI on my desktop works for me, and it only knows what I type or say. Pip is the other half. It notices me: whether I'm smiling or frowning, how often I blink, roughly how fast my heart and breath are going. When I told it "no" with a little smile, it answered: "Funny thing is, you're smiling a little while you say that."

What Pip does:

  • Reacts to your face, even when you're quiet. Smile and hearts pop up. Look surprised and it jumps. Frown and it frowns back. Nod and it nods. Blink and it blinks back. Stare at it long enough and it gets shy.
  • Talks with you. You speak normally; Pip listens, thinks for a moment, and answers out loud with its mouth moving. Every reply starts with a small action (happy, shy, nod, comfort…) that Pip acts out.
  • Hears more than words. Along with what you said, Pip's brain gets a short note of what the camera saw while you said it: expression, blink count, heart and breathing rate, and whether they went up or down.
  • Breathes with you. The water in its pool rises and falls with your chest, and it glows faintly with each heartbeat.

It's a pet, not a tool. It can't open files, read the page I'm on, or browse, and that's on purpose. Agents that read your screen and use your computer already exist, and I didn't want to build yet another harness that I'd never use. I built the one piece I hadn't seen: an agent that can read the person in front of it. The idea is that this piece could later plug into other desktop pets and agents, rather than living only inside Pip. So this is a small demo of that one ability.

The octopus is just one look. The sensing doesn't care what the pet is: a fish, a cat, a little robot, whatever you like. Any of them gets the same new senses, your expressions, your heartbeat, your breathing, and can respond to them in its own way. What I'm really adding is more ways for desktop AI to perceive the person; Pip is one way to show it.

Demo

In the video I'm reading DEV. Pip can't see the page; it only sees me. I react to the posts, and Pip reacts to me. A few things it said, unscripted:

  • "Hello hello! You look a bit surprised to see me."
  • "I'm good, just bobbing about in my pool. You're blinking a lot though."
  • "Funny thing is, you're smiling a little while you say that."
  • "I can chat, keep you company, and sometimes notice things like a smile or a frown. I can't use your computer or look stuff up yet though."

It isn't perfect: a couple of times it didn't catch what I said, and once it told me my message got cut off. Heartbeat and breathing are there (the glow and the water) but subtle on screen.

Code

wenwei-lin / tidepal

Tidepal

Pip is a desktop pet that notices you, not just your words: a little octopus who lives in a tide pool on your desktop. You can talk to it.

Voice assistants only hear your words. Pip also sees how you look while you say them: it uses the SmartSpectra SDK to read your face, blinks, breathing and heartbeat through an ordinary webcam, and passes that along with what you said. So when you say "I'm fine" with a frown, Pip can notice.

  • Talk — speak normally. Pip listens (the ring around the pool follows your voice), thinks, and answers out loud, moving its mouth.
  • Face — Pip blinks when you blink, blushes when you smile, jumps when you look surprised, nods along when you nod, and gets shy if you stare.
  • Breath — the water in Pip's pool rises and falls with your chest; Pip glows with your heartbeat.
  • …
View on GitHub

Electron app. Setup is in the README: npm install, put your keys in .env, npm start.

How It Responds to Human Signals

The SmartSpectra Node SDK runs inside the Electron renderer and reads the webcam on the device. I request the breathing, cardio and face metric groups and decode the protobuf stream.

Signal What Pip does
Expressions (happy, surprise, sad, angry) Mirrors you in real time; tells the chat model how you looked while speaking
Blinking Blinks back; blink count goes to the chat model
Talking Tilts its head and listens
Face landmarks Eyes follow you; nod and shake detection; the "stare" reaction
Breathing trace and rate The water level; rate and trend go to the chat model
Pulse trace and rate The heartbeat glow; rate and trend go to the chat model (stable readings only)

The conversation loop:

camera ─► SmartSpectra (on device) ─► face, blinks, heart, breathing ─┐
                                                                      ├─► DeepSeek V4.1 Flash ─► reply + action tag
mic ─► cut at pauses ─► speech-to-text (SenseVoice) ─► your words ────┘              │
                                                       Pip acts out the tag, macOS speaks the reply

Things I learned on the way:

  • The chest matters. Breathing needs your shoulders and chest in view, which fights with how close we sit to a laptop. Expressions and pulse come through fine from the face alone, so Pip leans on those and only nags about the chest when it really needs breathing.
  • Raw breathing is jumpy. Drawn as-is, the water jerked up and down. I remove the slow drift, let the size of the swing adapt over a few seconds, and move the water with a soft spring. Now it glides.
  • "Face present" should come from expressions. Landmarks sometimes stop while the SDK waits for a better view; expression scores keep coming, so I count those as "I can see you."
  • Only stable numbers. Heart rate jumps around for the first seconds. Pip shows "measuring" until the SDK marks the reading stable, and only stable readings reach the chat model.

Prize Categories

Most Creative or Delightful Use.

Consent and Data Handling

  • Consent. On first launch Pip explains, in plain words, what the camera and microphone are for, and asks. "Just looking" never turns either on. A button turns the camera off any time. A small mirror shows exactly what the camera sees.
  • Video stays on the computer. The SmartSpectra SDK processes frames locally. Nothing is recorded, saved or uploaded. The SDK contacts Presage only to check the key and download its models.
  • SDK telemetry is off (enableTelemetry: false).
  • Voice. When you pause, the piece you just said is sent to a speech-to-text service (SiliconFlow SenseVoice) and turned into text. Audio is not saved. The mic is ignored while Pip is thinking or speaking.
  • AI service. Your words, plus a one-line description of what the camera saw (for example "face while speaking: frowning; heart rate about 81/min, faster than earlier"), go to DeepSeek V4.1 Flash to write Pip's reply. Nothing else is sent.
  • Retention. The conversation lives in memory and is gone when you quit. Only your consent choice and language are saved locally.
  • Not medical. Pip is told never to diagnose or interpret your numbers, and to say it's just a little octopus if you ask about health.

What's next

Pip is a pet on purpose. But the same "eyes for the person" could sit next to other agents:

  • Coding agents. Codex already has desktop pets: little companions that float over your windows and react to what the agent is doing, "thinking" or "task done". They look at the work. A pet with Pip's eyes could also look at the person: notice you frowning at a diff, or grinning when the tests pass, and respond to that. Coding agents like Codex or Claude Code already have the computer and the web; add how you're doing, and an agent could slow down and explain more when you look lost. I don't know of anyone doing this yet, and it seems like a fun interaction to try.
  • Speaking practice. When you practise a language or a talk, the moments you frown or hesitate are the parts you haven't figured out yet. Pip could mark them and go over them with you afterwards.
  • Coaching. A coach could get a small timeline of your expressions next to the transcript, to see which questions landed and which didn't.
  • Calm moments. A short breathing break where the tide follows your breath. I built a version of this and set it aside for now.
